title: Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoint (Java)
remediation: Use Resilience4j @RateLimiter or Bucket4j for Spring Boot. Add account lockout logic.

title: Client-Controlled Price in Payment Processing
description: Detects payment processing where price/amount comes directly from user input (request body, query params) without server-side validation against the product catalog or cart.
remediation:
Never trust client-provided prices. Always look up the price server-side:
  product = Product.objects.get(id=request.data['product_id'])
  amount = product.price * validated_quantity
Validate against the product catalog before charging.

title: Client-Controlled Price in Payment Processing (JavaScript)
Negative Quantity or Negative Price Not Validated
remediation:
Always validate quantity > 0 and amount > 0:
  quantity = int(request.data['quantity'])
  if quantity <= 0 or quantity > MAX_QTY:
      raise ValidationError("Invalid quantity")

title: Missing Workflow State Validation (Step Skipping)
description: Detects multi-step processes (checkout, onboarding, verification) where the current step does not validate that previous steps were completed, enabling step-skipping attacks.
remediation:
Enforce workflow state machine:
  if order.status != OrderStatus.PAYMENT_CONFIRMED:
      raise PermissionDenied("Previous step not completed")
Use a state machine library (django-fsm, transitions).

title: Missing Workflow State Validation (JavaScript)
Coupon/Discount Code Applied Multiple Times
remediation:
Track coupon redemptions:
  if coupon.is_used or coupon.usage_count >= coupon.max_uses:
      raise ValidationError("Coupon already used")
  coupon.usage_count += 1
Use database constraints for atomicity.

title: Hardcoded Credentials in C# Source
description: Detects hardcoded API keys, passwords, tokens, and connection strings in C# source code including const declarations, string assignments, and inline authentication values used in HttpClient and service configurations.
impact: Hardcoded credentials in C# assemblies can be extracted through IL decompilation (ILSpy, dnSpy). This provides direct access to databases, APIs, and authenticated endpoints.
remediation: Use ASP.NET Core Configuration with User Secrets for development, Azure Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager for production. Never commit credentials to appsettings.json in source control.

title: JWT Validation Skip in ASP.NET
description: Detects insecure JWT handling in ASP.NET Core including disabled signature validation, missing issuer/audience checks, weak signing keys, and algorithm confusion vulnerabilities.
impact: Disabled JWT validation allows attackers to forge authentication tokens, impersonate any user, escalate privileges, and access protected API endpoints.
remediation: Enable all JWT validation parameters. Use strong signing keys (256+ bits). Validate issuer, audience, and lifetime. Use asymmetric keys (RSA/ECDSA) for production.

title: Weak Password Hashing in C#
description: Detects use of weak hashing algorithms (MD5, SHA1, SHA256 without salting) for password storage instead of proper password hashing functions like BCrypt, Argon2, or ASP.NET Identity's PasswordHasher.
impact: Weak password hashing enables offline brute-force and rainbow table attacks. MD5/SHA1 passwords can be cracked in seconds with modern hardware.
remediation: Use ASP.NET Identity PasswordHasher (PBKDF2) or BCrypt.Net: var hasher = new PasswordHasher<User>(); var hash = hasher.HashPassword(user, password); var result = hasher.VerifyHashedPassword(user, hash, input);

title: Missing Authentication on Controller/Action
description: Detects ASP.NET Core controllers or actions that handle sensitive operations without [Authorize] attribute while other controllers in the same project use authentication.
impact: Missing authentication allows unauthenticated users to perform sensitive operations including data modification, deletion, and privilege escalation.
remediation: Apply [Authorize] globally in Program.cs and use [AllowAnonymous] only for login/register. Use policy-based authorization for sensitive actions: [Authorize(Policy = "AdminOnly")]

title: Insecure Cookie Configuration in ASP.NET
description: Detects insecure cookie settings in ASP.NET Core including missing Secure flag, HttpOnly flag, SameSite attribute, and weak authentication cookie configuration.
impact: Insecure cookies can be stolen via XSS (no HttpOnly), intercepted via MITM (no Secure), or used in CSRF attacks (no SameSite).
remediation: Configure cookies with Secure=true, HttpOnly=true, SameSite=Strict: options.Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always; options.Cookie.HttpOnly = true; options.Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.Strict;

title: CSRF Protection Bypass in ASP.NET
description: Detects disabled or misconfigured CSRF protection including missing [ValidateAntiForgeryToken], disabled anti-forgery filters, and misconfigured CORS with credentials.
impact: CSRF enables attackers to perform actions on behalf of authenticated users including password changes, fund transfers, and data modification.
remediation:
Use [AutoValidateAntiforgeryToken] globally. Configure strict CORS: builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(); builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews(o =>
    o.Filters.Add(new AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute()));

title: Broken Access Control in ASP.NET MVC
description: Detects Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) and broken access control patterns where user-supplied IDs access resources without ownership verification in ASP.NET Core controllers.
impact: IDOR allows accessing, modifying, or deleting other users' data by manipulating resource IDs in requests.
remediation:
Always filter queries by the authenticated user's context: var userId = User.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value; var item = await _context.Items.FirstOrDefaultAsync(
    i => i.Id == id && i.UserId == userId);

title: Weak Session Management in ASP.NET
description: Detects weak session configuration including in-memory session storage in production, missing session timeout, predictable session IDs, and session fixation vulnerabilities.
impact: Weak session management enables session hijacking, fixation attacks, and data loss when in-memory cache resets.
remediation: Use distributed cache (Redis, SQL Server) for production sessions. Set reasonable timeouts. Regenerate session ID after login.

title: OAuth/OIDC Misconfiguration in ASP.NET Core
description: Detects insecure OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect configurations including disabled HTTPS, missing state/nonce validation, weak redirect URI validation, and insecure token storage.
impact: OAuth/OIDC misconfiguration enables token theft via MITM, CSRF via missing state parameter, and impersonation through redirect URI manipulation.
remediation: Always enable RequireHttpsMetadata=true in production. Validate state and nonce parameters. Use Configuration for client credentials.

title: ASP.NET Identity Misconfiguration
description: Detects weak ASP.NET Core Identity configuration including disabled password requirements, disabled lockout, weak password policies, and insecure token provider settings.
impact: Weak identity configuration allows users to set trivially guessable passwords and enables credential stuffing without lockout protection.
remediation: Configure strong password policies and lockout: options.Password.RequiredLength = 12; options.Password.RequireDigit = true; options.Lockout.MaxFailedAccessAttempts = 5; options.Lockout.DefaultLockoutTimeSpan = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15);

title: JWT Algorithm None Attack / Signature Bypass
description: Detects JWT implementations vulnerable to the "alg:none" attack where the algorithm is taken from the token header without validation, allowing attackers to forge tokens without a valid signature.
remediation: Always specify allowed algorithms explicitly: jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=['RS256']). Never accept the algorithm from the token header. Always verify signatures — never set verify=False. Use asymmetric algorithms (RS256, ES256) for public-facing APIs.

title: JWT Algorithm Confusion (RS256 → HS256)
description: Detects JWT configurations vulnerable to algorithm confusion where the public key (RS256) can be used as an HMAC secret (HS256), allowing attackers to forge tokens using the publicly available key.
remediation: Accept only ONE algorithm family. Never mix HMAC and RSA algorithms. Use algorithms=['RS256'] (asymmetric) or algorithms=['HS256'] (symmetric).

title: JWT Secret/Key Weakness
description: Detects JWT signing with weak, hardcoded, or default secrets.
remediation: Use environment variables or secret managers for JWT secrets. Secret must be >=256 bits (32+ chars) for HS256. Prefer RS256/ES256 with properly managed key pairs.

title: OAuth Open Redirect / Authorization Code Interception
description: Detects OAuth implementations vulnerable to redirect_uri manipulation, allowing attackers to intercept authorization codes or tokens.
remediation: Always validate redirect_uri against a strict allowlist of pre-registered URIs. Use exact string matching — never pattern/wildcard matching. Store allowed redirect URIs in OAuth client configuration.

title: OAuth State Parameter Missing (CSRF)
remediation: Always include a cryptographically random state parameter in OAuth requests. Validate the state parameter in the callback to prevent CSRF.

title: SAML Signature Validation Bypass
description: Detects SAML implementations that skip or improperly validate XML signatures on SAML assertions, enabling authentication bypass.
remediation: Always enable SAML signature validation: wantAssertionsSigned=true. Use strict mode in SAML libraries. Verify both the SAML Response and the Assertion signatures. Validate the SAML Assertion's audience restriction.

title: Session Fixation — No Regeneration After Login
description: Detects authentication flows that don't regenerate the session ID after successful login, enabling session fixation attacks.
remediation: Regenerate the session ID immediately after authentication: Python/Django: request.session.cycle_key() Python/Flask: session.regenerate() Java: request.changeSessionId() Node/Express: req.session.regenerate(callback) PHP: session_regenerate_id(true)

title: Session Cookie Security Flags Missing
remediation: Set all session cookies with: Secure=true, HttpOnly=true, SameSite=Strict or Lax.

title: Insecure Direct Object Reference — Missing Ownership Check
description: Detects API endpoints that access resources by user-supplied ID without verifying the current user's ownership/authorization to that resource.
remediation: Always include an ownership check in queries: Django: MyModel.objects.filter(pk=id, user=request.user) Express: Model.find({_id: id, userId: req.user.id}) Use object-level permission checks (DRF: check_object_permissions).

title: Mass Assignment / Over-Posting Leading to Privilege Escalation
remediation: Use allowlists for assignable fields. Django: use serializer with explicit fields. Rails: use strong_parameters with permit(). Node: pick only allowed fields from req.body.

title: Race Condition in Financial / State-Changing Operation
description: Detects state-changing operations (balance updates, inventory changes, vote counting) without proper locking or atomic operations, enabling race condition exploitation for double-spending or duplicate actions.
remediation: Use database-level atomic operations: Django: MyModel.objects.filter(pk=id).update(balance=F('balance') - amount)  SQL: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ? MongoDB: {$inc: {balance: -amount}} Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for check-then-modify patterns. Wrap in transaction with proper isolation level.

title: TOCTOU File Operation
description: Detects time-of-check-to-time-of-use vulnerabilities where a file's existence/permissions are checked separately from the file operation.
remediation: Use EAFP (Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission): try/except instead of check-then-act. Use os.open() with O_CREAT | O_EXCL for atomic file creation. Use tempfile.mkstemp() for secure temporary files.

title: Hardcoded API Keys in Go Source
description: Detects hardcoded API keys, tokens, and secrets in Go source code including constant declarations, variable assignments, and inline authentication values used in HTTP clients and service configurations.
impact: Hardcoded API keys in Go binaries can be extracted through reverse engineering or source code access. This provides direct access to external APIs, cloud services, and authenticated endpoints.
remediation: Use os.Getenv() for environment variables, Viper for configuration files, or a secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault. Never commit credentials to source control.

title: JWT Validation Skip in Go
description: Detects insecure JWT handling in Go applications including skipped signature verification, missing claims validation, acceptance of none algorithm, and improper use of jwt-go or golang-jwt libraries.
impact: Attackers can forge JWT tokens with arbitrary claims, bypass authentication, and impersonate any user including administrators when verification is skipped.
remediation: Always verify JWT signatures using jwt.Parse with a proper KeyFunc that validates the algorithm. Check token.Valid before accessing claims. Pin algorithms to RS256 or ES256.

title: Missing Authentication Middleware in Go
description: Detects HTTP routes in Go web frameworks (Gin, Echo, Chi, net/http) that handle sensitive operations without authentication middleware, leaving endpoints accessible to unauthenticated users.
impact: Missing authentication middleware allows unauthenticated users to access admin panels, modify user data, and perform privileged operations without any credentials.
remediation: Apply authentication middleware to all sensitive routes. Use route groups with auth middleware in Gin/Echo/Chi. Implement middleware chains that verify authentication before handler execution.

title: BCrypt Cost Factor Too Low in Go
description: Detects bcrypt password hashing in Go with a cost factor below the recommended minimum of 10, making brute-force attacks significantly faster after a database breach.
impact: Low bcrypt cost factor significantly reduces brute-force time. With MinCost (4), cracking is approximately 64x faster than with DefaultCost (10).
remediation: Use bcrypt.DefaultCost (10) or higher. Consider cost factor 12-14 for production. For stronger protection, use argon2.IDKey with recommended parameters.

title: Insecure Session Cookie Flags in Go
description: Detects session cookies in Go applications set without Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite flags, exposing session tokens to interception, XSS theft, or CSRF attacks.
impact: Insecure session cookies can be stolen via XSS (missing HttpOnly), intercepted over HTTP (missing Secure), or used in CSRF attacks (missing SameSite).
remediation: Set Secure: true, HttpOnly: true, and SameSite: http.SameSiteStrictMode on all session cookies. Use __Host- prefix for additional protection.

title: CORS Wildcard with Credentials in Go
description: Detects CORS configurations in Go applications that allow wildcard origins with credentials, or reflect arbitrary origins with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, enabling cross-origin credential theft.
impact: Wildcard CORS with credentials allows any malicious website to make authenticated requests to the API and read responses, enabling session hijacking and data theft.
remediation: Never use wildcard origins with credentials. Maintain a whitelist of allowed origins. Use AllowOriginFunc with proper validation. Set AllowCredentials to false for public APIs.

title: Password Comparison Timing Attack in Go
description: Detects password or token comparisons in Go using == or bytes.Equal instead of constant-time comparison functions, enabling timing-based side-channel attacks to extract secrets.
impact: Timing attacks allow attackers to extract secrets byte-by-byte by measuring response times. This can reveal API keys, tokens, and password hashes.
remediation: Use subtle.ConstantTimeCompare for all credential comparisons. Use bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword for password verification. Never use == or bytes.Equal for secret comparison.

title: OAuth2 Token Reuse and Replay in Go
description: Detects OAuth2 implementations in Go that fail to properly validate token freshness, allow token reuse across sessions, or do not verify audience and issuer claims, enabling token replay attacks.
impact: Token replay attacks allow attackers to reuse stolen or expired tokens to maintain unauthorized access. Missing audience validation allows tokens from one application to be used in another.
remediation: Always check token.Valid() before use. Use oauth2.ReuseTokenSource for automatic refresh. Validate audience, issuer, and expiry claims on ID tokens. Implement token rotation for refresh tokens.

title: API Key in URL Parameter in Go
description: Detects API keys and authentication tokens passed as URL query parameters in Go applications, exposing credentials in server logs, browser history, referrer headers, and proxy logs.
impact: API keys in URLs are logged by web servers, proxies, CDNs, and stored in browser history. This exposes credentials to log file access, referrer header leaks, and shoulder surfing.
remediation: Pass API keys in HTTP headers (Authorization or X-API-Key). Never include secrets in URL query parameters. Use POST body for sensitive data transmission.

title: Insecure TLS Configuration in Go
description: Detects insecure TLS configurations in Go applications including disabled certificate verification, weak TLS versions, insecure cipher suites, and skipped hostname verification enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.
impact: Disabled TLS verification allows man-in-the-middle attackers to intercept all HTTPS traffic including authentication credentials, API keys, and sensitive data transmitted between services.
remediation: Never set InsecureSkipVerify to true in production. Use MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12 or tls.VersionTLS13. Configure proper CA certificates. Use certificate pinning for critical connections.

title: Spring Security Misconfiguration
description: Detects Spring Security configurations that disable critical protections such as permitAll on sensitive endpoints, disabled authentication, or overly permissive security filter chains.
impact: Misconfigured Spring Security allows unauthenticated users to access admin panels, APIs, and sensitive operations. This bypasses all authentication and authorization controls.
remediation: Configure Spring Security with authenticated() for sensitive endpoints. Only use permitAll() for truly public paths like /login, /register, and /health. Use @PreAuthorize for method-level security.

title: Hardcoded Credentials in Java Source
description: Detects hardcoded passwords, API keys, and credentials in Java source code including connection strings, configuration constants, and inline authentication values.
impact: Hardcoded credentials can be extracted from compiled JAR files, decompiled class files, or source repositories. This provides direct access to databases, APIs, and services.
remediation: Use Spring @Value with externalized properties, environment variables, or a secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault. Use Spring Cloud Config for centralized secret management.

title: Missing @PreAuthorize on Sensitive Methods
description: Detects Spring controller methods handling sensitive operations without @PreAuthorize, @Secured, or @RolesAllowed annotations for method-level security enforcement.
impact: Without method-level security, any authenticated user can access admin functionality, modify other users data, and perform privileged operations.
remediation: Add @PreAuthorize annotations to all sensitive controller methods. Enable method-level security with @EnableMethodSecurity. Use hasRole() or hasAuthority() for role-based access control.

title: JDBC Credential Exposure
description: Detects hardcoded database credentials in JDBC connection strings, DataSource configurations, and Hibernate properties within Java source code.
impact: Exposed JDBC credentials allow direct database access, enabling attackers to read, modify, or delete all data.
remediation: Use Spring Boot externalized configuration with ${DB_PASSWORD}. Store credentials in environment variables, AWS Secrets Manager, or HashiCorp Vault.

title: JWT Verification Bypass in Java
description: Detects insecure JWT handling in Java applications including disabled signature verification, missing algorithm pinning, use of none algorithm, and acceptance of unsigned tokens.
impact: Attackers can forge JWT tokens with arbitrary claims, bypass authentication entirely, and impersonate any user including administrators.
remediation: Always use Jwts.parserBuilder().setSigningKey(key).build() with JJWT. Pin algorithms to RS256 or ES256. Use Spring Security NimbusJwtDecoder for standard JWT validation.

title: Spring CSRF Protection Disabled
description: Detects Spring Security configurations where CSRF protection is explicitly disabled. Critical for session-based applications where CSRF enables attackers to forge state-changing requests.
impact: CSRF disabled on session-based applications lets attackers forge requests that modify data, transfer funds, or change settings on behalf of authenticated users.
remediation: Do not disable CSRF for session-based applications. Use CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse() for SPAs. Only disable CSRF for purely stateless JWT-based APIs.

title: Session Management Weakness
description: Detects insecure session management in Spring applications including missing session fixation protection, excessive timeout, and insecure session cookie settings.
impact: Disabled session fixation protection lets attackers fix a known session ID and hijack authenticated sessions. Missing HttpOnly allows XSS theft.
remediation: Use sessionFixation().migrateSession() or changeSessionId(). Set maximumSessions(1). Enable HttpOnly and Secure flags on session cookies.

title: BCrypt Cost Factor Too Low
description: Detects BCrypt password hashing with a cost factor below the recommended minimum. Low cost factors allow faster brute-force attacks.
impact: Low BCrypt cost factor significantly reduces brute-force time. At cost 4, cracking is approximately 64x faster than cost 10.
remediation: Use BCryptPasswordEncoder with cost factor 12 or higher. Consider Argon2PasswordEncoder for stronger protection.

title: HTTP Basic Authentication Without HTTPS
description: Detects HTTP Basic authentication in Spring Security that may expose base64-encoded credentials over unencrypted connections.
impact: HTTP Basic sends base64-encoded (not encrypted) credentials in every request. Without HTTPS, any network observer can intercept them.
remediation: Always enforce HTTPS with HTTP Basic. Use requiresChannel().anyRequest() .requiresSecure(). Prefer token-based authentication instead.

title: Role-Based Access Control Bypass
description: Detects patterns where Spring Security role-based access control can be bypassed through incorrect role hierarchy, missing role checks, or permissive custom AccessDecisionVoter implementations.
impact: Incorrect RBAC allows regular users to access admin functionality and perform privileged operations. This is vertical privilege escalation.
remediation: Use @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on admin endpoints. Implement proper RoleHierarchy. Ensure custom AccessDecisionVoters deny by default.

title: Hardcoded JWT Secret Key
description: Detects hardcoded secret keys used to sign or verify JSON Web Tokens. Hardcoded secrets in source code can be extracted by anyone with repository access, enabling token forgery, privilege escalation, and full authentication bypass across all users.
impact: An attacker who retrieves the hardcoded secret can forge arbitrary JWT tokens, impersonate any user including administrators, and fully bypass authentication. This leads to complete system compromise.
remediation: Store JWT secrets in environment variables or a secrets management service such as AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or Azure Key Vault. Rotate secrets periodically and use asymmetric key pairs (RS256/ES256) for production systems.

title: JWT Algorithm None Bypass
description: Detects configurations where the JWT library accepts 'none' as a valid signing algorithm. This allows attackers to craft unsigned tokens that the server treats as valid, completely bypassing authentication.
impact: Attackers can create unsigned JWT tokens that the server accepts as valid. This allows complete authentication bypass, impersonation of any user, and unauthorized access to all protected resources.
remediation: Always specify a strict allow-list of algorithms in jwt.verify() options, e.g., algorithms: ['RS256']. Never include 'none' in allowed algorithms. Use asymmetric algorithms (RS256, ES256) in production.

title: Missing Authentication Middleware on Sensitive Routes
description: Detects Express.js or similar framework routes that handle sensitive operations without authentication middleware. Unprotected routes allow unauthenticated users to access restricted functionality.
impact: Unauthenticated users can access sensitive API endpoints, view or modify protected data, perform administrative actions, or access other users' resources without any credentials.
remediation: Add authentication middleware to all sensitive routes. Use app.use() or router.use() to apply authentication globally, then whitelist public endpoints explicitly. Prefer a deny-by-default approach.

title: Broken Access Control - Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
description: Detects patterns where user-supplied identifiers are used directly to access resources without verifying that the authenticated user is authorized to access those specific resources. This enables horizontal privilege escalation.
impact: Attackers can access, modify, or delete resources belonging to other users by manipulating object identifiers. This leads to data breaches, privacy violations, and unauthorized modifications.
remediation: Always verify that the authenticated user is authorized to access the requested resource. Scope database queries to the current user (e.g., where userId = req.user.id). Use UUIDs instead of sequential integer IDs. Implement an authorization layer.

title: Session Fixation Vulnerability
description: Detects session management patterns where session IDs are not regenerated after authentication, allowing attackers to fixate a known session ID and hijack authenticated sessions.
impact: An attacker can fixate a session ID on the victim's browser, wait for the victim to authenticate, and then use the known session ID to access the victim's authenticated session, gaining full access to their account.
remediation: Always call req.session.regenerate() immediately after successful authentication and before storing any user data in the session. Destroy the old session first. Use secure session configuration with httpOnly and secure cookie flags.

title: Insecure Cookie Settings
description: Detects session or authentication cookies configured without essential security flags such as httpOnly, secure, and sameSite. Missing flags expose cookies to theft via XSS, man-in-the-middle attacks, and cross-site request forgery.
impact: Cookies without httpOnly can be stolen via XSS attacks. Cookies without secure flag can be intercepted over unencrypted HTTP connections. Missing SameSite enables CSRF. All can lead to session hijacking and account compromise.
remediation: Set httpOnly: true, secure: true, and sameSite: 'strict' (or 'lax') for all session and authentication cookies. Use __Host- or __Secure- cookie prefixes where possible. Review all res.cookie() calls for proper flags.

title: Password Stored in localStorage
description: Detects patterns where passwords or authentication credentials are stored in the browser's localStorage or sessionStorage. These storage mechanisms are accessible to any JavaScript running on the page, making credentials vulnerable to XSS-based theft.
impact: Any XSS vulnerability on the site allows attackers to read passwords from localStorage. Passwords in browser storage persist across sessions and can be accessed by browser extensions, shared computer users, or malware.
remediation: Never store passwords or raw credentials in localStorage or sessionStorage. Use secure httpOnly cookies for session management. If a token must be stored client-side, use short-lived tokens and store them in memory only.

title: OAuth State Parameter Missing
description: Detects OAuth 2.0 authorization flows that do not generate or validate the state parameter. The missing state parameter makes the application vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery attacks against the OAuth callback.
impact: Without a state parameter, an attacker can initiate an OAuth flow and trick a victim into completing it, linking the attacker's account to the victim's session. This enables account takeover or unauthorized access.
remediation: Always generate a cryptographically random state parameter and store it in the server-side session before initiating the OAuth flow. Validate the state parameter in the callback handler. Use PKCE for public clients.

title: CORS Misconfiguration with Credentials
description: Detects CORS configurations that allow credentials (cookies, HTTP authentication) with overly permissive origins, including wildcard or dynamically reflected origins. This allows malicious third-party sites to make authenticated requests on behalf of users.
impact: A malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin requests to the vulnerable API, reading sensitive data or performing actions as the victim user. This enables data theft, account manipulation, and further attacks.
remediation: Never use wildcard origin with credentials. Maintain a strict whitelist of allowed origins and validate against it. Use exact string matching for origin validation. Avoid reflecting the request Origin header directly.

title: Rate Limiting Bypass on Authentication Endpoints
description: Detects authentication endpoints (login, registration, password reset) that lack rate limiting middleware. Without rate limiting, attackers can perform brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and enumeration at scale.
impact: Without rate limiting, attackers can perform brute-force password attacks, credential stuffing with leaked credential databases, and user enumeration. This can lead to mass account compromise.
remediation: Apply rate limiting middleware to all authentication endpoints using express-rate-limit or rate-limiter-flexible. Implement progressive delays and account lockout. Add CAPTCHA after multiple failed attempts. Use both IP-based and account-based limiting.

title: Flask Route ID Parameter Used Directly in Database Query
description: Detects Flask route handlers that accept an ID path parameter (<int:id>, <int:doc_id>, <uuid:user_id>) and pass it directly to a database query (Model.query.get(id), filter_by(id=id)) without any authorization or ownership check. This is the canonical IDOR pattern in Flask applications.
impact: Horizontal privilege escalation. Attacker manipulates the ID parameter (incrementing integers, enumerating UUIDs) to access objects belonging to other users or tenants: documents, invoices, profiles, API keys, and financial records. Sequential integer IDs are trivially enumerable.

title: Object Retrieved by ID Without Ownership or Tenant Verification
description: Detects patterns where an object fetched by user-supplied ID is used (serialized, modified, deleted) without an intervening ownership or tenant validation check. This Layer 2 rule has lower confidence than LOGIC-IDOR-001 because the authorization check may exist in a decorator or middleware not visible in the immediate code context. Confidence is boosted when corroborated by LOGIC-MT-001/002 in the same file.
impact: Unauthorized access to arbitrary objects via ID manipulation. Depending on the endpoint type: data disclosure (GET), data modification (PUT/PATCH), or data destruction (DELETE). In multi-tenant context, enables cross-tenant operations.

title: Nested Resource Access Without Parent Object Validation
description: Detects access to nested/child resources using both parent and child IDs where the parent-child relationship is not validated. Example: /tenants/<tid>/items/<item_id> where item_id is fetched without verifying it belongs to the tenant identified by tid. The URL implies hierarchical scoping but the implementation may not enforce it.
impact: Cross-tenant or cross-user resource access through hierarchical URL manipulation. The nested URL structure suggests access is scoped (e.g., /tenants/1/items/5) but the implementation fetches the child resource without verifying it belongs to the specified parent.

title: Bulk Fetch by User-Supplied IDs Without Ownership Validation
description: Detects endpoints that accept an array of IDs from the request body or parameters and fetch all matching objects without filtering by tenant or user ownership. Batch/bulk endpoints amplify IDOR impact because a single request can exfiltrate multiple objects.
impact: Amplified IDOR — single request exfiltrates multiple objects across tenants. Attacker submits array of sequential or guessed IDs to extract bulk data. Impact multiplied by batch size. Can be used for mass enumeration or targeted extraction of specific high-value records.

title: File or Document Access by ID Without Authorization
description: Detects file access endpoints where a document/file ID is used to retrieve or serve a file without ownership validation. File endpoints are particularly sensitive because they may contain PII, financial reports, contracts, or internal documents. Low-entropy sequential IDs make enumeration trivial.
impact: Direct exfiltration of files and documents belonging to other users or tenants. Common targets: financial reports, contracts, tax documents, medical records, government IDs, internal memos. Single-file access can be automated to enumerate and download entire document repositories.

title: Object Mutation (Update/Delete) via IDOR Without Ownership Check
description: Detects update or delete operations on objects fetched by user-supplied ID without ownership or tenant verification. Mutation endpoints (PUT, PATCH, DELETE) have higher impact than read-only IDOR because they enable data destruction and integrity compromise, not just disclosure. This is a chain-capable rule — severity escalates when corroborated by LOGIC-MT-004 (bulk operations without tenant scope).
impact: Data integrity compromise and data destruction across tenants. Attacker can modify arbitrary records (changing financial data, escalating permissions, altering audit logs) or delete them entirely. In multi-tenant SaaS, this enables cross-tenant data manipulation.
remediation:
Always validate ownership before mutation:
@app.delete('/items/<int:item_id>') @login_required def delete_item(item_id):
    # WRONG:
    item = Item.query.get_or_404(item_id)
    db.session.delete(item)
    db.session.commit()

    # RIGHT:
    item = Item.query.filter_by(
        id=item_id,
        tenant_id=g.tenant_id
    ).first_or_404()
    db.session.delete(item)
    db.session.commit()

title: Unscoped ORM Query — All Records Without Tenant Filter
description: Detects ORM queries that retrieve all records without any filtering (.query.all(), .objects.all(), session.query(Model).all()). In multi-tenant applications, unscoped queries return data across ALL tenants, enabling cross-tenant data leakage. Each query must include an explicit tenant_id/org_id filter.
impact: Cross-tenant data exposure. Every record in the table is returned regardless of tenant ownership. In multi-tenant SaaS, this means Tenant A's users see Tenant B's data: customers, invoices, documents, audit logs, and PII. Severity scales with the sensitivity of the model being queried.

title: ORM Filter by Non-Tenant Fields — Missing Tenant Scope in Query
description: Detects ORM filter/filter_by calls that filter by non-tenant fields (id, status, email, name, etc.) without including a tenant_id or org_id parameter. In multi-tenant context, filtering by only non-tenant fields returns records from all tenants matching the criteria. This rule uses line-level anti-patterns from the intelligence layer for per-finding suppression when tenant_id appears nearby.
impact: Cross-tenant data leakage through unscoped filters. Filtering by non-unique fields like status or email without tenant scope returns records from all tenants. Attacker can enumerate and access other tenants' records by manipulating filter parameters.
remediation:
Always include tenant scope in filter queries:
# WRONG: users = User.query.filter_by(status='active').all()
# RIGHT: users = User.query.filter_by(
    tenant_id=g.tenant_id,
    status='active'
).all()

title: Direct ID Fetch Without Tenant Validation — Cross-Tenant Access
description: Detects direct database lookups using an ID parameter (Model.query.get(), get_or_404(), session.get()) without subsequent tenant ownership validation. In multi-tenant applications, retrieving an object by its primary key without verifying it belongs to the current tenant enables IDOR-style cross-tenant access. This is detection_layer 2: confidence is boosted when corroborated by LOGIC-MT-001 or LOGIC-MT-002 in the same file.
impact: Direct cross-tenant object access. Attacker changes the ID parameter (incrementing integer IDs, guessing UUIDs) to access objects belonging to other tenants: documents, invoices, user profiles, API keys. This is the most common multi-tenant vulnerability pattern.
remediation:
Always validate tenant ownership after fetching by ID:
# WRONG: doc = Document.query.get_or_404(doc_id) return jsonify(doc.to_dict())
# RIGHT: doc = Document.query.get_or_404(doc_id) if doc.tenant_id != g.tenant_id:
    abort(404)  # Return 404, not 403, to prevent enumeration
return jsonify(doc.to_dict())
# BEST: scope the query itself doc = Document.query.filter_by(
    id=doc_id, tenant_id=g.tenant_id
).first_or_404()

title: Bulk Operation Without Tenant Scope — Cross-Tenant Modification
description: Detects bulk delete or update operations on ORM querysets that lack a visible tenant filter. Unscoped bulk operations can modify or destroy data across ALL tenants in a single request. This is detection_layer 2 because bulk operations in system jobs (migrations, cleanup tasks) are intentionally unscoped — file-level context determines risk.
impact: Mass data destruction or modification across all tenants. A single unscoped bulk delete could erase every record in a table. Unscoped bulk updates could modify financial data, permissions, or status fields for all tenants simultaneously.
remediation:
Always include tenant_id in bulk operation filters:
# WRONG: Order.query.filter_by(status='cancelled').delete()
# RIGHT: Order.query.filter_by(
    tenant_id=g.tenant_id,
    status='cancelled'
).delete()
Additionally, add a pre-delete/pre-update hook that validates tenant scope is present in the query's WHERE clause.

title: Loop-Nested Secondary Query Without Tenant Filter
description: Detects a secondary database query executed inside a loop body (for item in results: sub = SubModel.query.filter_by(parent_id=...)) where the inner query lacks tenant scoping. Even if the outer query is tenant-scoped, the inner query may leak cross-tenant related records. This is a Layer 2 contextual rule requiring loop context.
impact: Cross-tenant data leakage through related object queries. Even when the primary query is correctly scoped, nested queries that fetch child or related records by parent_id (without tenant_id) can return records belonging to other tenants with matching foreign keys.
remediation:
Scope all nested queries to the current tenant:
# WRONG: for order in tenant_orders:
    items = OrderItem.query.filter_by(order_id=order.id).all()

# RIGHT: for order in tenant_orders:
    items = OrderItem.query.filter_by(
        order_id=order.id,
        tenant_id=g.tenant_id  # Redundant but defensive
    ).all()

Preferred: use eager loading with scoped relationships: orders = Order.query.filter_by(tenant_id=g.tenant_id).options(
    joinedload(Order.items)
).all()

title: List Comprehension with Unscoped Database Call
description: Detects list comprehensions or generator expressions that embed a database query call without tenant scoping. Patterns like [get_data(item.id) for item in request.json['ids']] are common in batch API endpoints and frequently omit tenant validation.
impact: Batch cross-tenant data access. Attacker supplies arbitrary IDs in a batch API request body to fetch objects from other tenants. List comprehension patterns bypass per-item tenant validation.
remediation:
Validate tenant ownership for batch fetches:
# WRONG: items = [Item.query.get(id) for id in request.json['ids']]
# RIGHT: items = Item.query.filter(
    Item.id.in_(request.json['ids']),
    Item.tenant_id == g.tenant_id
).all()

title: Export Endpoint Without Tenant Scoping — Bulk Data Exfiltration
description: Detects export, download, or bulk data retrieval endpoints that query data without explicit tenant filtering. Export endpoints are high-value targets because they return large datasets — a single missing tenant filter can expose the entire table across all tenants. This is detection_layer 2 — the export context amplifies the severity of any co-occurring LOGIC-MT-001/002 findings.
impact: Mass data exfiltration across all tenants via a single export request. Attacker downloads CSV/Excel/JSON containing every record in the table: customer data, financial records, PII, API keys, internal documents. Impact scales linearly with number of tenants and records.
remediation:
Always scope export queries to the current tenant:
@app.get('/export/users') @login_required def export_users():
    # WRONG: users = User.query.all()
    # RIGHT:
    users = User.query.filter_by(tenant_id=g.tenant_id).all()
    # ... generate CSV from scoped results

For async exports, pass tenant_id explicitly to the background job: export_task.delay(tenant_id=g.tenant_id, format='csv')

title: Raw SQL Without Tenant-Scoped WHERE Clause
description: Detects raw SQL execution (db.session.execute, cursor.execute, db.engine.execute, connection.execute) with SELECT/DELETE/UPDATE statements that lack a tenant_id or org_id parameter. Raw SQL bypasses ORM-level scoping abstractions and is frequently written without tenant awareness.
impact: Raw SQL queries bypass all ORM-level tenant isolation. Missing tenant_id in WHERE clause returns or modifies data across all tenants. Combined with SQL injection risk from string interpolation.
remediation:
Include tenant_id in all raw SQL queries:
# WRONG: db.session.execute(text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE status = :status"),
                   {"status": "active"})

# RIGHT: db.session.execute(text(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE tenant_id = :tid AND status = :status"
), {"tid": g.tenant_id, "status": "active"})
Prefer ORM queries with automatic tenant scoping over raw SQL.

title: Direct HTTP Header Privilege Trust — Forgeable Authorization Source
description: Detects code that reads privilege-related HTTP headers (X-Is-Admin, X-Role, X-Permissions, X-Auth-Level, etc.) using request.headers.get(), request.headers[], request.META.get(), or WSGI environ. HTTP headers are fully client-controlled and trivially forgeable. Any value read from a privilege-named header MUST be treated as untrusted user input.
impact: Complete privilege escalation. Any unauthenticated attacker can add a forged header (e.g., X-Is-Admin: true) via curl, Burp Suite, or browser DevTools to bypass all authorization checks. This grants full admin access to multi-tenant data, user management, audit logs, and potentially destructive operations like bulk deletion or export.
remediation:
Never derive authorization from HTTP headers. Use server-side sessions, JWT tokens with cryptographic signature verification, or database-backed role lookups. Example fix:
# WRONG: g.is_admin = request.headers.get('X-Is-Admin') == 'true' # RIGHT: g.is_admin = current_user.has_role('admin')  # DB-backed
If reverse-proxy headers are required (e.g., X-Forwarded-For), validate them against a trusted proxy allowlist and never use them for privilege determination.

title: Privilege Flag Assignment from HTTP Header — Forgeable Escalation
description: Detects assignment of an HTTP header value to a privilege-related variable or attribute (g.is_admin, is_superuser, user_role, etc.). This pattern is more dangerous than mere header reading because it establishes a trusted privilege flag from an untrusted source.
impact: Establishes a server-side privilege flag from a forgeable source. All downstream authorization decisions that check this flag are compromised. Attacker sends X-Is-Admin: true header and gains full admin access to the application, including tenant management, user deletion, billing modification, and audit log access.
remediation:
Replace header-derived privilege assignments with database-backed lookups:
# WRONG: g.is_admin = request.headers.get('X-Is-Admin') == 'true'
# RIGHT: user = User.query.get(session['user_id']) g.is_admin = user.has_role('admin')
Or use JWT claims with signature verification: claims = jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=['HS256']) g.is_admin = claims.get('role') == 'admin'

title: Authorization Conditional Using Forgeable Header-Derived Value
description: Detects authorization branches (if/else) that gate sensitive operations on privilege flags known to be derived from HTTP headers. This is a Layer 2 contextual rule — the conditional itself is only dangerous when corroborated by LOGIC-PRIV-001 or LOGIC-PRIV-002 firing in the same file (proving the flag originates from a forgeable header).
impact: Authorization bypass. If the conditional guards admin-only operations (user deletion, data export, configuration changes), an attacker who forges the source header gains unrestricted access. Impact depends on the operations gated by the conditional.
remediation:
Replace header-derived privilege checks with verified sources:
# WRONG: if g.is_admin:  # where g.is_admin was set from X-Is-Admin header
    delete_all_users()

# RIGHT: if current_user.has_role('admin'):  # DB-backed role check
    delete_all_users()

title: Admin Endpoint Protected Only by Header-Derived Authorization
description: Detects admin or privileged endpoints (routes containing /admin/, /manage/, /internal/, /audit/) that rely on header-based authorization checks. This is a chain rule (Layer 2) — it gains maximum severity when corroborated by LOGIC-PRIV-001 or LOGIC-PRIV-002 in the same file, proving the admin endpoint's access control is entirely forgeable.
impact: Full administrative access via trivially forgeable HTTP header. Attacker gains access to admin panels, user management, tenant administration, billing configuration, audit logs, and bulk data export. In a multi-tenant SaaS context, this enables cross-tenant data access, mass data exfiltration, and service disruption.
remediation:
Protect admin endpoints with cryptographically verified authentication:
@app.route('/admin/users') @login_required @admin_required  # Decorator checks DB-backed role def admin_list_users():
    ...

Never use header-derived flags as the sole access control for admin endpoints. Implement defense-in-depth: authentication + authorization + audit logging for all admin operations.

title: Insecure Keychain Access
description: Detects keychain items stored without proper access control flags.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: Weak Biometric Authentication
description: Detects LAContext usage without fallback validation.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

description: Detects hardcoded passwords in Objective-C source code.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: Missing SSL Certificate Pinning
description: Detects NSURLSession without certificate pinning delegates.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: Disabled App Transport Security
description: Detects ATS exceptions allowing insecure connections.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: Weak Encryption Algorithm
description: Detects usage of weak or deprecated encryption algorithms.
impact: Weak cryptography can be broken, compromising data confidentiality and integrity
remediation: Use industry-standard algorithms (AES-256-GCM, SHA-256+, Argon2) and proper key management

title: ECB Mode Usage
description: Detects usage of ECB block cipher mode.
impact: Weak cryptography can be broken, compromising data confidentiality and integrity
remediation: Use industry-standard algorithms (AES-256-GCM, SHA-256+, Argon2) and proper key management

title: Hardcoded Encryption Key
description: Detects hardcoded cryptographic keys in source code.
impact: Weak cryptography can be broken, compromising data confidentiality and integrity
remediation: Use industry-standard algorithms (AES-256-GCM, SHA-256+, Argon2) and proper key management

title: Insecure Random Number Generation
description: Detects use of weak random number generators.
impact: Weak cryptography can be broken, compromising data confidentiality and integrity
remediation: Use industry-standard algorithms (AES-256-GCM, SHA-256+, Argon2) and proper key management

title: Weak Hash for Password Storage
description: Detects MD5/SHA1 used for password hashing.
impact: Weak cryptography can be broken, compromising data confidentiality and integrity
remediation: Use industry-standard algorithms (AES-256-GCM, SHA-256+, Argon2) and proper key management

title: Dynamic Library Loading
description: Detects dynamic library loading from untrusted paths.
impact: Remote code execution enables complete system compromise and lateral movement
remediation: Avoid dynamic code execution, sandbox untrusted input, use allowlists

title: Insecure Deserialization
description: Detects NSKeyedUnarchiver usage without secure coding.
impact: Remote code execution enables complete system compromise and lateral movement
remediation: Avoid dynamic code execution, sandbox untrusted input, use allowlists

title: URL Scheme Handler Without Validation
description: Detects custom URL scheme handling without input validation.
impact: Remote code execution enables complete system compromise and lateral movement
remediation: Avoid dynamic code execution, sandbox untrusted input, use allowlists

title: Pasteboard Data Leakage
description: Detects sensitive data being stored in pasteboard.
impact: Remote code execution enables complete system compromise and lateral movement
remediation: Avoid dynamic code execution, sandbox untrusted input, use allowlists

title: Insecure WebView Configuration
description: Detects WKWebView with JavaScript enabled and insecure settings.
impact: Remote code execution enables complete system compromise and lateral movement
remediation: Avoid dynamic code execution, sandbox untrusted input, use allowlists

title: Hardcoded Passwords in PHP Source
description: Detects hardcoded passwords, API keys, and credentials in PHP source code including database connection strings, configuration constants, and inline authentication values in PHP applications.
impact: Hardcoded credentials in PHP files are directly readable from source code. PHP files may be exposed through misconfigured web servers, source code leaks, or backup files (.php.bak).
remediation: Use environment variables with getenv() or PHP dotenv. In Laravel, use env() helper. Never commit .env files to version control. Use a secrets manager for production credentials.

title: MD5/SHA1 for Password Hashing in PHP
description: Detects use of MD5 or SHA1 for password hashing in PHP applications. These algorithms are cryptographically broken for password storage and allow rapid brute-force attacks.
impact: MD5 and SHA1 are computationally fast, allowing billions of attempts per second on modern GPUs. Rainbow tables exist for common passwords. After database breach, most passwords can be cracked in minutes.
remediation: Use password_hash() with PASSWORD_BCRYPT or PASSWORD_ARGON2ID. Use password_verify() for comparison. These functions handle salting and use appropriate cost factors automatically.

title: SQL Injection in Login Query
description: Detects SQL injection vulnerabilities in PHP authentication queries where user-supplied credentials are concatenated directly into SQL strings without parameterization or escaping.
impact: SQL injection in login queries allows complete authentication bypass. Attacker uses ' OR 1=1 -- to log in as any user without knowing the password. Can also extract database contents.
remediation: Use PDO prepared statements with parameterized queries. Never concatenate user input into SQL strings. In Laravel, use Eloquent ORM or query builder with parameter binding.

title: Session Fixation in PHP
description: Detects PHP applications vulnerable to session fixation attacks where the session ID is not regenerated after authentication, allowing attackers to fix a known session ID and hijack authenticated sessions.
impact: Session fixation allows attackers to set a known session ID before authentication. After the victim logs in, the attacker uses the pre-set session ID to access the authenticated session.
remediation: Always call session_regenerate_id(true) immediately after successful authentication. Use session.use_strict_mode=1 in php.ini. In Laravel, use Session::regenerate(). Never accept session IDs from URL parameters.

title: Missing CSRF Token Verification in PHP
description: Detects PHP forms and state-changing endpoints that lack CSRF token generation and verification, allowing cross-site request forgery attacks on authenticated operations.
impact: Missing CSRF protection allows attackers to forge requests that perform actions on behalf of authenticated users, including data modification, account changes, and financial transactions.
remediation: Generate a unique CSRF token per session and include it in all forms as a hidden field. Verify the token on every state-changing request. In Laravel, use @csrf directive. In WordPress, use wp_nonce_field().

title: Insecure Remember-Me Token in PHP
description: Detects insecure remember-me token implementations in PHP that use predictable values, store plaintext credentials, or lack proper token rotation and expiration mechanisms.
impact: Insecure remember-me tokens allow attackers to forge persistent login cookies. Storing passwords in cookies exposes credentials. Predictable tokens enable brute-force of valid sessions.
remediation: Generate cryptographically random tokens with bin2hex(random_bytes(32)). Store only the token hash in the database. Implement token rotation on each use. Set proper expiration and HttpOnly/Secure flags.

title: strcmp/strcasecmp Bypass for Authentication in PHP
description: Detects use of strcmp or strcasecmp for password or token comparison in PHP. These functions return 0 (equal) when comparing a string to an array, enabling authentication bypass through type juggling.
impact: strcmp returns NULL when given an array instead of string. In PHP, NULL == 0 is true with loose comparison, bypassing password checks entirely. Any user can authenticate without valid credentials.
remediation: Use password_verify() for password comparison. Use hash_equals() for token comparison. If using strcmp, always use strict comparison (===). Validate input types before comparison.

title: Type Juggling in Password Comparison
description: Detects PHP authentication code using loose comparison (==) for password hash verification, which is vulnerable to type juggling attacks where specially crafted strings compare as equal to numeric values.
impact: PHP type juggling with loose comparison allows authentication bypass. MD5 hashes starting with 0e are treated as zero in scientific notation. Multiple known strings produce 0e-prefixed MD5 hashes.
remediation: Always use password_verify() for password comparison. Use strict comparison (===) for all hash comparisons. Use hash_equals() for constant-time string comparison.

title: extract() and register_globals Abuse in Authentication
description: Detects use of extract() on user input or patterns mimicking register_globals in PHP authentication code, allowing attackers to overwrite authentication variables with arbitrary values.
impact: extract() on user input allows attackers to overwrite any PHP variable in the current scope. Sending is_admin=1 or authenticated=true in POST data directly sets those variables, bypassing all authentication.
remediation: Never use extract() on user input. Access $_POST, $_GET directly by key. If extract is necessary, use EXTR_SKIP or EXTR_PREFIX_ALL. Whitelist expected input keys.

title: Insecure PHP Session Configuration
description: Detects insecure PHP session configuration settings including disabled cookie_httponly, cookie_secure, use_strict_mode, and use of file-based sessions with world-readable permissions.
impact: Insecure session configuration exposes session cookies to XSS theft (missing HttpOnly), network interception (missing Secure), and session fixation attacks (missing strict mode).
remediation: Set session.cookie_httponly=1, session.cookie_secure=1, session.use_strict_mode=1, session.use_only_cookies=1, and session.cookie_samesite=Strict in php.ini or via ini_set().

title: Django SECRET_KEY Hardcoded in Source Code
description: Detects hardcoded SECRET_KEY in Django settings files. The SECRET_KEY is used for session signing, CSRF tokens, password reset tokens, and all cryptographic operations. A leaked key enables session forgery and complete authentication bypass.
impact: A leaked SECRET_KEY allows attackers to forge session cookies, predict CSRF tokens, create password reset tokens, and impersonate any user including administrators. This leads to complete authentication bypass.
remediation: Store SECRET_KEY in environment variables using os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY']. Use python-decouple or django-environ for configuration management. Generate keys with django.core.management.utils.get_random_secret_key().

title: Flask Session Secret Weak or Hardcoded
description: Detects weak, short, or hardcoded Flask session secrets. Flask uses the secret_key for signing session cookies. A weak or predictable secret allows attackers to forge or tamper with session data.
impact: A weak Flask secret allows attackers to brute-force the session signing key, forge arbitrary session cookies, and impersonate any user in the application including administrators.
remediation: Generate a strong secret using os.urandom(32) or secrets.token_hex(32). Store it in an environment variable. Never use common words or short strings as Flask secret keys.

title: Django @login_required Missing on Sensitive Views
description: Detects Django views handling sensitive operations without the @login_required decorator or LoginRequiredMixin. Unprotected views allow anonymous users to access restricted functionality.
impact: Anonymous users can access administrative panels, user data, payment operations, and settings pages without any authentication. This leads to data exposure and unauthorized actions.
remediation: Add @login_required to all sensitive function-based views. Use LoginRequiredMixin for class-based views. Set LOGIN_URL in settings. Consider using a deny-by-default middleware approach.

title: Flask-Login Authentication Bypass
description: Detects Flask routes handling sensitive operations without Flask-Login @login_required decorator, or patterns where Flask-Login protections are weakened or bypassed through misconfiguration.
impact: Unauthenticated users can access sensitive endpoints including admin panels, user management, and payment processing. LOGIN_DISABLED=True globally removes all authentication requirements.
remediation: Apply @login_required to all sensitive routes. Never set LOGIN_DISABLED=True in production. Ensure unauthorized_handler returns 401 or redirects to login. Use Flask-Login's fresh_login_required for critical operations.

title: Password Stored in Plaintext
description: Detects patterns where passwords are stored or compared in plaintext without any hashing. Plaintext password storage is the most severe credential management vulnerability.
impact: Plaintext passwords exposed in any database breach will immediately compromise all user accounts. Attackers gain credentials usable for credential stuffing across other services.
remediation: Always use bcrypt, argon2, or PBKDF2 for password hashing. In Django, use set_password() and check_password(). In Flask, use generate_password_hash() from werkzeug.security.

title: Insecure Password Hashing with MD5 or SHA1
description: Detects usage of MD5, SHA1, or SHA256 without proper key derivation for password hashing. These fast hash algorithms allow rapid brute-force attacks on leaked password databases.
impact: MD5 passwords can be cracked at billions of hashes per second on GPU. SHA1 is only marginally better. Rainbow tables instantly reverse unsalted hashes. A database breach exposes all user credentials within hours.
remediation: Use bcrypt with cost factor 12+, argon2id, or PBKDF2 with 600,000+ iterations. In Django, use the default PASSWORD_HASHERS. In Flask, use werkzeug.security.generate_password_hash with method='pbkdf2:sha256'.

title: Django CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE Set to False
description: Detects Django settings where CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE is explicitly set to False, allowing CSRF tokens to be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections. This enables man-in-the-middle attackers to steal CSRF tokens.
impact: CSRF tokens transmitted over HTTP can be intercepted by network-level attackers. Combined with insecure session cookies, this enables both CSRF attacks and session hijacking on unencrypted connections.
remediation: Set CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE=True, SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True, CSRF_COOKIE_SAMESITE='Lax', and SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE='Lax' in production Django settings. Enforce HTTPS with SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT=True.

title: Session Timeout Not Configured
description: Detects Django and Flask applications where session timeout (SESSION_COOKIE_AGE / PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME) is not configured or set to an excessively long value. Long-lived sessions increase the window for session hijacking.
impact: Long-lived sessions increase the window for session hijacking via XSS, network interception, or shared computer access. Sessions that persist for weeks leave stolen tokens valid for extended periods.
remediation: Set SESSION_COOKIE_AGE to 3600 (1 hour) or 7200 (2 hours) for sensitive applications. Enable SESSION_EXPIRE_AT_BROWSER_CLOSE=True in Django. Set PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME=timedelta(hours=1) in Flask.

title: Permission Decorator Bypass
description: Detects patterns where Django or DRF permission decorators are present but can be bypassed due to misconfiguration, such as custom permission classes that always return True, missing object-level permissions, or DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES set to AllowAny.
impact: Permissive permission classes allow unauthorized users to access, modify, or delete resources they should not have access to. This leads to data breaches and unauthorized operations.
remediation: Set DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES to [IsAuthenticated] in DRF settings. Implement proper has_permission and has_object_permission in custom permission classes. Always verify ownership in object-level permissions.

title: OAuth2 Token Validation Missing
description: Detects OAuth2 token handling in Python applications where tokens are accepted without proper validation, including missing signature verification, expiration checks, audience validation, or issuer verification.
impact: Without proper token validation, attackers can forge tokens, use expired tokens, or use tokens issued for different services. This enables authentication bypass and impersonation of any user.
remediation: Always validate JWT tokens with algorithms pinned to RS256 or ES256. Enable signature verification, expiration checks, audience validation, and issuer verification. Use established libraries like PyJWT with strict options.

remediation: Use Rails credentials (rails credentials:edit), ENV vars, or secret managers

title: Use of DES or Triple DES (3DES) Encryption
description: Detects usage of DES or Triple DES (3DES) algorithms in C# code via DESCryptoServiceProvider, TripleDESCryptoServiceProvider, or their factory methods. DES uses a 56-bit key that is trivially brute-forced with modern hardware in hours. 3DES is deprecated by NIST as of 2023 and is vulnerable to the Sweet32 birthday attack on its 64-bit block cipher after processing approximately 32 GB of data under the same key. Both RC2CryptoServiceProvider and related weak symmetric ciphers are also flagged. Applications must migrate to AES-256-GCM or AES-256-CBC with HMAC authentication.
impact:
DES can be brute-forced in hours with commodity hardware or cloud resources.
3DES is vulnerable to the Sweet32 birthday attack after processing ~32 GB
under the same key. RC2 has variable key length with known weaknesses.
Encrypted data protected by these algorithms should be considered recoverable
by determined attackers. Non-compliance with PCI-DSS, NIST SP 800-131A,
and FIPS 140-3.

title: Use of MD5 or SHA1 for Security-Critical Hashing
description: Detects usage of cryptographically broken hash algorithms MD5 and SHA1 through .NET's System.Security.Cryptography namespace. MD5CryptoServiceProvider, SHA1CryptoServiceProvider, SHA1Managed, MD5.Create(), and HashAlgorithm.Create("MD5"/"SHA1") are all vulnerable. MD5 is fully broken for collision resistance, and SHA1 has demonstrated practical collision attacks (SHAttered). Neither algorithm is safe for password hashing, digital signatures, certificate validation, or integrity verification in security contexts.
impact:
Using MD5/SHA1 in .NET applications creates severe vulnerabilities:
- MD5 collisions generated in seconds on commodity hardware
- SHA1 chosen-prefix collisions demonstrated (SHAttered, Shambles)
- Password hashes crackable at billions of attempts per second via hashcat
- ASP.NET Forms Authentication with MD5/SHA1 enables account takeover
- Digital signatures and HMAC-based tokens become forgeable
- Non-compliance with NIST SP 800-131A, PCI-DSS, FIPS 140-3

title: Use of ECB (Electronic Codebook) Block Cipher Mode
description: Detects explicit use of ECB mode for block cipher operations in C# via CipherMode.ECB assignment or related patterns. ECB mode encrypts identical plaintext blocks to identical ciphertext blocks, leaking data patterns. This is famously demonstrated by the ECB Penguin problem where encrypted images retain visible structure. ECB also enables block-swapping attacks where an adversary can rearrange ciphertext blocks to manipulate decrypted output. ECB should never be used for encrypting data longer than a single block.
impact:
ECB mode and improper IVs break encryption security in .NET:
- ECB mode produces identical ciphertext for identical plaintext blocks
- Static/zero IVs enable chosen-plaintext attacks in CBC mode
- IV = Key catastrophically ties confidentiality to a single secret
- Pattern leakage enables content analysis without key recovery
- Block swapping attacks can manipulate decrypted output
- Non-compliance with NIST SP 800-38A, SP 800-38D

title: Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys in Source Code
description: Detects hardcoded cryptographic keys in C# source code including byte array literals used with symmetric ciphers, hardcoded key constants, and key material embedded in source files. .NET applications are compiled to IL which is trivially decompilable using tools like dnSpy, ILSpy, or dotPeek. Hardcoded keys in .NET assemblies provide false security since the keys are easily extractable from compiled DLLs and EXEs. Key rotation requires code changes and redeployment.
impact:
Hardcoded keys in C# applications are trivially extractable:
- .NET assemblies (DLL/EXE) are easily decompiled to readable C# code
- dnSpy, ILSpy, dotPeek, and JustDecompile recover source-level code
- NuGet packages with embedded keys expose them to all consumers
- Docker images with embedded keys expose them in image layers
- Key rotation requires rebuild and redeployment
- Violates PCI-DSS 3.5, NIST SP 800-57, SOC2 CC6.1

title: Weak RSA Key Size (Below 2048 bits)
description: Detects RSACryptoServiceProvider or RSA instances created with insufficient key sizes (below 2048 bits) in .NET applications. The default RSACryptoServiceProvider constructor generates a 1024-bit key in older .NET Framework versions. RSA.Create() defaults to 2048 bits in newer versions but developers may explicitly specify smaller sizes. RSA-512 and RSA-768 have been publicly factored, and RSA-1024 is factorable by state-level attackers using the General Number Field Sieve. NIST recommends a minimum of 2048 bits with 3072 or 4096 bits preferred for long-term security.
impact:
Insufficient RSA key sizes in .NET applications create security risks:
- RSA-512 and RSA-768 have been publicly factored
- RSA-1024 factorable by well-resourced attackers
- Default RSACryptoServiceProvider() in old .NET Framework uses 1024 bits
- Weak certificates enable MITM via key factoring
- Digital signatures become forgeable with recovered private key
- Non-compliance with NIST SP 800-131A, PCI-DSS, FIPS 140-3

title: Use of System.Random for Security-Sensitive Operations
description: Detects usage of System.Random for generating security-sensitive values instead of System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator. System.Random uses a subtraction PRNG that is not cryptographically secure and produces predictable output given the seed. The default constructor uses Environment.TickCount as seed, which is predictable from server startup time. .NET 6+ added RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes/GetInt32 as convenient CSPRNG methods. System.Random should never be used for tokens, keys, nonces, salts, OTPs, or session IDs.
impact:
Using System.Random for security operations in .NET is exploitable:
- Default seed (Environment.TickCount) is predictable from server start time
- Internal state recoverable from observed outputs
- Same-seed Random instances produce identical sequences
- Random.Shared is convenient but not cryptographically secure
- Password reset tokens, CSRF tokens, OTPs become predictable

title: Disabled or Bypassed SSL/TLS Certificate Validation
description: Detects code that disables SSL/TLS certificate validation by setting ServerCertificateValidationCallback to always return true, configuring HttpClientHandler to skip certificate checks, or using deprecated TLS/SSL protocol versions. ServicePointManager.ServerCertificateValidationCallback affects ALL connections globally in the process. This completely negates TLS protection, allowing trivial man-in-the-middle attacks on every HTTPS connection the application makes including payment gateways and auth providers.
impact:
Disabling certificate validation and using deprecated protocols enables attacks:
- Any attacker on the network path can intercept HTTPS with a self-signed cert
- SSLv3 vulnerable to POODLE attack (plaintext recovery)
- TLS 1.0 vulnerable to BEAST attack
- ServicePointManager settings affect ALL connections globally in the process
- Payment gateway, auth provider, and API communications all compromised
- Violates PCI-DSS 4.0, HIPAA, GDPR transport security requirements

title: Custom Cryptographic Algorithm Implementation
description: Detects attempts to implement custom cryptographic algorithms instead of using well-tested standard libraries from System.Security.Cryptography. Custom implementations of encryption (XOR ciphers, substitution ciphers), hashing, key exchange, or random number generation are almost always weaker than standard implementations due to subtle mathematical, timing, and implementation flaws. This rule also detects weak key derivation patterns including PasswordDeriveBytes (PBKDF1) and Rfc2898DeriveBytes with insufficient iterations, as well as raw password-to-key conversions.
impact:
Custom cryptographic implementations typically have fatal weaknesses:
- XOR ciphers are trivially broken with known-plaintext attacks
- Custom hashes have collision and preimage vulnerabilities
- PasswordDeriveBytes (PBKDF1) uses only MD5/SHA1 with limited output
- Rfc2898DeriveBytes with low iterations is GPU brute-forceable
- Raw password bytes as key limits entropy to password entropy
- Data protected by custom crypto should be considered unprotected

title: Weak Hash Algorithm Usage (crypto/md5 or crypto/sha1)
description: Detects usage of cryptographically broken hash algorithms MD5 and SHA1 through Go's crypto/md5 and crypto/sha1 packages for security-sensitive operations. Go's standard library explicitly provides these packages but their documentation warns against using them for security purposes. MD5 collisions are trivially generatable, and SHA1 was broken by the SHAttered attack. These must not be used for password hashing, digital signatures, certificate validation, or HMAC where collision resistance matters.
impact:
Using crypto/md5 or crypto/sha1 for security in Go applications creates vulnerabilities:
- MD5 collisions generatable in seconds on commodity hardware
- SHA1 chosen-prefix collisions demonstrated (SHAttered, Shambles)
- Password hashes crackable via rainbow tables and GPU brute force
- Digital signatures using these algorithms can be forged
- HMAC-MD5/HMAC-SHA1 weaker than HMAC-SHA256 for new applications
- Non-compliance with NIST SP 800-131A, PCI-DSS, FIPS 140-3
remediation:
Replace with crypto/sha256 or stronger alternatives:

```go
// VULNERABLE: MD5 for hashing
import "crypto/md5"
hash := md5.Sum([]byte(data))

// SECURE: SHA-256 for integrity
import "crypto/sha256"
hash := sha256.Sum256([]byte(data))

// SECURE: bcrypt for password hashing
import "golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt"
hashed, err := bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword([]byte(password), 12)
err = bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword(hashed, []byte(password))

// SECURE: argon2 for password hashing
import "golang.org/x/crypto/argon2"
hash := argon2.IDKey([]byte(password), salt, 3, 64*1024, 4, 32)

// SECURE: HMAC-SHA256
import "crypto/hmac"
import "crypto/sha256"
mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, key)
mac.Write(data)
signature := mac.Sum(nil)
```

title: Weak Cipher Usage (DES/RC4)
description: Detects usage of weak or deprecated cipher algorithms in Go applications including crypto/des (DES and Triple DES) and crypto/rc4 (RC4/ARC4). DES uses a 56-bit key brute-forceable in hours. Triple DES is vulnerable to Sweet32 birthday attacks on its 64-bit block size. RC4 has well-documented keystream biases exploitable in TLS and WPA. Go's standard library includes these packages for legacy compatibility but they should never be used for new encryption operations.
impact:
Using weak ciphers in Go applications exposes encrypted data:
- DES 56-bit key exhaustion in hours using FPGA clusters
- 3DES/Triple DES vulnerable to Sweet32 birthday attack after ~32GB
- RC4 keystream biases enable plaintext recovery
- Blowfish 64-bit block size enables birthday attacks
- All modern compliance standards prohibit these algorithms
- Data encrypted with these ciphers should be considered compromised
remediation:
Replace with AES-256-GCM or XChaCha20-Poly1305:

```go
// VULNERABLE: DES encryption
import "crypto/des"
block, _ := des.NewCipher(key8bytes)

// SECURE: AES-256-GCM
import (
    "crypto/aes"
    "crypto/cipher"
    "crypto/rand"
)
block, err := aes.NewCipher(key32bytes) // 256-bit key
gcm, err := cipher.NewGCM(block)
nonce := make([]byte, gcm.NonceSize())
rand.Read(nonce)
ciphertext := gcm.Seal(nonce, nonce, plaintext, nil)

// SECURE: XChaCha20-Poly1305
import "golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20poly1305"
aead, err := chacha20poly1305.NewX(key32bytes)
nonce := make([]byte, aead.NonceSize())
rand.Read(nonce)
ciphertext := aead.Seal(nonce, nonce, plaintext, nil)
```

title: Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys in Go Code
description: Detects hardcoded cryptographic keys, secrets, and passwords embedded directly in Go source code. Go binaries, while compiled, can be analyzed with tools like strings and Go-specific reverse engineering tools (go tool objdump, Ghidra with Go plugins). Hardcoded keys in Go are particularly dangerous because Go binaries are often distributed as single static binaries, making key extraction straightforward. String constants in Go are stored unencrypted in the binary data section.
impact:
Hardcoded keys in Go applications are extractable and compromise all protected data:
- Go binaries contain strings in their data section, extractable via `strings` command
- Go-specific tools (go tool objdump, Ghidra) can identify key material in binaries
- Single static binaries are easily shared and analyzed
- Docker images with embedded keys expose keys in image layers
- Key rotation requires rebuilding and redeploying all binaries
- Violates PCI-DSS 3.5, NIST SP 800-57, SOC2 CC6.1

title: math/rand Used Instead of crypto/rand
description: Detects usage of Go's math/rand package for generating security-sensitive values instead of crypto/rand. math/rand uses a deterministic PRNG (source-based) that produces predictable output given the seed. The default source is not safe for concurrent use and produces identical sequences with the same seed. Even math/rand/v2 with modern algorithms is not cryptographically secure. crypto/rand reads from the OS CSPRNG (/dev/urandom on Unix, CryptGenRandom on Windows) and must be used for all security operations.
impact:
Using math/rand for security operations in Go applications enables prediction:
- math/rand with known seed produces entirely deterministic output
- Time-based seeds (time.Now().UnixNano()) narrow search space to ~1 billion values
- Default math/rand (before Go 1.20) uses seed 1, producing identical sequences
- Attackers observing outputs can recover state and predict future values
- Password reset tokens, session IDs, OTPs become predictable
- Even math/rand/v2 is explicitly documented as not cryptographically secure
remediation:
Use crypto/rand for all security-sensitive random operations:

```go
// VULNERABLE: math/rand for token generation
import "math/rand"
rand.Seed(time.Now().UnixNano())
token := rand.Int63()

// SECURE: crypto/rand for random bytes
import "crypto/rand"
token := make([]byte, 32)
_, err := rand.Read(token)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal("CSPRNG failure:", err)
}
tokenStr := hex.EncodeToString(token)

// SECURE: crypto/rand for random integers
import "crypto/rand"
import "math/big"
n, err := rand.Int(rand.Reader, big.NewInt(900000))
otp := n.Int64() + 100000
```
