title: Composer Autoloader Exploitation via Deserialization Gadget Chains
description: Detects conditions where PHP deserialization occurs in applications using Composer autoloading, which dramatically expands the attack surface for gadget chain exploitation. When Composer autoloading is active (require 'vendor/autoload.php'), any class from any installed package can be instantiated during deserialization. This means gadget chains from popular packages like Monolog, Guzzle, Symfony, Doctrine, Laravel, and PHPUnit become available. The presence of both deserialization and Composer autoloading creates a high-risk combination for PHP object injection attacks.
impact:
Composer autoloader exploitation through deserialization can lead to:
- Remote Code Execution through dozens of known gadget chains
- File system manipulation (read/write/delete)
- SQL injection through ORM gadget chains
- SSRF through HTTP client gadget chains
- Complete server compromise via any of the 100+ PHPGGC chains
remediation:
1. Use json_decode instead of unserialize for all user data.
2. If unserialize is required, use strict allowed_classes:
   ```php
   $data = unserialize($input, ['allowed_classes' => false]);
   ```
3. Remove development dependencies in production:
   ```bash
   composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
   ```
4. Use PHPGGC for security audit of installed packages:
   ```bash
   phpggc -l  # List available chains for installed packages
   ```
5. Implement runtime deserialization monitoring.

title: Laravel Queue Job Deserialization Enabling Remote Code Execution
description: Detects vulnerabilities in Laravel queue job deserialization where serialized job payloads from queue backends (Redis, SQS, Beanstalkd, database) are deserialized using PHP's unserialize. Laravel queue workers deserialize job payloads to reconstruct Eloquent models and job classes. If the queue backend is compromised (e.g., exposed Redis) or if job payloads can be tampered with, an attacker can inject malicious serialized objects that exploit gadget chains in Laravel's framework classes. CVE-2022-31279 demonstrated RCE through crafted queue payloads in Laravel.
impact:
Laravel queue deserialization exploitation can lead to:
- Remote Code Execution on queue worker processes
- Background job manipulation and injection
- Data corruption through tampered job payloads
- Privilege escalation via crafted job objects
- Persistent backdoor through recurring malicious queue jobs
remediation:
1. Secure Redis with authentication and network restrictions:
   ```env
   REDIS_PASSWORD=strong_random_password_here
   REDIS_HOST=127.0.0.1
   ```
2. Use encrypted and signed queue payloads (Laravel 8+):
   ```php
   // In queue job class
   class ProcessPayment implements ShouldQueue, ShouldBeEncrypted
   {
       use SerializesModels;
   }
   ```
3. Restrict network access to queue backends.
4. Use database queue with parameterized queries.
5. Implement queue job HMAC verification at the worker level.

title: Doctrine ORM Object Hydration with Untrusted Data
description: Detects Doctrine ORM object hydration patterns where user-controlled data is used to hydrate entity objects without proper validation. Doctrine's ObjectHydrator and custom hydration modes can reconstruct entity objects from database results or external data. When combined with PHP's type juggling and Doctrine's proxy object mechanism, attacker-controlled data can lead to unexpected object instantiation, lazy-loading proxy exploitation, and in certain configurations, deserialization of stored serialized column data. Doctrine entities with lifecycle callbacks (PostLoad, PrePersist) can amplify the impact of object injection.
impact:
Doctrine ORM hydration exploitation can lead to:
- Object injection through serialized column types (object/array)
- Remote Code Execution via gadget chains during hydration
- Data manipulation through lifecycle callback abuse
- Privilege escalation via proxy class exploitation
- Indirect SQL injection through type conversion

title: PHPGGC Gadget Chain Entry Points in Application Code
description: Detects code patterns that serve as entry points for PHP Generic Gadget Chains (PHPGGC). This rule identifies classes and methods commonly found in popular PHP frameworks and libraries that are used as initial links in deserialization gadget chains. The rule targets magic methods (__destruct, __wakeup, __toString, __call, __get, __set) in classes from Laravel, Symfony, Monolog, Guzzle, Doctrine, SwiftMailer, and other widely-used packages that are documented in the PHPGGC repository as exploitable gadget chains.
impact:
PHPGGC gadget chain exploitation leads to:
- Remote Code Execution through system()/exec()/eval()
- Arbitrary file write for webshell deployment
- Arbitrary file read for sensitive data extraction
- Server-Side Request Forgery through HTTP client gadgets
- SQL injection through ORM gadget chains
- Complete server compromise through chained operations
remediation:
1. Prevent deserialization of untrusted data (root cause):
   ```php
   // Use json_decode instead of unserialize
   $data = json_decode($input, true);
   ```
2. Use allowed_classes to prevent gadget chain class instantiation:
   ```php
   $data = unserialize($input, ['allowed_classes' => false]);
   ```
3. Remove unused framework packages to reduce gadget surface:
   ```bash
   composer remove unused/package
   composer install --no-dev
   ```
4. Audit magic methods in application code:
   ```bash
   grep -rn '__destruct\|__wakeup\|__toString\|__call' src/
   ```
5. Implement runtime deserialization monitoring (e.g., Snuffleupagus).

title: Pickle Deserialization of Untrusted Data Leading to Remote Code Execution
description: Detects usage of pickle.loads(), pickle.load(), cPickle.loads(), cPickle.load(), or _pickle.loads() on data originating from untrusted sources. Python's pickle module can serialize and deserialize arbitrary Python objects including code objects. The __reduce__ method allows any class to define custom reconstruction logic that executes during unpickling. An attacker who can control pickled data can achieve arbitrary code execution by crafting a payload that invokes os.system, subprocess.Popen, or any other callable during deserialization.
impact:
Pickle deserialization of untrusted data leads to:
- Arbitrary Remote Code Execution with server process privileges
- Full server compromise including file system access
- Data exfiltration from databases and internal services
- Lateral movement within the network
- Persistent backdoor installation
- Complete confidentiality, integrity, and availability compromise

title: PyYAML yaml.load Without SafeLoader Enabling Code Execution
description: Detects usage of yaml.load() without specifying Loader=yaml.SafeLoader or Loader=yaml.BaseLoader. In PyYAML versions prior to 6.0, yaml.load() defaults to yaml.FullLoader (or yaml.Loader in older versions) which supports Python-specific YAML tags such as !!python/object, !!python/object/apply, and !!python/module. These tags allow instantiation of arbitrary Python objects during YAML parsing, leading to remote code execution when processing untrusted YAML input.
impact:
Unsafe YAML deserialization in Python can result in:
- Remote Code Execution via !!python/object/apply tags
- Arbitrary object instantiation leading to server compromise
- File system access through crafted YAML constructors
- Denial of Service via billion-laughs YAML bomb
- Information disclosure through object attribute access
remediation:
1. Always use yaml.safe_load instead of yaml.load:
   ```python
   import yaml
   data = yaml.safe_load(user_input)
   ```
2. If yaml.load is required, always specify SafeLoader:
   ```python
   data = yaml.load(user_input, Loader=yaml.SafeLoader)
   ```
3. For multiple documents, use yaml.safe_load_all:
   ```python
   for doc in yaml.safe_load_all(user_input):
       process(doc)
   ```
4. Set YAML input size limits to prevent DoS attacks.
5. Upgrade PyYAML to version 6.0+ which warns on unsafe usage.

title: shelve or dbm Module Deserialization of Untrusted Database Files
description: Detects usage of Python's shelve module or direct dbm usage on database files from untrusted sources. The shelve module uses pickle internally to serialize and deserialize values stored in dbm-style databases. Opening a shelve database file from an untrusted source and accessing any value triggers pickle deserialization, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Similarly, crafted dbm files can exploit parser bugs in the underlying database library.
impact:
Shelve/dbm deserialization of untrusted files can lead to:
- Remote Code Execution via pickle payloads in shelve values
- Arbitrary file system access through path traversal
- Data corruption of legitimate shelve databases
- Denial of Service through malformed database files
- Privilege escalation if shelve is accessed by privileged processes
remediation:
1. Never open shelve databases from untrusted sources:
   ```python
   # Bad: user-controlled path
   db = shelve.open(user_provided_path)

   # Good: use fixed, application-controlled paths
   db = shelve.open(os.path.join(APP_DATA_DIR, 'internal_cache'))
   ```
2. Replace shelve with a safe database solution:
   ```python
   import sqlite3
   conn = sqlite3.connect(os.path.join(APP_DATA_DIR, 'data.db'))
   ```
3. If shelve must be used, validate and sanitize file paths.
4. Use JSON-based storage for user-submitted data.
5. Implement file upload validation to reject shelve database file types.

title: marshal.loads Deserialization of Untrusted Data
description: Detects usage of Python's marshal module (marshal.loads, marshal.load) on untrusted input. The marshal module is designed for reading and writing Python bytecode (.pyc files) and can deserialize code objects. Processing untrusted marshal data can lead to code execution when the deserialized code object is subsequently evaluated, and can cause crashes or undefined behavior due to malformed bytecode. The Python documentation explicitly warns against unmarshalling untrusted data.
impact:
Marshal deserialization of untrusted data can lead to:
- Arbitrary code execution through deserialized code objects
- Python interpreter crash via malformed bytecode
- Denial of Service through resource exhaustion
- Information disclosure through code object introspection
- Full server compromise when code objects are executed
remediation:
1. Never use marshal with untrusted data:
   ```python
   # Bad: marshal on untrusted input
   code = marshal.loads(user_data)

   # Good: use JSON for data exchange
   import json
   data = json.loads(user_data)
   ```
2. The marshal module is for internal Python use only (pyc files).
3. Use safe serialization formats (JSON, MessagePack) for external data.
4. If code execution is required, use a sandboxed environment.
5. Implement strict input validation before any deserialization.

title: jsonpickle Decode of Untrusted Data Enabling Object Injection
description: Detects usage of jsonpickle.decode() or jsonpickle.loads() on data from untrusted sources. jsonpickle embeds Python type information in JSON using a special py/object key, allowing reconstruction of arbitrary Python objects during decoding. Since jsonpickle transparently handles complex Python types including classes with __reduce__, __setstate__, and __getattr__ methods, an attacker can craft a JSON payload that instantiates malicious objects during deserialization, achieving arbitrary code execution.
impact:
jsonpickle deserialization of untrusted data can lead to:
- Arbitrary code execution through py/reduce or py/object payloads
- Object injection with attacker-controlled class instantiation
- Information disclosure through serialized internal state
- Privilege escalation via crafted object attribute injection
- Server compromise through chained object construction
remediation:
1. Never use jsonpickle with untrusted data. Use standard json module:
   ```python
   import json
   data = json.loads(user_input)
   ```
2. If jsonpickle is needed for internal use, validate data source:
   ```python
   import hmac
   import hashlib

   def safe_decode(data, key):
       payload, signature = data.rsplit('|', 1)
       expected = hmac.new(key, payload.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
       if not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected):
           raise ValueError('Invalid signature')
       return jsonpickle.decode(payload)
   ```
3. Use jsonpickle's safe mode if available (unpicklable=False for encode).
4. Replace jsonpickle with pydantic or marshmallow for data serialization.
5. Implement input schema validation before jsonpickle.decode.

title: dill or cloudpickle Deserialization of Untrusted Data
description: Detects usage of dill or cloudpickle modules for deserializing data from untrusted sources. Both dill and cloudpickle extend Python's pickle module to support serialization of a broader range of Python objects including lambda functions, closures, nested functions, and dynamically created classes. These extended capabilities make them even more dangerous than standard pickle when processing untrusted data, as they can serialize and deserialize virtually any Python object including arbitrary code.
impact:
dill/cloudpickle deserialization of untrusted data leads to:
- Full remote code execution including lambda/closure reconstruction
- Arbitrary module import and function execution
- Complete server compromise
- Data exfiltration from ML pipelines and compute environments
- Lateral movement in distributed computing clusters
- Supply chain attacks through malicious serialized functions
remediation:
1. Never deserialize dill/cloudpickle data from untrusted sources:
   ```python
   # Bad: deserializing user input
   func = dill.loads(request.data)

   # Good: use safe alternatives
   import json
   config = json.loads(request.data)
   ```
2. For ML model serialization, use safe formats:
   ```python
   # Use ONNX, SavedModel, or safetensors instead
   import safetensors
   model = safetensors.torch.load_file('model.safetensors')
   ```
3. Sign serialized functions with HMAC before transmission.
4. Use process sandboxing for untrusted code execution (gVisor, Firecracker).
5. Validate data source authenticity before deserialization.

title: Django Session Deserialization Using PickleSerializer
description: Detects Django applications configured to use PickleSerializer for session serialization. Django's session framework can use different serializers for storing session data. When PickleSerializer is configured (SESSION_SERIALIZER = 'django.contrib.sessions.serializers.PickleSerializer'), session data is stored using pickle. If an attacker can forge session cookies (via secret key leakage, session fixation, or cookie tampering), they can inject pickle payloads that execute arbitrary code when the session is loaded on the server side.
impact:
Django PickleSerializer usage can lead to:
- Remote Code Execution through forged session cookies
- Complete server compromise via pickle deserialization
- Privilege escalation from any authenticated user to superuser
- Data exfiltration from the Django application database
- Persistent backdoor via modified session data
- Compliance violations (PCI DSS, GDPR)
remediation:
1. Switch to JSONSerializer (Django default since 1.6):
   ```python
   # settings.py
   SESSION_SERIALIZER = 'django.contrib.sessions.serializers.JSONSerializer'
   ```
2. Ensure SECRET_KEY is strong and not exposed:
   ```python
   import secrets
   SECRET_KEY = secrets.token_hex(50)
   ```
3. Enable secure session cookie flags:
   ```python
   SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True
   SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
   SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = 'Lax'
   ```

5. Rotate SECRET_KEY periodically and after any suspected exposure.

title: XML Deserialization via xmlrpc Enabling SSRF and Data Exfiltration
description: Detects usage of Python's xmlrpc.server or xmlrpc.client modules with untrusted data, as well as unsafe XML parsing that can lead to XML External Entity (XXE) injection, Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), and in some cases deserialization attacks. The xmlrpc protocol serializes Python objects as XML, and processing untrusted XML-RPC requests or responses can lead to entity expansion attacks (billion laughs), external entity loading (XXE/SSRF), and object injection through crafted XML type tags.
impact:
XML-RPC deserialization vulnerabilities can lead to:
- Server-Side Request Forgery through ServerProxy URL manipulation
- XML External Entity (XXE) injection for file disclosure
- Denial of Service via billion laughs entity expansion
- Information disclosure through XML error messages
- Method traversal on registered instances (allow_dotted_names)
- SSRF to internal services bypassing network segmentation
remediation:
1. Use defusedxml for XML parsing in XML-RPC:
   ```python
   import defusedxml.xmlrpc
   defusedxml.xmlrpc.monkey_patch()
   ```
2. Disable dotted name access on registered instances:
   ```python
   server.register_instance(handler, allow_dotted_names=False)
   ```
3. Validate and restrict XML-RPC client URLs:
   ```python
   from urllib.parse import urlparse
   url = urlparse(user_url)
   if url.hostname not in ALLOWED_HOSTS:
       raise ValueError('Disallowed host')
   proxy = xmlrpc.client.ServerProxy(user_url)
   ```
4. Implement request size limits for XML-RPC servers.
5. Use gRPC or REST/JSON APIs instead of XML-RPC for new services.

title: Unsafe Ruby Marshal or YAML Deserialization
description: Detects Marshal.load() or YAML.load() with untrusted input in Ruby, enabling arbitrary object instantiation and remote code execution through deserialization gadget chains.
impact:
Ruby Marshal.load and YAML.load can instantiate arbitrary objects,
enabling RCE through deserialization gadget chains. Rails applications
are particularly at risk due to the rich class hierarchy available for
gadget chain construction. Historical CVEs (CVE-2013-0156) demonstrate
the severity of this class of vulnerability in Rails.
remediation:
- Use YAML.safe_load instead of YAML.load
- Use JSON.parse for data exchange
- Never deserialize Marshal data from untrusted sources
- If YAML.load is needed, use permitted_classes and permitted_symbols
- Framework-specific guidance:
  - Ruby on Rails: Ensure config.active_support.use_yaml_unsafe_load
    is set to false (default in Rails 7+). Use ActiveSupport::JSON
    for serialization. Configure Active Record serialized attributes
    with coder: JSON instead of default YAML.
  - Rails Sessions: Use cookie_store with encrypted cookies (the
    default in Rails 5.2+). Never use Marshal-based session stores
    with untrusted data. Set config.action_dispatch.cookies_serializer
    to :json.
  - Sidekiq: Use JSON serialization for job arguments. Set
    Sidekiq.strict_args! to enforce JSON-compatible arguments.
  - Rails API: Use ActionController::API mode with JSON rendering.
    Reject requests with Content-Type: application/x-yaml.
  - Sinatra: Use JSON.parse for request body parsing. Never use
    YAML.load on user input in route handlers.
  - General Ruby: Use Oj gem with mode: :strict for fast, safe JSON
    parsing. Use Psych.safe_load with explicit permitted_classes
    when YAML is required.

title: Unsafe Go gob or JSON Deserialization with Interface Types
description: Detects Go JSON or gob deserialization into interface{} types with user-controlled input, potentially enabling type confusion, data integrity violations, and logic bypasses.
impact:
Deserializing into interface{} types loses type safety and can lead to
type confusion, unexpected behavior, or logic bypasses. While Go is
memory-safe and does not have the same RCE risk as Java or Python
deserialization, type confusion can still lead to authorization bypass,
data corruption, and denial of service through panics. The gob package
additionally allows registered types to be instantiated from network
input, expanding the attack surface.
remediation:
- Deserialize into concrete struct types with explicit fields
- Use struct tags for JSON field mapping
- Validate deserialized data with a validation library
- Prefer JSON over gob for external data
- Framework-specific guidance:
  - Gin: Use c.ShouldBindJSON(&typedStruct) with binding tags for
    automatic validation. Define strict struct types with
    `json:"field" binding:"required"` tags. Use gin.H{} only for
    response serialization, never for input deserialization.
  - Echo: Use c.Bind(&typedStruct) with validator tags. Configure
    echo.DefaultBinder with strict type mapping. Use
    echo.Validator interface for custom validation rules.
  - Fiber: Use c.BodyParser(&typedStruct) with explicit struct
    types. Never parse into map[string]interface{} or any.
  - Standard library: Always define concrete structs for
    json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&typedStruct). Use
    json.Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields() to reject unexpected
    fields. Implement json.Unmarshaler for custom validation.
  - gRPC: Use Protocol Buffers with generated Go types for
    type-safe serialization. Never use gob for cross-service
    communication.
  - gob: Only use gob for trusted, internal communication between
    Go services over authenticated channels. Never expose gob
    decoders to untrusted network input. Avoid gob.Register()
    with types that have side effects in their methods.
  - General: Use the go-playground/validator library for struct
    validation after deserialization. Implement custom
    UnmarshalJSON methods for complex validation logic.

description: Detects CI/CD pipeline configurations where untrusted inputs (PR titles, branch names, issue comments) are interpolated into shell commands without sanitization — enabling arbitrary code execution.

title: npm Dependency Confusion — Missing Scope / Registry Pin
description: Detects npm packages that could be vulnerable to dependency confusion attacks where a malicious public package with the same name as an internal package is installed instead.
remediation: Use npm scopes (@company/package-name) for all internal packages. Pin the internal registry in .npmrc: @company:registry=https://internal-registry. Use package-lock.json to lock resolved registries.

title: pip Dependency Confusion — Extra Index URL
remediation: Use --index-url (not --extra-index-url) to replace the default PyPI. Or use --extra-index-url with --only-binary :all: and hash verification. Pin packages with hashes in requirements.txt.

title: npm Lifecycle Script Executing External Code
description: Detects npm package.json lifecycle scripts (preinstall, postinstall, install) that download or execute external code, a common malware vector.
remediation: Audit all lifecycle scripts in dependencies. Use npm install --ignore-scripts for initial install, then audit. Consider using npm config set ignore-scripts true globally.

title: pip Install from Git/URL (Unverified Source)
remediation: Pin git dependencies to specific commit hashes, not branches. Use pip install git+https://...@COMMIT_HASH. Prefer publishing internal packages to a private registry.

title: Lockfile Registry Mismatch / Tampering Indicator
remediation: Review lockfile changes in code review — especially resolved URLs. Use npm ci (not npm install) in CI/CD for lockfile integrity. Enable npm audit signatures verification.
