title: Privileged Container Configuration
description: Detects Kubernetes pod or container configurations running with privileged mode enabled, granting full host access. Privileged containers bypass nearly all kernel-level isolation and gain direct access to host devices, filesystems, and kernel modules. This is one of the most dangerous misconfigurations in Kubernetes environments.
impact:
Privileged containers have full access to the host's devices, kernel
modules, and filesystem. An attacker who compromises a privileged container
effectively gains root access to the underlying host node. This is
categorized as a critical finding by CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Pod Security Standards
- Set privileged: false (default) in all container securityContext blocks
- Apply the PSS restricted profile: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1: Minimize the admission of privileged containers
- CIS Docker Benchmark 5.4: Ensure privileged containers are not used

## Helm Chart Hardening
- Override values.yaml: securityContext.privileged=false
- Use helm-values security scanning (e.g., checkov, kubesec)
- Template validation: helm template . | kubesec scan -

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  container.securityContext.privileged == true
  msg := sprintf("Privileged container not allowed: %v", [container.name])
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Use specific capabilities instead of full privilege escalation
- Apply seccomp and AppArmor profiles for fine-grained access control
- Deploy Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper to enforce at admission time
- Use Pod Security Admission controller in enforce mode

title: Privilege Escalation Allowed
description: Detects containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation set to true, enabling processes to gain more privileges than their parent. This allows setuid binaries and other privilege escalation vectors within the container, potentially allowing a non-root process to gain root-level access through SUID/SGID binaries, kernel exploits, or capability manipulation.
impact:
Allows container processes to escalate privileges via setuid binaries,
capabilities, or other kernel mechanisms, potentially gaining root.
This violates the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards restricted profile
and CIS Benchmark 5.2.5.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Pod Security Standards
- Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false in securityContext
- Apply the PSS restricted profile which requires this by default

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.5: Minimize the admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation
- Ensure no-new-privileges is set at the container runtime level

## Helm Chart Hardening
- Default securityContext in values.yaml:
  securityContext:
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    capabilities:
      drop: ["ALL"]

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == true
  msg := sprintf("Privilege escalation not allowed for container: %v", [container.name])
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Drop all capabilities: capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
- Set runAsNonRoot: true
- Remove all SUID/SGID binaries from container images

title: Host Network Namespace Sharing
description: Detects pods configured to use the host's network namespace, PID namespace, or IPC namespace, enabling access to host network interfaces, processes, and inter-process communication. This breaks container isolation boundaries and allows the pod to interact directly with host-level services, sniff traffic, and access host process information.
impact:
Pods sharing host namespaces can access host-level network services,
processes, and IPC mechanisms, bypassing network policies and enabling
lateral movement within the cluster. This violates CIS Kubernetes
Benchmark 5.2.4 (hostNetwork), 5.2.2 (hostPID), and 5.2.3 (hostIPC).
remediation:
## Kubernetes Pod Security Standards
- Set hostNetwork: false (default)
- Set hostPID: false and hostIPC: false
- Apply the PSS baseline profile which prohibits host namespaces

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.4: Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host network namespace
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2: Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host process ID namespace
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.3: Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host IPC namespace

## Helm Chart Hardening
- Set hostNetwork: false as default in values.yaml
- Add conditional checks: {{- if not .Values.hostNetwork }}
- Validate templates: helm template . | conftest test -

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.object.spec.hostNetwork == true
  msg := "Pods with host network access are not allowed"
}
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.object.spec.hostPID == true
  msg := "Pods with host PID namespace are not allowed"
}
```

## Network Policy Enforcement
- Use Kubernetes NetworkPolicies for pod-to-pod communication
- Deploy Calico or Cilium for advanced network policy enforcement
- Use Istio AuthorizationPolicy for service mesh mTLS
- Only use host networking for system-level DaemonSets when required

title: Hardcoded Secrets in YAML Configuration
description: Detects hardcoded passwords, tokens, keys, and credentials in Kubernetes manifests, Docker Compose files, and CI/CD configuration. Secrets committed to version control persist in git history even after removal and can be harvested by anyone with repository access, including through leaked backups, forks, and CI/CD logs.
impact:
Hardcoded secrets in YAML configurations are committed to version control,
exposing credentials to anyone with repository access, including in CI/CD logs.
This violates CIS Benchmark 5.4.1 and can lead to full system compromise
through credential reuse attacks.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Pod Security Standards
- Use Kubernetes Secrets with encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration)
- Never store secrets in ConfigMaps or plain YAML manifests

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.4.1: Prefer using secrets as files over secrets as environment variables
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.4.2: Consider external secret storage

## Helm Chart Hardening
- Use external-secrets operator with Helm charts
- Reference secrets via secretKeyRef in values.yaml
- Use sealed-secrets for GitOps: kubeseal --format yaml < secret.yaml > sealed-secret.yaml
- Never commit values files with actual secrets

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "ConfigMap"
  value := input.request.object.data[key]
  re_match("(?i)(password|secret|token|api.?key)", key)
  msg := sprintf("ConfigMap contains potential secret key: %v", [key])
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Use sealed-secrets for GitOps workflows
- Use HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault
- Use SOPS for encrypting secrets in git
- Implement git pre-commit hooks (detect-secrets, gitleaks)
- Rotate all exposed credentials immediately
- Scan git history: gitleaks detect --source=.

title: CI/CD Pipeline Secret Exposure
description: Detects CI/CD pipeline configurations that may expose secrets through logging, artifact caching, insecure environment variable handling, or command-line argument passing. Secrets printed to CI/CD logs are typically stored indefinitely and accessible to anyone with build log access, third-party integrations, and webhook consumers.
anti_patterns: # safe: value is not a secret
impact:
Secrets printed or logged in CI/CD pipelines are exposed in build logs,
which may be accessible to team members, third-party integrations,
or attackers who compromise the CI/CD system. Build artifacts and
caches containing secrets can persist beyond the build lifecycle.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Pod Security Standards
- Ensure CI/CD-deployed workloads follow PSS restricted profile
- Use OIDC federation instead of long-lived secrets for cloud access

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Software Supply Chain Security Guide: Section 3 - Build Pipelines
- Never echo or print environment variables containing secrets

## Helm Chart Hardening
- Use CI/CD native secret injection for Helm values
- Never pass secrets via helm --set on command line (visible in process lists)
- Use helm-secrets plugin with SOPS encryption

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package cicd.security
deny[msg] {
  step := input.jobs[_].steps[_]
  contains(step.run, "echo")
  contains(step.run, "secrets.")
  msg := "CI/CD step echoes secrets to logs"
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Use ::add-mask:: in GitHub Actions to mask values
- Use CI/CD platform native secret management
- Avoid passing secrets as command-line arguments (visible in process lists)
- Audit CI/CD logs for accidental secret exposure
- Use OIDC tokens instead of static credentials where possible
- Exclude .env files and credential files from artifact uploads
- Implement pipeline security scanning with tools like actionlint

title: Container Running as Root
description: Detects containers without runAsNonRoot or with explicit runAsUser: 0, indicating the container process runs as the root user (UID 0). Running as root inside containers significantly increases the blast radius of a container compromise, as the root user can modify system files, install packages, and exploit kernel vulnerabilities more easily.
anti_patterns: # requires root for binding to port 80
impact:
Containers running as root can modify system files, install packages,
and exploit kernel vulnerabilities for container escapes. This violates
CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.6 and the Pod Security Standards
restricted profile.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Pod Security Standards
- Set runAsNonRoot: true in securityContext
- Set runAsUser to a non-zero UID (e.g., 1000 or 65534)
- Apply the PSS restricted profile which requires runAsNonRoot

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.6: Minimize the admission of root containers
- CIS Docker Benchmark 4.1: Ensure a user for the container has been created

## Helm Chart Hardening
- Default values.yaml:
  podSecurityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    fsGroup: 1000
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  container.securityContext.runAsUser == 0
  msg := sprintf("Container %v must not run as root (UID 0)", [container.name])
}
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  not input.request.object.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg := "Pod must set runAsNonRoot: true"
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Use distroless or minimal base images
- Use USER directive in Dockerfiles
- Use user namespaces for UID remapping
- Set supplementalGroups and fsGroup to non-zero values

title: Missing Resource Limits
description: Detects Kubernetes containers without CPU/memory resource limits, enabling resource exhaustion attacks. Without resource limits, a single container can consume all available node resources, starving other workloads and potentially crashing the node. This is a common vector for denial-of-service attacks within shared Kubernetes clusters.
impact:
Containers without resource limits can consume all available CPU and
memory on a node, causing denial of service for other workloads.
This violates CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.4.3 and can result in
Kubernetes BestEffort QoS class assignment, making the pod the
first candidate for eviction under resource pressure.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Pod Security Standards
- Set both requests and limits for CPU and memory on every container
- Ensure Guaranteed QoS by setting requests equal to limits for critical workloads

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.4.3: Apply Security Context to Your Pods and Containers
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.8: Ensure resource limits are set

## Helm Chart Hardening
- Always define default resources in values.yaml:
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
    limits:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 512Mi
- Add resource validation in Helm chart tests

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  not container.resources.limits.memory
  msg := sprintf("Container %v must have memory limits", [container.name])
}
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  not container.resources.limits.cpu
  msg := sprintf("Container %v must have CPU limits", [container.name])
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Apply LimitRange objects for namespace-level defaults
- Use ResourceQuota for namespace-level totals
- Monitor resource usage with Prometheus/Grafana
- Use VerticalPodAutoscaler (VPA) for right-sizing
- Set ephemeral-storage limits to prevent disk exhaustion

title: Writable Root Filesystem
description: Detects containers without readOnlyRootFilesystem set to true, or with it explicitly set to false, allowing filesystem modifications within the container. Writable root filesystems enable attackers to modify application binaries, install backdoors, write web shells, tamper with configuration files, and establish persistence mechanisms within the container.
impact:
Writable root filesystems allow attackers to modify application binaries,
install backdoors, or write to system directories within the container.
This violates CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.7 and undermines immutable
infrastructure principles.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Pod Security Standards
- Set readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in securityContext
- The PSS restricted profile recommends (but does not require) this setting

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.7: Minimize the admission of containers with writable root filesystems
- CIS Docker Benchmark 5.12: Ensure the container's root filesystem is mounted as read only

## Helm Chart Hardening
- Default values.yaml:
  securityContext:
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
- Define emptyDir volumes for writable paths:
  volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
    - name: cache
      mountPath: /var/cache
  volumes:
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir: {}
    - name: cache
      emptyDir:
        sizeLimit: 100Mi

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  not container.securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem
  msg := sprintf("Container %v must have readOnlyRootFilesystem: true", [container.name])
}
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  container.securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem == false
  msg := sprintf("Container %v has writable root filesystem", [container.name])
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Use emptyDir volumes for writable temporary directories
- Use ConfigMaps and Secrets for configuration files
- Use tmpfs mounts with size limits for temporary data
- Build container images with all necessary files baked in at build time

title: Dangerous Kubernetes Capabilities
description: Detects containers granted dangerous Linux capabilities such as SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, NET_ADMIN, NET_RAW, SYS_MODULE, DAC_OVERRIDE, or ALL. These capabilities provide near-root privileges and can be exploited for container escapes, network sniffing, kernel module loading, and bypassing file permission checks. The principle of least privilege requires dropping all capabilities and only adding specific ones that are strictly necessary.
impact:
Capabilities like SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, and SYS_PTRACE provide near-root
privileges and can be exploited for container escapes. SYS_ADMIN alone
is essentially equivalent to full root privileges. This violates CIS
Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.8 and 5.2.9, and the Pod Security Standards
restricted profile.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Pod Security Standards
- Drop all capabilities by default: capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
- Add only specific needed capabilities (e.g., NET_BIND_SERVICE for port 80)
- Apply the PSS restricted profile which only allows NET_BIND_SERVICE

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.8: Minimize the admission of containers with added capabilities
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.9: Minimize the admission of containers with capabilities assigned
- CIS Docker Benchmark 5.3: Restrict Linux Kernel Capabilities within containers

## Helm Chart Hardening
- Default values.yaml:
  securityContext:
    capabilities:
      drop:
        - ALL
      add: []  # Empty by default, override only when justified
- Document justification for any added capabilities in chart README

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission

# List of dangerous capabilities
dangerous_caps := {"SYS_ADMIN", "SYS_PTRACE", "NET_ADMIN", "NET_RAW",
                    "SYS_MODULE", "DAC_OVERRIDE", "ALL", "SETUID", "SETGID"}

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  cap := container.securityContext.capabilities.add[_]
  dangerous_caps[cap]
  msg := sprintf("Dangerous capability %v added to container %v", [cap, container.name])
}

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
  not container.securityContext.capabilities.drop
  msg := sprintf("Container %v must drop ALL capabilities", [container.name])
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Use Pod Security Standards restricted profile
- Audit capability usage with tools like kube-bench
- Use seccomp profiles to further restrict system calls
- Use AppArmor profiles for mandatory access control
- Apply Calico network policies to restrict NET_RAW at the network level

title: Missing Network Policy
description: Detects Kubernetes namespaces and workloads without associated NetworkPolicy resources, allowing unrestricted pod-to-pod communication across the cluster. By default, Kubernetes does not enforce any network segmentation, meaning every pod can communicate with every other pod. This flat network model enables lateral movement, data exfiltration, and cross-namespace attacks once an attacker compromises a single pod.
impact:
Without NetworkPolicies, all pods can communicate freely with every other
pod in the cluster, enabling lateral movement after an initial compromise.
An attacker who gains access to one pod can reach databases, internal APIs,
and control plane components. This violates CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.3.2
and zero-trust network principles.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Network Policies
- Create default-deny NetworkPolicies for each namespace
- Explicitly allow only required ingress and egress traffic
- Apply namespace-level isolation as a baseline

## Default Deny Policy Template
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: my-namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
```

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.3.2: Ensure that all Namespaces have Network Policies defined

## Additional Remediation
- Use Calico or Cilium for advanced network policy features
- Implement DNS-based egress policies to restrict external communication
- Use Istio AuthorizationPolicy for L7 traffic control
- Audit network policies with kubectl-who-can and network-policy-viewer

title: Exposed Kubernetes Dashboard
description: Detects Kubernetes Dashboard deployments with insecure configurations such as skip-login enabled, exposed via NodePort or LoadBalancer, cluster-admin role bindings, or missing authentication. The Kubernetes Dashboard provides full cluster management capabilities and, when exposed without proper authentication, grants attackers complete control over the cluster including deploying workloads, reading secrets, and deleting resources.
impact:
An exposed Kubernetes Dashboard with skip-login or cluster-admin
privileges gives any network-accessible user full control over
the entire cluster. Attackers can deploy cryptominers, read all
secrets including TLS certificates and database credentials,
delete critical workloads, and establish persistent backdoors.
The Tesla cryptojacking incident (2018) was caused by exactly
this misconfiguration.
remediation:
## Secure Dashboard Configuration
- Remove --enable-skip-login flag
- Remove --enable-insecure-login flag
- Use token-based authentication with RBAC
- Never bind the dashboard ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin

## Access Control
- Use kubectl proxy for local access instead of NodePort/LoadBalancer
- Deploy an OAuth2 proxy (e.g., oauth2-proxy, dex) in front of the dashboard
- Bind dashboard ServiceAccount to namespace-scoped roles only

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 1.2.6: Ensure that the --enable-admission-plugins argument includes NodeRestriction
- Restrict dashboard access to cluster administrators only

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Deployment"
  contains(input.request.object.metadata.name, "dashboard")
  args := input.request.object.spec.template.spec.containers[_].args
  arg := args[_]
  contains(arg, "--enable-skip-login")
  msg := "Dashboard skip-login must not be enabled"
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Consider removing the dashboard entirely in production
- Use Lens, k9s, or headlamp as safer alternatives
- Apply NetworkPolicy to restrict dashboard access to admin CIDRs only

title: Missing Pod Disruption Budget
description: Detects Kubernetes Deployments, StatefulSets, and ReplicaSets without corresponding PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) resources. Without a PDB, voluntary disruptions such as node drains, cluster upgrades, and autoscaler scale-downs can simultaneously terminate all replicas of a workload, causing application downtime. In adversarial scenarios, an attacker with node-level access can trigger mass pod evictions to cause denial of service.
impact:
Without PodDisruptionBudgets, cluster operations like node drains,
upgrades, and autoscaler events can terminate all replicas of a
workload simultaneously, causing application downtime. For
stateful workloads, this can result in data loss or corruption.
This is critical for meeting SLA and uptime requirements.
remediation:
## PodDisruptionBudget Configuration
- Create a PDB for every production Deployment and StatefulSet with > 1 replica
- Use minAvailable or maxUnavailable to guarantee minimum availability

## PDB Template
```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: my-app-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
```

## Best Practices
- Set minAvailable to at least 1 for critical workloads
- Use percentage-based values for dynamic scaling: minAvailable: "50%"
- Ensure PDB selector labels match the Deployment/StatefulSet pod template labels
- Test PDB effectiveness: kubectl drain node --dry-run

## Additional Remediation
- Use Helm chart helpers to auto-generate PDBs alongside Deployments
- Enforce PDB creation via OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno policies
- Monitor PDB violations in cluster events
- Set appropriate terminationGracePeriodSeconds for graceful shutdown

title: Insecure Service Account Token Auto-Mount
description: Detects pods and service accounts with automountServiceAccountToken set to true (or not explicitly disabled), which automatically mounts the Kubernetes API token inside every pod. This token grants API access corresponding to the service account's RBAC permissions and can be stolen by an attacker who compromises the pod to escalate privileges, enumerate cluster resources, and move laterally within the cluster.
impact:
Auto-mounted service account tokens provide every pod with API
credentials that can be used to query the Kubernetes API, list
secrets, create workloads, and escalate privileges depending on
the service account's RBAC bindings. This violates the principle
of least privilege and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.1.6.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Service Account Security
- Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on all pods that do not need API access
- Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on service accounts by default
- Use projected volume tokens with audience and expiration constraints

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.1.5: Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.1.6: Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted where necessary

## Pod-Level Disable Template
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-pod
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:latest
```

## OPA Rego Policy
```rego
package kubernetes.admission
deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  not input.request.object.spec.automountServiceAccountToken == false
  msg := "Pods must set automountServiceAccountToken: false"
}
```

## Additional Remediation
- Use bound service account tokens (TokenRequest API) with short TTL
- Apply least-privilege RBAC roles to service accounts
- Block API server access with NetworkPolicies where possible
- Use Workload Identity (GKE) or IAM Roles for Service Accounts (EKS) instead

title: Missing Ingress TLS Configuration
description: Detects Kubernetes Ingress resources without TLS configuration, exposing web traffic in cleartext over HTTP. Without TLS termination at the ingress level, all traffic between clients and the cluster is transmitted unencrypted, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks, credential interception, session hijacking, and data exfiltration. This applies to both external and internal ingress endpoints.
impact:
Ingress resources without TLS expose all web traffic in cleartext,
enabling interception of authentication credentials, session tokens,
API keys, and sensitive data. This violates PCI-DSS Requirement 4.1
(encrypt transmission of cardholder data), HIPAA security rules, and
general security best practices for transport encryption.
remediation:
## Kubernetes Ingress TLS Configuration
- Add TLS section to every Ingress resource
- Enable SSL redirect annotations to force HTTPS
- Use cert-manager for automated certificate management

## TLS Ingress Template
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: my-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - app.example.com
      secretName: app-tls-cert
  rules:
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: my-service
                port:
                  number: 443
```

## CIS Benchmark References
- Ensure all externally facing services use TLS 1.2+
- Configure HSTS headers for web applications
- Use end-to-end encryption from ingress to backend pods

## Additional Remediation
- Deploy cert-manager with Let's Encrypt for auto-renewal
- Use HSTS preloading for critical domains
- Enforce TLS via OPA/Kyverno admission policies
- Monitor certificate expiration with cert-manager alerts

title: Unencrypted etcd Data at Rest
description: Detects Kubernetes API server and etcd configurations that lack encryption at rest for stored data. By default, Kubernetes stores all data (including Secrets, ConfigMaps, and custom resources) in etcd as base64-encoded plaintext. Without an EncryptionConfiguration specifying AES-CBC, AES-GCM, or KMS-based encryption, anyone with direct etcd access or etcd backup access can read all cluster secrets in cleartext.
impact:
Without encryption at rest, all Kubernetes Secrets (database passwords,
TLS certificates, API keys, service account tokens) are stored as
base64-encoded plaintext in etcd. Anyone with direct etcd access,
etcd backup access, or host filesystem access to etcd data directories
can decode and steal all cluster secrets. This violates CIS Kubernetes
Benchmark 1.2.29 and compliance frameworks requiring data-at-rest
encryption (PCI-DSS 3.4, HIPAA 164.312(a)(2)(iv)).
remediation:
## Kubernetes Encryption at Rest
- Create an EncryptionConfiguration with aescbc, aesgcm, or kms provider
- Pass --encryption-provider-config to kube-apiserver
- Ensure the encryption provider is listed BEFORE identity in the providers list

## EncryptionConfiguration Template
```yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - aescbc:
          keys:
            - name: key1
              secret: <base64-encoded-32-byte-key>
      - identity: {}
```

## CIS Benchmark References
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 1.2.29: Ensure that the --encryption-provider-config argument is set as appropriate
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 1.2.30: Ensure that encryption providers are appropriately configured

## KMS-Based Encryption (Recommended for Production)
- Use AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, or Azure Key Vault for key management
- Configure KMS provider plugin for automatic key rotation
- Ensure etcd data directory has restrictive file permissions (700)

## Additional Remediation
- Encrypt existing secrets: kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -
- Rotate encryption keys periodically
- Enable etcd TLS for transport encryption
- Restrict etcd access to API server nodes only
- Monitor etcd access logs for unauthorized reads

title: Missing ValidateAntiForgeryToken in ASP.NET MVC
description: Detects ASP.NET MVC controller actions that accept POST, PUT, or DELETE requests without the [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] attribute. Without this protection, forms and state-changing endpoints are vulnerable to cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attacks where malicious sites can submit forged requests on behalf of authenticated users.
impact:
Without CSRF protection, an attacker can create a malicious webpage
that submits forms or AJAX requests to the vulnerable application.
When an authenticated user visits the attacker's page, the browser
automatically includes the authentication cookie. The application
processes the request as a legitimate action by the user, enabling
unauthorized fund transfers, account modifications, data deletion,
and privilege changes.

title: Kestrel Server Exposed Without Reverse Proxy
description: Detects ASP.NET Core applications that configure Kestrel to listen on public interfaces or high-traffic ports without being behind a reverse proxy (nginx, IIS, or a cloud load balancer). Kestrel is designed as an edge-case web server and lacks the hardening, rate limiting, request filtering, and DoS protection that a reverse proxy provides. Direct exposure risks denial of service and exploitation of edge-case HTTP parsing vulnerabilities.
impact:
Exposing Kestrel directly to the internet without a reverse proxy
removes multiple layers of defense. Kestrel lacks advanced request
filtering, rate limiting, connection draining, and slow-loris attack
protection that servers like nginx or IIS provide. Attackers can
exploit HTTP parsing edge cases, perform denial-of-service attacks
with relatively low bandwidth, and bypass security controls that
would normally be enforced at the reverse proxy layer.

title: Detailed Errors Exposed in Production ASP.NET Application
description: Detects ASP.NET applications that display detailed error information in production, including stack traces, source code, and configuration details. This occurs when UseDeveloperExceptionPage() is used without environment checks, custom error pages are disabled, or customErrors/httpErrors are set to Off in web.config.
impact:
Detailed error pages in production reveal full stack traces with source
code, file paths, database connection strings, internal class names,
method signatures, and configuration values. This information enables
targeted attacks by revealing the application's internal structure,
technology stack, and potential vulnerability points. SQL exceptions
may reveal database schemas. File path exceptions reveal server layout.

title: Missing HTTPS Redirection in ASP.NET Application
description: Detects ASP.NET applications that do not enforce HTTPS through UseHttpsRedirection(), UseHsts(), or the [RequireHttps] attribute. Without HTTPS enforcement, sensitive data including credentials, session tokens, and personal information is transmitted in cleartext, vulnerable to interception by network attackers via man-in-the-middle attacks, Wi-Fi eavesdropping, and traffic sniffing.
impact:
Without HTTPS enforcement, all data transmitted between the client
and server is vulnerable to interception. Attackers on the same
network can capture login credentials, session cookies, API tokens,
personal data, and financial information. This violates PCI DSS,
HIPAA, GDPR, and other compliance frameworks that require encryption
in transit for sensitive data.

title: Insecure CORS Policy in ASP.NET Core
description: Detects ASP.NET Core applications that configure CORS with overly permissive policies, such as AllowAnyOrigin(), AllowAnyMethod(), or combining AllowAnyOrigin with AllowCredentials. This enables any website to make cross-origin requests to the API, potentially with the user's authentication cookies, leading to data theft and unauthorized actions.
impact:
An insecure CORS policy allows any website to make cross-origin
requests and read responses from the ASP.NET API. When combined
with AllowCredentials(), the attacker's page can make authenticated
requests using the victim's session cookies. This enables complete
data theft, account manipulation, and unauthorized API access from
any domain the attacker controls.

title: Over-Posting via Model Binding Without Bind Attribute in ASP.NET
description: Detects ASP.NET MVC and Web API controllers that bind request data directly to domain models without using [Bind], view models (DTOs), or explicit property whitelisting. This enables mass assignment (over-posting) attacks where attackers add extra fields to requests that modify properties the developer did not intend to be user-settable, such as IsAdmin, Price, or AccountBalance.
impact:
Mass assignment (over-posting) allows attackers to modify model
properties that should not be user-settable. Attackers can set
IsAdmin=true to gain admin access, modify Price or Balance fields
for financial fraud, change ownership fields to take over resources,
or modify internal state fields to bypass business logic. Entity
Framework auto-saves these changes to the database.

title: Missing Helmet Middleware in Express Application
description: Detects Express.js applications that initialize an Express server without applying the Helmet middleware. Helmet sets various HTTP security headers (X-Content-Type-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options, etc.) that protect against clickjacking, MIME-type sniffing, and other common web vulnerabilities. Omitting Helmet leaves the application exposed to a wide range of client-side attacks by default.
impact:
Without Helmet, the Express application serves responses lacking critical
HTTP security headers. Attackers can exploit this to perform clickjacking
attacks (missing X-Frame-Options), MIME-type confusion (missing
X-Content-Type-Options), and downgrade attacks (missing HSTS). This is
classified as a security misconfiguration that affects every response.

title: Disabled or Overly Permissive CORS Configuration in Express
description: Detects Express.js applications that configure CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) with a wildcard origin or reflect any origin without validation. This allows any website to make credentialed cross-origin requests to the application, enabling data theft, CSRF bypass, and unauthorized API access from attacker-controlled domains.
impact:
An overly permissive CORS configuration allows any website to make
authenticated cross-origin requests to the API. When combined with
credentials: true, attackers can steal sensitive user data, perform
actions on behalf of users, and bypass CSRF protections. This
effectively turns every authenticated endpoint into an exploitable
attack surface.

title: Trust Proxy Misconfiguration in Express Application
description: Detects Express.js applications that improperly configure or fail to configure the 'trust proxy' setting. When Express runs behind a reverse proxy (nginx, AWS ALB, Cloudflare), incorrect trust proxy settings can lead to IP spoofing, rate limit bypass, and incorrect protocol detection. Setting trust proxy to true without specifying hops trusts all proxies, allowing X-Forwarded-For header manipulation.
impact:
When trust proxy is set to true without specifying the number of proxy
hops, Express trusts all values in the X-Forwarded-For chain. An attacker
can inject arbitrary IP addresses into this header, bypassing rate
limiters, IP-based access controls, geo-restrictions, and audit logging.
This can enable brute-force attacks, account takeover, and forensic
evidence tampering.

title: Body-Parser Size Limit Missing or Excessive in Express
description: Detects Express.js applications that use body-parser or express.json() without configuring a request body size limit, or with an excessively large limit. Without a limit, attackers can send extremely large payloads causing denial of service through memory exhaustion, event loop blocking, or disk consumption.
impact:
Without body size limits, attackers can send multi-gigabyte request
bodies that consume all available memory, causing the Node.js process
to crash with an out-of-memory error. This creates a denial of service
condition. Even with automatic restarts, sustained attacks can keep the
service unavailable. Large JSON payloads can also block the event loop
during parsing.

title: Next.js API Route Without Authentication Check
description: Detects Next.js API routes (pages/api/ or app/api/) that handle requests without any form of authentication or authorization check. Unprotected API routes expose server-side functionality directly to the internet, allowing unauthorized access to data and operations. Next.js API routes are publicly accessible by default and require explicit auth middleware.
impact:
Unprotected Next.js API routes allow any unauthenticated user to access
server-side functionality. Attackers can read sensitive data, modify
records, delete resources, and invoke privileged operations. Since Next.js
API routes run server-side with full access to databases, environment
variables, and internal services, the impact can be catastrophic.

title: getServerSideProps Data Exposure in Next.js
description: Detects Next.js pages using getServerSideProps that pass excessive or sensitive data to the client-side page component via props. Data returned from getServerSideProps is serialized to JSON and embedded in the HTML page source, making it visible to anyone who views the page source. Developers often inadvertently expose database fields, internal IDs, secrets, or user data from other accounts.
impact:
Data returned from getServerSideProps is serialized and embedded in the
HTML page within the __NEXT_DATA__ script tag. Any data included in props
is visible to the end user by viewing page source. This can leak database
passwords, API keys, internal user data, and fields from other users'
records. This data exposure violates data privacy regulations and may
enable further attacks.

title: Unsafe Redirect in Next.js Middleware
description: Detects Next.js middleware that performs redirects based on user-controlled input without proper validation. Attackers can manipulate query parameters, headers, or cookies to redirect users to malicious external sites, enabling phishing, credential theft, and OAuth token interception. Open redirects in middleware affect all routes matched by the middleware matcher.
impact:
Open redirect vulnerabilities in Next.js middleware affect all routes
covered by the middleware matcher. Attackers can construct URLs that
appear to point to the legitimate application but redirect to malicious
sites. This enables convincing phishing attacks, OAuth token theft via
redirect_uri manipulation, and bypass of security controls that trust
the application domain.

title: SSR Injection via dangerouslySetInnerHTML in Next.js
description: Detects Next.js components that use dangerouslySetInnerHTML with data sourced from user input, database queries, or external APIs without proper sanitization. In a server-side rendering context, this can lead to stored XSS, reflected XSS, and in some cases server-side template injection. Because Next.js renders on the server first, injected scripts are included in the initial HTML response.
impact:
Using dangerouslySetInnerHTML with unsanitized data in Next.js enables
cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. Since Next.js performs server-side
rendering, the malicious script is embedded in the initial HTML response,
making it effective even against users with JavaScript-heavy client-side
protections. Attackers can steal session cookies, redirect users,
modify page content, and perform actions on behalf of the victim.

title: Dependency Confusion - Private Package Name Leak
description: Detects package.json files that may be vulnerable to dependency confusion attacks by using unscoped private package names
impact: Attackers can publish malicious packages with the same name to public registries
remediation: Use scoped packages (@org/package), set private: true, configure .npmrc with registry

title: Dependency Confusion - requirements.txt Private Package
description: Detects Python requirements.txt with packages that may exist only in private registries
impact: Extra index URLs alongside PyPI enable dependency confusion attacks
remediation: Use --index-url (not --extra-index-url) for private registries, or use pip-compile

title: Dependency Confusion - .npmrc Misconfiguration
description: Detects .npmrc configurations that don't properly scope private registries
impact: Global registry override can expose both public and private packages to confusion
remediation: Use scoped registry config: @myorg:registry=https://private-registry/

title: Supply Chain - Malicious Install Script
description: Detects suspicious pre/post install scripts in package.json
impact: Malicious install scripts execute code as soon as a package is installed
remediation: Audit install scripts, use npm audit, consider --ignore-scripts flag

title: Supply Chain - Typosquatting Indicators
description: Detects dependencies that look like typosquatted versions of popular packages
impact: Typosquatted packages install malicious code instead of the intended library
remediation: Double-check package names, use npm audit, enable package-lock.json

title: Spring Security Filter Chain Bypass
description: Detects Spring Security misconfigurations that allow filter chain bypass
impact: Security filter bypass allows unauthenticated access to protected endpoints
remediation: Always end filter chain with .anyRequest().authenticated(), use requestMatchers

title: Spring Actuator Exposure
description: Detects exposed Spring Boot Actuator endpoints without authentication
impact: Exposed actuator endpoints leak sensitive config, environment vars, and heap dumps
remediation: Restrict exposure to health/info only, require authentication for all actuators

title: Spring SpEL Injection
description: Detects Spring Expression Language injection via user input
impact: SpEL injection enables arbitrary code execution on Spring servers
remediation: Use SimpleEvaluationContext (read-only), never parse user input as SpEL

title: Express.js Middleware Order Bypass
description: Detects routes defined before authentication/authorization middleware
impact: Routes before auth middleware are accessible without authentication
remediation: Define authentication middleware before any route handlers

title: Express.js Uncaught Error Information Leak
description: Detects Express error handlers that expose stack traces in production
impact: Stack traces in error responses reveal internal code structure and file paths
remediation: Return generic error messages in production, log details server-side only

title: Flask Debug Mode in Production
description: Detects Flask debug mode enabled which exposes Werkzeug debugger
impact: Flask debug mode exposes interactive Werkzeug debugger allowing RCE
remediation: Never enable debug mode in production, use environment variables for config

title: Flask Secret Key Weakness
description: Detects weak or hardcoded Flask secret keys
impact: Weak secret keys allow forging Flask session cookies to bypass authentication
remediation: Use os.urandom(32).hex() or os.environ.get('SECRET_KEY') with a strong random value

title: Next.js Server-Side Data Exposure
description: Detects sensitive data in getServerSideProps/getStaticProps passing to client
impact: Server-side props are serialized to HTML and visible in page source
remediation: Never pass sensitive data in props; filter/transform server data before returning

title: Next.js API Route Without Authentication
description: Detects Next.js API routes that handle sensitive operations without authentication checks
impact: Unprotected API routes allow unauthorized data manipulation
remediation: Add authentication middleware or check session/token in all mutating API routes

title: Django Raw SQL Without Parameters
description: Detects Django raw SQL queries using string formatting instead of parameters
impact: SQL injection via Django ORM raw() bypasses all ORM safety features
remediation: Use parameterized queries: Model.objects.raw('SELECT ... WHERE id=%s', [user_id])

title: Django Security Middleware Disabled
description: Detects disabled Django security middleware in settings
impact: Disabled security middleware removes defense-in-depth protections
remediation: Enable all security middleware in production: SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT=True, etc.

title: Flask Debug Mode Enabled in Production
description: Detects Flask applications that run with debug mode enabled, which exposes the interactive Werkzeug debugger. This debugger allows remote code execution through its interactive console, provides full stack traces with source code, and reveals environment variables. Debug mode should never be enabled in production as it provides attackers a direct path to server compromise.
impact:
When Flask debug mode is enabled in production, the Werkzeug debugger
exposes an interactive Python console accessible to anyone who can
trigger an application error. This allows remote code execution,
reading files from the server, accessing environment variables
(including secrets), and full server compromise. Detailed stack traces
also reveal application source code, file paths, and internal logic.
remediation:
Ensure debug mode is disabled in production:

```python
import os
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

# Never hardcode debug=True
app.config['DEBUG'] = False

# Use environment-specific configuration
class ProductionConfig:
    DEBUG = False
    TESTING = False

class DevelopmentConfig:
    DEBUG = True

config = {
    'production': ProductionConfig,
    'development': DevelopmentConfig,
}

app.config.from_object(config[os.environ.get('FLASK_ENV', 'production')])

# Use a production WSGI server
# gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 app:app
```

title: Missing CORS Configuration in Flask Application
description: Detects Flask applications that either lack CORS configuration entirely or configure flask-cors with overly permissive settings such as wildcard origins, allowing any domain to make cross-origin requests. Without proper CORS configuration, the API is either completely inaccessible to legitimate frontends or open to abuse from malicious origins.
impact:
Overly permissive CORS configuration allows malicious websites to make
authenticated cross-origin requests to the Flask API. When combined
with supports_credentials=True, attackers can steal session cookies,
CSRF tokens, and user data. A wildcard CORS policy effectively
disables the same-origin policy protection for the API.
remediation:
Configure Flask-CORS with explicit origin whitelist:

```python
from flask import Flask
from flask_cors import CORS

app = Flask(__name__)

CORS(app, origins=[
    'https://app.example.com',
    'https://admin.example.com',
], supports_credentials=True,
   allow_headers=['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
   methods=['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE'])
```

title: Flask Secret Key Hardcoded in Source Code
description: Detects Flask applications that define the SECRET_KEY configuration value directly in source code rather than loading it from a secure external source. The secret key is critical for signing session cookies, CSRF tokens, and other cryptographic operations. A hardcoded key committed to version control allows anyone with repository access to forge sessions and bypass security mechanisms.
impact:
A hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY allows attackers with source code access
to forge session cookies, impersonate any user including administrators,
bypass CSRF protections, and decrypt any data encrypted with the key.
Since the key is in version control, all developers, CI/CD systems,
and anyone with repository access can exploit this vulnerability.
remediation:
Load the secret key from a secure external source:

```python
import os
import secrets
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

# Load from environment variable (preferred)
app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = os.environ['SECRET_KEY']

# Or generate securely if not set (development only)
app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = os.environ.get(
    'SECRET_KEY',
    secrets.token_hex(32)  # Only for development!
)

# For production, use a secret manager:
# - AWS Secrets Manager
# - HashiCorp Vault
# - Azure Key Vault
# - GCP Secret Manager
```

title: Unsafe File Upload Handling in Flask
description: Detects Flask applications that handle file uploads without proper validation of file type, size, content, and storage location. Unsafe file upload handling can lead to arbitrary file write, path traversal, remote code execution via uploaded web shells, and denial of service through oversized files. Flask's request.files does not enforce any restrictions by default.
impact:
Unsafe file upload handling allows attackers to upload malicious files
such as web shells, server-side scripts, or oversized files. Without
filename sanitization, path traversal can write files anywhere on the
filesystem. Without extension validation, executable files can be
uploaded to web-accessible directories. Without size limits, denial
of service through resource exhaustion is possible.
remediation:
Implement comprehensive file upload validation:

```python
import os
import uuid
from flask import Flask, request
from werkzeug.utils import secure_filename

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config['MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH'] = 5 * 1024 * 1024  # 5MB
ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS = {'png', 'jpg', 'jpeg', 'gif', 'pdf'}
UPLOAD_FOLDER = '/var/uploads'  # Outside web root

def allowed_file(filename):
    return '.' in filename and \
           filename.rsplit('.', 1)[1].lower() in ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS

@app.route('/upload', methods=['POST'])
def upload_file():
    file = request.files.get('file')
    if not file or not allowed_file(file.filename):
        return 'Invalid file', 400

    # Use UUID filename to prevent path traversal
    ext = secure_filename(file.filename).rsplit('.', 1)[1].lower()
    safe_name = f"{uuid.uuid4().hex}.{ext}"
    file.save(os.path.join(UPLOAD_FOLDER, safe_name))
    return 'Uploaded', 200
```

title: Django DEBUG=True in Production Settings
description: Detects Django applications with the DEBUG setting set to True in production configuration files. When DEBUG is True, Django displays detailed error pages with full stack traces, local variables, settings values, and SQL queries. This exposes sensitive application internals, database credentials, API keys, and code paths to any user who triggers an error.
impact:
With DEBUG=True in production, any unhandled exception displays a
detailed debug page revealing the full Python traceback, local
variables (potentially including passwords), Django settings (including
SECRET_KEY and database credentials), installed applications, and
middleware stack. The 404 debug page reveals all URL patterns. This
information enables sophisticated follow-up attacks.
remediation:
Ensure DEBUG is False in production:

```python
# settings/production.py
import os
from decouple import config

DEBUG = False  # Always False in production

# Or safely from environment:
DEBUG = config('DEBUG', default=False, cast=bool)

# Ensure ALLOWED_HOSTS is set (required when DEBUG=False)
ALLOWED_HOSTS = config('ALLOWED_HOSTS', cast=lambda v: [
    s.strip() for s in v.split(',')
])
```

title: Django ALLOWED_HOSTS Wildcard Configuration
description: Detects Django applications with ALLOWED_HOSTS set to a wildcard ['*'] or empty list (with DEBUG=False). The ALLOWED_HOSTS setting validates the Host header to prevent HTTP Host header attacks. A wildcard allows any Host header value, enabling cache poisoning, password reset poisoning, and server-side request routing attacks.
impact:
A wildcard ALLOWED_HOSTS setting allows attackers to inject arbitrary
Host headers. This enables password reset poisoning (reset links sent
to attacker's domain), cache poisoning (malicious content cached for
other users), and SSRF through URL generation functions that trust the
Host header. Combined with Django's URL building functions, this can
redirect users to malicious sites.
remediation:
Set ALLOWED_HOSTS to specific, trusted hostnames:

```python
# settings/production.py
ALLOWED_HOSTS = [
    'example.com',
    'www.example.com',
    'api.example.com',
]

# Or from environment variable:
ALLOWED_HOSTS = os.environ.get('ALLOWED_HOSTS', '').split(',')

# Never use wildcard in production
# ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']  # NEVER DO THIS
```

title: Unsafe mark_safe Usage in Django Templates
description: Detects Django code that uses mark_safe() or the |safe template filter with data that originates from user input, database fields, or external sources without prior sanitization. mark_safe() tells Django's template engine to skip HTML escaping for the marked string, creating XSS vulnerabilities when applied to untrusted data.
impact:
Using mark_safe() with unsanitized user data creates cross-site
scripting vulnerabilities. Django's auto-escaping is the primary
defense against XSS, and mark_safe explicitly bypasses it. Attackers
can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript that execute in victims'
browsers, enabling session theft, account takeover, and data exfiltration.
remediation: Use format_html() instead of mark_safe() for dynamic content: ```python from django.utils.html import format_html, escape # BAD - XSS vulnerable # return mark_safe(f'{name}') # GOOD - auto-escapes arguments return format_html('{}', url, name) # For rich text from users, use a sanitization library: import nh3 clean_html = nh3.clean( user_html, tags={'b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'a', 'p', 'br', 'ul', 'li'}, attributes={'a': {'href', 'title'}}, ) return mark_safe(clean_html) ```

title: Missing Security Middleware in Django Settings
description: Detects Django applications that are missing critical security middleware from the MIDDLEWARE setting. Django provides built-in middleware for CSRF protection, clickjacking prevention, XSS filtering, HTTPS enforcement, and HSTS. Omitting these middleware components leaves the application vulnerable to common web attacks that Django is designed to prevent.
impact:
Missing Django security middleware exposes the application to multiple
attack vectors. Without CsrfViewMiddleware, all POST endpoints are
vulnerable to cross-site request forgery. Without SecurityMiddleware,
HSTS and HTTPS redirect are disabled. Without XFrameOptionsMiddleware,
pages can be embedded in iframes for clickjacking attacks. These are
foundational protections that Django provides by default.
remediation:
Ensure all security middleware is properly configured:

```python
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware',
]

# Security settings
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000
SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS = True
SECURE_HSTS_PRELOAD = True
SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF = True
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True
X_FRAME_OPTIONS = 'DENY'
```

title: Missing Authentication Middleware on Gin Router Groups
description: Detects Gin web framework route groups that handle sensitive operations without authentication middleware. Gin uses router groups to organize routes, and middleware is applied per-group. When route groups for administrative, user, or API endpoints lack authentication middleware, all routes within that group become publicly accessible, exposing sensitive functionality to unauthenticated users.
impact:
Missing authentication middleware on Gin route groups exposes all
routes within the group to unauthenticated access. Attackers can
read sensitive data, modify records, delete resources, and perform
administrative operations without any credentials. Since Gin route
groups often organize related API endpoints, a single missing
middleware call can expose an entire feature area.

title: Insecure CORS Configuration in Gin Application
description: Detects Gin applications that configure CORS with overly permissive settings using the gin-contrib/cors package or manual header setting. This includes wildcard origins, reflecting all origins, allowing all methods and headers, or combining wildcards with credentials. Permissive CORS in Go APIs enables cross-origin data theft and CSRF bypass.
impact:
Overly permissive CORS configuration allows any website to make
cross-origin requests to the Gin API. When AllowCredentials is true,
the attacker's page can include the victim's cookies, enabling theft
of authenticated API responses. This effectively bypasses same-origin
policy and enables data exfiltration, unauthorized API access, and
CSRF attacks against the Go backend.

title: Gin Debug Mode Enabled in Production
description: Detects Gin applications running in debug mode (gin.DebugMode) in production deployments. Debug mode enables verbose logging of all routes, request details, and internal framework operations. It also disables certain performance optimizations and can expose route structure, middleware chain details, and internal error messages to attackers who trigger errors or observe response headers.
impact:
Gin debug mode in production logs all registered routes with their
handlers on startup, making route discovery trivial for attackers
with access to logs. Debug mode also outputs detailed request/response
information, may include verbose error messages in responses, and
disables performance optimizations. While less critical than Flask or
Django debug modes, it still constitutes information disclosure and
security misconfiguration.

title: Missing CSRF Middleware in Echo Application
description: Detects Echo web framework applications that handle state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE) without CSRF middleware. Echo does not enable CSRF protection by default, and the middleware must be explicitly added. Without CSRF protection, forms and API endpoints that use cookie-based authentication are vulnerable to cross-site request forgery attacks.
impact:
Without CSRF middleware, Echo applications using cookie-based or
session-based authentication are vulnerable to cross-site request
forgery attacks. Attackers can create malicious pages that submit
forms to the Echo API, executing state-changing operations with
the victim's session. This enables unauthorized fund transfers,
account modifications, data deletion, and privilege changes.

title: Permissive CORS Configuration in Echo Application
description: Detects Echo framework applications with overly permissive CORS configurations using the echo middleware.CORSWithConfig or manual header setting. This includes wildcard origins, allowing all methods and headers, or reflecting any origin with credentials. Permissive CORS in Echo APIs exposes authenticated endpoints to cross-origin data theft.
impact:
Permissive CORS configuration in Echo allows any website to make
cross-origin requests and read API responses. Combined with
AllowCredentials, attackers can make authenticated requests using
the victim's session cookies. This bypasses the same-origin policy,
enabling unauthorized data access, account manipulation, and
exfiltration of sensitive API responses.

title: Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints in Echo
description: Detects Echo applications that have login, registration, password reset, or OTP verification endpoints without rate limiting middleware. Without rate limiting, these endpoints are vulnerable to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, account enumeration, and denial of service. Authentication endpoints are prime targets for automated attacks and require explicit rate limiting to be secure.
impact:
Without rate limiting on authentication endpoints, attackers can
perform brute-force attacks at thousands of attempts per second.
A 6-digit OTP can be brute-forced within minutes. Credential
stuffing attacks using leaked password databases can compromise
accounts with reused passwords. Password reset endpoints without
rate limiting enable email bombing and account enumeration.
This directly leads to account takeover.

title: Laravel APP_DEBUG=true in Production Environment
description: Detects Laravel applications with APP_DEBUG set to true in production configuration. When debug mode is enabled, Laravel displays detailed error pages via Ignition or Whoops, revealing full stack traces, database queries with parameters, environment variables (including APP_KEY, database passwords, API secrets), and the complete application configuration. This has historically led to critical RCE vulnerabilities such as CVE-2021-3129 (Ignition RCE).
impact:
Laravel debug mode in production exposes APP_KEY (allowing session
forgery and encryption bypass), database credentials, mail server
passwords, third-party API keys, and full application source code
via stack traces. The Ignition debug page has historically been
exploitable for RCE (CVE-2021-3129). An exposed APP_KEY alone allows
attackers to forge session cookies and decrypt all application data.

title: Laravel Mass Assignment Without Fillable or Guarded
description: Detects Laravel Eloquent models that accept mass assignment without defining $fillable or $guarded properties. Without these protections, attackers can modify any database column through request input, including fields like is_admin, role, password, balance, and owner_id. Models with $guarded = [] (empty array) are also vulnerable as they explicitly disable all protection.
impact:
Without mass assignment protection, attackers can set any column in
the database by including extra fields in their request. Common
exploits include setting is_admin=true for privilege escalation,
modifying price/balance for financial fraud, changing owner_id for
resource theft, and setting verification flags to bypass checks.
Laravel's Eloquent ORM processes all provided fields by default.

title: Unvalidated File Upload in Laravel
description: Detects Laravel controllers that handle file uploads without proper validation of file type, MIME type, size, and content. Laravel's request file handling stores uploaded files without restriction unless validation rules are explicitly applied. Missing validation enables attackers to upload PHP web shells, bypass file type restrictions using double extensions, and exploit path traversal vulnerabilities.
impact:
Unvalidated file uploads allow attackers to upload PHP web shells
that execute arbitrary commands on the server. If files are stored
in web-accessible directories (public/), the attacker can execute
the uploaded PHP file directly. Without filename sanitization, path
traversal attacks can overwrite critical files. Without size limits,
attackers can exhaust disk space.

title: Symfony Debug Mode Enabled in Production
description: Detects Symfony applications that run with kernel.debug set to true or the Symfony Web Profiler and Debug Toolbar enabled in production. The debug mode exposes the Web Profiler which reveals detailed request and response information, database queries, security context, services container, and environment variables. The debug toolbar provides real-time introspection of every request component.
impact:
Symfony debug mode in production exposes the Web Profiler at /_profiler/
which reveals complete request/response details, database queries with
parameters, security token contents, logged-in user details, service
container configuration, environment variables, and mail contents.
Detailed exception pages reveal source code, file paths, and the full
call stack with local variables.
remediation:
Ensure debug mode is disabled in production:

```bash
# .env.local (or server environment)
APP_ENV=prod
APP_DEBUG=0
```

```yaml
# config/packages/prod/web_profiler.yaml
web_profiler:
    toolbar: false
    intercept_redirects: false
framework:
    profiler:
        enabled: false
        collect: false
```

```php
// public/index.php
$kernel = new Kernel(
    $_SERVER['APP_ENV'] ?? 'prod',
    (bool) ($_SERVER['APP_DEBUG'] ?? false)
);
```

title: Missing CSRF Token Validation in Symfony Forms
description: Detects Symfony applications where CSRF protection is disabled on forms or controllers that handle state-changing operations. Symfony provides built-in CSRF protection through the CsrfExtension and CSRF token manager, but this protection must be explicitly enabled or can be accidentally disabled through form configuration or missing annotations.
impact:
Without CSRF protection, any website can submit forms to the Symfony
application on behalf of authenticated users. Attackers craft hidden
forms that auto-submit when victims visit their page. The browser
includes the session cookie, and the application processes the request
as legitimate. This enables unauthorized transactions, data
modifications, and account changes.

title: Unsafe Twig raw Filter Usage in Symfony Templates
description: Detects Symfony Twig templates that use the |raw filter or {% autoescape false %} with data that originates from user input, database records, or external APIs. The |raw filter disables Twig's automatic output escaping, which is the primary defense against XSS in Symfony applications. Using |raw with untrusted data creates XSS vulnerabilities.
impact:
Using the |raw filter with untrusted data disables Twig's automatic
HTML escaping, allowing attacker-controlled HTML and JavaScript to be
rendered in the browser. This enables stored XSS (from database
content), reflected XSS (from request parameters), and DOM-based XSS.
Attackers can steal session cookies, redirect users, modify page
content, and perform actions as the victim.

title: Spring Security permitAll Misconfiguration
description: Detects Spring Security configurations that use permitAll() on sensitive endpoints or overly broad URL patterns, effectively disabling authentication for routes that should require it. This is a common misconfiguration where developers permit access too broadly during development and fail to restrict it before production deployment.
impact:
Using permitAll() on sensitive URL patterns disables Spring Security's
authentication and authorization for those endpoints. Attackers can
access admin panels, user management APIs, data endpoints, and
privileged operations without any credentials. Combined with disabled
CSRF, this allows full exploitation of all protected functionality.

title: Spring Boot Actuator Endpoints Exposed Without Authentication
description: Detects Spring Boot applications that expose Actuator endpoints (health, env, configprops, heapdump, threaddump, mappings, etc.) without requiring authentication. Actuator endpoints provide deep operational insight into the running application including environment variables, configuration properties, heap dumps containing secrets, and application mappings. In Spring Boot 1.x, all actuator endpoints are exposed by default.
impact:
Exposed actuator endpoints can reveal database credentials, API keys,
cloud provider secrets, and internal configuration. The /actuator/env
endpoint shows all environment variables. The /actuator/heapdump allows
downloading a JVM heap dump containing in-memory secrets, session data,
and encryption keys. The /actuator/shutdown endpoint enables remote
application shutdown (DoS). The /actuator/gateway/routes can reveal
internal service topology.
remediation:
Restrict actuator endpoint exposure and require authentication:

```yaml
# application.yml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus
    enabled-by-default: false
  endpoint:
    health:
      enabled: true
      show-details: when-authorized
    info:
      enabled: true
  server:
    port: 9090  # Separate management port
    address: 127.0.0.1  # Only localhost
```

```java
// Secure actuator endpoints
http.requestMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())
    .authorizeRequests()
    .anyRequest().hasRole("ACTUATOR_ADMIN");
```

title: Spring CORS Wide-Open Configuration
description: Detects Spring applications that configure CORS with overly permissive settings, such as allowing all origins, all methods, or all headers. This includes @CrossOrigin annotations without restrictions, global CorsRegistry configuration with wildcards, and CorsConfiguration bean definitions that permit any origin. Wide-open CORS enables cross-origin attacks on authenticated endpoints.
impact:
Wide-open CORS configuration allows any website to make cross-origin
requests to the Spring application. When combined with credentials
(cookies, authorization headers), attackers can read authenticated
responses, steal data, and perform actions on behalf of users from
any origin. This effectively bypasses same-origin policy protections.

title: SpEL Injection via @Value or Expression Evaluation
description: Detects Spring applications that use Spring Expression Language (SpEL) with user-controlled input in @Value annotations, SpelExpressionParser, or other expression evaluation contexts. SpEL injection allows remote code execution by evaluating arbitrary expressions that can access Java runtime, execute system commands, and read/write files.
impact:
SpEL injection allows attackers to execute arbitrary Java code on the
server. Through SpEL, attackers can invoke Runtime.exec() to run system
commands, access the Java ClassLoader to load arbitrary classes, read
and write files, access Spring beans and application context, and
exfiltrate environment variables and secrets. This typically results
in complete server compromise.

title: Missing Method-Level Security in Spring Controllers
description: Detects Spring controllers and service methods that perform sensitive operations without method-level security annotations (@PreAuthorize, @Secured, @RolesAllowed). While URL-level security in HttpSecurity provides a first layer of defense, method-level security ensures authorization checks at the business logic layer. Without it, URL pattern changes or misconfigurations can expose privileged operations.
impact:
Without method-level security, authorization depends entirely on
URL-pattern matching in HttpSecurity configuration. If URL patterns
change, new endpoints are added, or patterns overlap, privileged
operations may become accessible to unauthorized users. Method-level
security provides defense-in-depth ensuring that each operation
independently verifies the caller's authorization.

title: Insecure OAuth2 Resource Server Configuration in Spring
description: Detects Spring Security OAuth2 resource server configurations that are insecure, including disabled token validation, permissive JWT verification, missing audience validation, or use of symmetric keys that can be brute-forced. Improper OAuth2 configuration can allow attackers to forge access tokens and gain unauthorized access to protected resources.
impact:
Insecure OAuth2 resource server configuration allows attackers to forge
or manipulate JWT tokens. With a weak symmetric key, tokens can be
brute-forced offline. Without audience validation, tokens issued for
one service can be reused on another. Without proper issuer validation,
tokens from any authorization server are accepted. This results in
unauthorized access to all protected resources.

title: SQL Injection via Dynamic WHERE Clause
description: Detects SQL injection via dynamic WHERE clause construction in ABAP.
impact:
Dynamic WHERE clauses allow SQL injection in SAP systems,
potentially compromising business-critical data.
remediation:
Use static WHERE clauses or cl_abap_dyn_prg=>check_whitelist_str:
  DATA(lv_safe) = cl_abap_dyn_prg=>check_whitelist_str(
    val = lv_input allowed_chars = '0123456789ABCDEF' ).

title: OS Command Injection
description: Detects OS command execution with user-controlled input in ABAP.
impact:
OS command injection on SAP application servers can compromise
the entire SAP landscape.
remediation:
Use SM69 to define allowed external commands.
Always perform AUTHORITY-CHECK before executing commands.

title: ABAP Code Injection via Dynamic Programming
description: Detects dynamic ABAP code generation and execution.
impact: Dynamic ABAP code injection allows execution of arbitrary ABAP on the system.
remediation:
Avoid GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL with user input.
Use AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'S_DEVELOP' for development-related operations.

impact: Exposed secrets enable unauthorized access to systems, APIs, and sensitive data

title: Cross-Client Data Access

impact: Framework misconfiguration can disable security controls and expose sensitive functionality

description: Detects SOQL queries built with string concatenation of user input.

title: Unsafe JSON Deserialization

remediation: Use safe serialization formats (JSON), implement type filtering, avoid deserializing untrusted data

title: Governor Limit Vulnerability (SOQL in Loop)
description: Detects SOQL queries inside loops which can hit governor limits.
impact: Framework misconfiguration can disable security controls and expose sensitive functionality

title: SQL Injection in Embedded SQL
description: Detects dynamic SQL construction with string concatenation in COBOL.
impact:
SQL injection in COBOL mainframe applications can compromise
entire enterprise databases (DB2, IMS, VSAM).
remediation:
Use host variables in embedded SQL:
  EXEC SQL SELECT * FROM ACCOUNTS WHERE ID = :WS-ACCOUNT-ID END-EXEC.
Never concatenate user input into SQL strings.

title: CICS Command Injection

impact: CICS command injection can execute arbitrary transactions on mainframes.
remediation:
Validate program names and transaction IDs against allowlists.
Use RACF/ACF2/TopSecret for resource access control.

title: Command Injection via system() or popen()
description: Detects use of system(), popen(), or exec*() family with user-controlled input in C++ applications, enabling arbitrary OS command execution.
impact:
Remote code execution through OS command injection in native applications.
C++ applications often run with elevated privileges, making command injection
especially dangerous. Successful exploitation can lead to full system compromise,
data exfiltration, lateral movement, or persistent backdoor installation.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - POSIX: use fork()/execvp() with explicit argument arrays
  - Windows: use CreateProcessW() with explicit argument lists, avoid ShellExecute with user input
  - Qt: use QProcess with argument list instead of single command string
  - Boost: use boost::process::child with args vector
Secure libraries:
  - POSIX posix_spawn() / posix_spawnp() with argv arrays
  - Boost.Process with explicit argument vectors
  - Qt QProcess::start(program, arguments) with separate arguments
Prevention strategies:
  - Use exec*() family without shell interpretation
  - Use fork()/execvp() with explicit argument arrays
  - Validate input against strict character allowlists (alphanumeric only)
  - Use POSIX spawn() instead of system()
  - Never pass user input through a shell interpreter
  - Apply SELinux/AppArmor policies to restrict process capabilities
  - Use compile-time checks and static analysis (Coverity, Clang-Tidy)

title: Format String Vulnerability
description: Detects format string vulnerabilities where user-controlled input is passed as the format string to printf/sprintf family functions, enabling memory reads, writes, and potential code execution.
impact:
Format string attacks enable reading stack memory (information disclosure),
writing to arbitrary memory addresses (code execution via GOT overwrite
or return address manipulation), crashing applications (denial of service),
and bypassing ASLR/stack canaries through information leaks.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - C: always use explicit format strings: printf("%s", user_input)
  - C++: prefer std::cout, std::format (C++20), or fmt::format over printf family
  - Syslog: always use syslog(priority, "%s", user_message)
  - Qt: use qDebug() << variable instead of printf-style formatting
Secure libraries:
  - {fmt} library (fmtlib/fmt) for type-safe formatting
  - spdlog for type-safe logging
  - std::format (C++20) for compile-time checked formatting
  - Boost.Format for safe string formatting
Prevention strategies:
  - Never pass user input as the format string parameter
  - Use compiler warnings: -Wformat -Wformat-security -Werror=format-security
  - Use static analysis tools (Coverity, Clang-Tidy, cppcheck) to detect format string bugs
  - Enable FORTIFY_SOURCE: compile with -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2
  - Use GCC's __attribute__((format)) to validate format string functions
  - Deploy with ASLR, stack canaries, and non-executable stack as defense in depth

title: Buffer Overflow via Unsafe String Functions
description: Detects use of unsafe C string functions (strcpy, strcat, gets, sprintf) that do not perform bounds checking, leading to buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
impact:
Buffer overflow enables stack smashing, heap corruption, code execution
via return address overwrite, ROP chain exploitation, and denial of service.
Modern exploit mitigations (ASLR, stack canaries, DEP/NX) reduce but do
not eliminate the risk. Information leaks from other bugs (e.g., format
strings) can be chained to bypass these protections.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - POSIX/Linux: replace strcpy with strlcpy (BSD) or strncpy with null termination
  - Windows: use StringCchCopy/StringCbCopy from strsafe.h or strcpy_s from safecrt
  - Qt: use QString instead of C-style char arrays
  - Embedded: use bounded copy functions with explicit size parameters
Secure libraries:
