SQLAlchemy Core:
  stmt = text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :id")
  result = connection.execute(stmt, {"id": user_id})

SQLAlchemy ORM:
  session.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()

Flask-SQLAlchemy:
  User.query.filter_by(username=user_input).first()

FastAPI with async databases:
  query = users.select().where(users.c.id == user_id)
  await database.fetch_one(query)

psycopg2:
  cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", (user_id,))

asyncpg:
  await conn.fetchrow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", user_id)

Never use f-strings, .format(), or % formatting in SQL statements.
Use an ORM whenever possible. If raw SQL is required, always use
parameterized placeholders native to the database driver.

title: Command Injection via os.system or subprocess with shell=True
description: Detects use of os.system(), os.popen(), or subprocess with shell=True accepting user-controlled input.
impact:
Remote code execution. Attacker can execute arbitrary system commands on the
server, potentially gaining full control, accessing sensitive files, or
pivoting to internal systems.
remediation:
General best practices:
  - Use subprocess.run() with shell=False (default) and pass args as a list
  - Use shlex.split() for safe argument parsing
  - Use shlex.quote() for individual argument escaping if shell is needed
  - Prefer Python libraries (shutil, pathlib) over shell commands
  - Apply strict input validation with allowlists

Django:
  - Use django.core.management.call_command() for management commands
  - Use pathlib or shutil for file operations instead of shell commands
  - Validate input against a strict allowlist before any subprocess usage

Flask:
  - Use secure_filename() from werkzeug.utils for filename handling
  - Avoid passing Flask request data to any subprocess or os.system call
  - Implement a command builder pattern with strict allowlists

FastAPI:
  - Use Pydantic models to validate and constrain input before system calls
  - Use asyncio.create_subprocess_exec (NOT _shell) with list arguments
  - Implement typed enums for any command-selection logic

Secure library recommendations:
  - shlex: For safe shell argument handling
  - pathlib: For filesystem operations instead of shell commands
  - shutil: For file copy/move/delete instead of shell commands
  - plumbum: For type-safe subprocess management

title: Code Injection via eval/exec with User Input
description: Detects use of eval(), exec(), or compile() with user-controlled input, enabling arbitrary Python code execution.
impact:
Arbitrary Python code execution in the application context. Attackers can
import modules, access the file system, read environment variables, establish
reverse shells, or pivot laterally.
remediation:
General:
  - Never use eval()/exec() with user input under any circumstances
  - Use ast.literal_eval() for safe literal evaluation of strings, numbers, tuples, lists, dicts, booleans, and None
  - Use json.loads() for JSON parsing
  - Implement a safe expression parser (e.g., pyparsing, simpleeval) for math expressions

Django:
  - Use Django template language for dynamic rendering instead of eval
  - Use Django forms and model validation for input processing
  - For dynamic filtering, use Q objects: Q(**{field: value})
  - Never pass user input to eval for dynamic queryset construction

Flask:
  - Use Flask-WTF forms for input validation
  - For calculator-type features, use simpleeval or numexpr libraries
  - Use Jinja2 filters and template logic instead of eval for dynamic output

FastAPI:
  - Use Pydantic validators to parse and constrain input types
  - For dynamic computation, define allowed operations as a mapping of string keys to functions
  - Use dependency injection to safely resolve dynamic behavior

If code execution is truly required:
  - Use RestrictedPython with a minimal set of allowed builtins
  - Run user code in a sandboxed container (Docker, gVisor)
  - Use WebAssembly-based sandboxes (Pyodide) for client-side execution
  - Enforce execution time limits and memory constraints

Secure library recommendations:
  - ast.literal_eval: For safely evaluating literal Python expressions
  - simpleeval: For safe mathematical expression evaluation
  - numexpr: For safe numerical expression evaluation
  - RestrictedPython: For sandboxed Python execution
  - pyparsing: For building safe custom parsers

title: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)
description: Detects Jinja2, Mako, or Django template rendering with user-controlled template strings, enabling server-side template injection.
impact:
Server-side template injection allows attackers to execute arbitrary code
within the template engine context. In Jinja2, this can lead to full RCE
via __class__.__mro__ traversal or os module access.
remediation:
General:
  - Use render_template() with file-based templates, never render_template_string()
  - If dynamic templates are needed, use Jinja2 SandboxedEnvironment
  - Enable autoescape=True
  - Never pass user input as a template string
  - Validate and sanitize all dynamic template content

Django:
  - Always use file-based templates with render(request, 'template.html', context)
  - Use Django's built-in template engine with autoescape enabled (default)
  - Never instantiate django.template.Template() with user input
  - Use the mark_safe() function only on trusted content, never on user input
  - Use django.utils.html.escape() for any user content rendered in templates

Flask:
  - Use render_template('template.html', **context) with file-based templates
  - Never use render_template_string() with user-controlled content
  - Enable Jinja2 autoescape (enabled by default for .html templates)
  - Use markupsafe.escape() for user input that must be rendered
  - If dynamic templates are required, use jinja2.sandbox.SandboxedEnvironment

FastAPI:
  - Use Jinja2Templates(directory="templates") with file-based templates
  - Pass user data only as template context variables, never as template source
  - Enable autoescape=True in the Jinja2 environment configuration
  - Use Pydantic validation on all user inputs before passing to templates

Mako:
  - Use file-based templates with TemplateLookup
  - Enable strict_undefined=True and default_filters=['h']
  - Never pass user input to mako.template.Template() constructor

Secure library recommendations:
  - jinja2.sandbox.SandboxedEnvironment: For restricted Jinja2 execution
  - markupsafe: For safe HTML string handling
  - bleach: For HTML sanitization

title: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection
description: Detects XML parsing with external entity processing enabled, allowing XXE attacks for file disclosure and SSRF.
impact:
XXE attacks enable local file disclosure (/etc/passwd, application configs),
server-side request forgery to internal services, denial of service via
billion laughs attack, and port scanning of internal networks.
remediation:
General:
  - Use defusedxml library as a drop-in replacement for standard XML parsers
  - For lxml: XMLParser(resolve_entities=False, no_network=True)
  - Disable DTD processing entirely
  - Use JSON instead of XML where possible
  - If XML is required, validate against a strict schema

Django:
  - Use Django REST Framework with JSONParser instead of XMLParser
  - If XML is needed, use defusedxml in custom parsers:
      from defusedxml.ElementTree import parse
  - Remove XMLParser from REST_FRAMEWORK parser_classes
  - Configure Django REST Framework:
      REST_FRAMEWORK = {
          'DEFAULT_PARSER_CLASSES': [
              'rest_framework.parsers.JSONParser',
          ]
      }

Flask:
  - Use request.get_json() instead of parsing XML from request.data
  - If XML endpoints are required, use defusedxml:
      from defusedxml.ElementTree import fromstring
      data = fromstring(request.data)
  - Consider Flask-RESTX with JSON-only endpoints

FastAPI:
  - Accept JSON via Pydantic models instead of raw XML
  - If XML processing is required, create a custom dependency:
      from defusedxml.ElementTree import fromstring
      async def parse_xml(request: Request):
          return fromstring(await request.body())
  - Avoid using python-multipart or other parsers that process XML

lxml-specific hardening:
  - parser = lxml.etree.XMLParser(resolve_entities=False, no_network=True, dtd_validation=False, load_dtd=False)
  - tree = lxml.etree.parse(source, parser=parser)

Secure library recommendations:
  - defusedxml: Drop-in secure replacement for all stdlib XML parsers
  - lxml (hardened): With resolve_entities=False, no_network=True
  - xmltodict: For simple XML-to-dict conversion (use with defusedxml.expat)

title: Pickle Deserialization Injection
description: Detects deserialization of untrusted data via pickle.loads, pickle.load, shelve, or joblib where user-controlled bytes are deserialized. Pickle executes arbitrary Python code during deserialization via __reduce__.
impact:
Pickle deserialization executes arbitrary Python code via __reduce__.
Attackers can achieve full RCE, data exfiltration, and system compromise.
remediation:
- Never deserialize untrusted pickle data.
- Use JSON, MessagePack, or Protocol Buffers instead.
- If pickle is required, use RestrictedUnpickler with allowlisted classes.
- Validate data integrity with HMAC before deserialization.

title: YAML Deserialization Injection
description: Detects use of yaml.load() or yaml.unsafe_load() without SafeLoader, enabling arbitrary Python object instantiation and code execution via YAML tags like !!python/object/apply.
impact:
YAML deserialization with unsafe Loader allows arbitrary Python code
execution via !!python/object tags. Full RCE is trivially achievable.
remediation:
- Always use yaml.safe_load() or Loader=yaml.SafeLoader.
- Never use yaml.load() without explicitly specifying SafeLoader.
- Use yaml.safe_load_all() for multi-document streams.

title: MongoDB NoSQL Injection via PyMongo
description: Detects NoSQL injection where user-controlled input is passed directly to PyMongo query operators ($where, $regex, $gt, $ne), enabling query manipulation, authentication bypass, and data exfiltration.
impact:
NoSQL injection allows authentication bypass, data exfiltration, and
arbitrary JavaScript execution via $where operator in MongoDB.
remediation:
- Validate input types strictly (expect string, reject dicts with $ keys).
- Use mongo-sanitize or equivalent input sanitization.
- Never pass raw request body to MongoDB operations.

title: XPath Injection via lxml/ElementTree
description: Detects XPath queries constructed with user-controlled input via string formatting in lxml or xml.etree, enabling data extraction and authentication bypass through XPath manipulation.
impact:
XPath injection enables extraction of arbitrary XML data, authentication
bypass, and information disclosure from XML data stores.
remediation:
- Use lxml XPath variables: tree.xpath("//user[@name=$name]", name=user_input).
- Validate and restrict input to expected character sets.
- Use parameterized XPath via lxml's variable binding.

title: Format String Injection via str.format
description: Detects use of str.format() or str.format_map() where the format string itself is user-controlled, enabling access to object attributes and methods through Python's format specification mini-language.
impact:
Format string injection enables reading of object attributes, application
secrets, and internal state. Can lead to information disclosure and in
some cases code execution.
remediation:
- Never use user input as a format string template.
- Use f-strings with pre-defined templates.
- If dynamic templates needed, use a safe template engine (Jinja2 sandboxed).

title: HTTP Header / CRLF Injection
description: Detects HTTP header injection via user-controlled values in response headers, enabling CRLF injection for response splitting, XSS, and cache poisoning attacks.
impact:
CRLF injection enables HTTP response splitting, allowing XSS via
injected headers, cache poisoning, and session fixation attacks.
remediation:
- Strip or reject \\r and \\n characters from header values.
- Use framework-provided redirect functions instead of manual Location headers.
- URL-encode user input before placing in header values.

title: ReDoS via re.compile with User-Controlled Pattern
description: Detects use of re.compile() or re.match/search/findall with user-controlled regex patterns, enabling Regular Expression Denial of Service attacks via catastrophic backtracking.
impact:
ReDoS causes CPU exhaustion, making the application unresponsive.
Attackers can craft patterns with exponential time complexity.
remediation:
- Escape user input with re.escape() before using in re.compile().
- Use Google's re2 library for linear-time regex.
- Set timeouts on regex operations.

title: Django/Flask ORM Raw Query Injection
description: Detects SQL injection via Django's .raw(), .extra(), or SQLAlchemy's text() with string formatting of user input, bypassing ORM protections.
impact:
SQL injection via ORM raw queries bypasses normal ORM protections and
enables full database compromise including data exfiltration and RCE.
remediation:
- Use .raw() with parameterized placeholders: Model.objects.raw("SELECT * WHERE id=%s", [id]).
- Use SQLAlchemy text().bindparams() for parameterized raw queries.
- Avoid .extra() entirely; use annotations and aggregations instead.

title: LDAP Injection via python-ldap
description: Detects LDAP injection where user-controlled input is interpolated into LDAP filter strings or DN values without sanitization, enabling authentication bypass and directory enumeration.
impact:
LDAP injection allows authentication bypass, user enumeration, and
extraction of sensitive directory attributes (passwords, email, groups).
remediation:
- Use ldap.filter.escape_filter_chars() for filter values.
- Use ldap.dn.escape_dn_chars() for DN components.
- Validate input against strict character allowlists.

title: subprocess shell=True with User Arguments
description: Detects subprocess.run/call/Popen invocations with shell=True where command arguments are constructed from user-controlled input, enabling shell metacharacter injection even when the base command is hardcoded.
impact:
Command injection via subprocess with shell=True enables arbitrary OS
command execution, full server compromise, and persistent backdoors.
remediation:
- Use subprocess.run(["cmd", "arg1", "arg2"]) with shell=False (default).
- Pass arguments as a list, never as a concatenated string.
- Use shlex.quote() if shell=True is unavoidable.
- Use shlex.split() to safely parse command strings.

title: SQL Injection via String Operations
description: Detects SQL injection in embedded SQL within RPG programs.
impact:
SQL injection on IBM i can compromise DB2 for i databases
and potentially access IFS file system.
remediation:
Use parameter markers in embedded SQL:
  EXEC SQL SELECT * FROM CUSTFILE WHERE CUSTNO = :wsCustNo;

title: Command Injection via QCMDEXC
description: Detects OS command execution via QCMDEXC with dynamic commands.
impact: QCMDEXC command injection can execute arbitrary CL commands on IBM i.
remediation:
Use constant command strings. Validate user input against allowlists.
Use specific APIs instead of QCMDEXC when possible.

title: Hardcoded Credentials in RPG
description: Detects hardcoded passwords or credentials in RPG programs.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: Missing Object Authority Check
description: Detects file operations without authority verification.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: Weak Encryption in RPG
description: Detects weak or custom encryption in RPG programs.
impact: Weak cryptography can be broken, compromising data confidentiality and integrity
remediation: Use industry-standard algorithms (AES-256-GCM, SHA-256+, Argon2) and proper key management

title: Sensitive Data in Job Log
description: Detects sensitive data written to job log via DSPLY.
impact: Exposed secrets enable unauthorized access to systems, APIs, and sensitive data
remediation: Use secret management systems, environment variables, and rotate exposed credentials immediately

title: Program Adopted Authority Exposure
description: Detects programs using adopted authority which can escalate privileges.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: SQL Injection via String Interpolation in ActiveRecord
description: Detects ActiveRecord queries using string interpolation with user-controlled input instead of parameterized conditions.
impact:
SQL injection via ActiveRecord string interpolation bypasses ORM protections.
Rails applications are especially susceptible when developers use raw SQL strings
with interpolation instead of parameterized conditions. Can lead to full database
compromise, data exfiltration, and in some database configurations, remote code
execution.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Rails ActiveRecord: use parameterized conditions
      User.where("name = ?", params[:name])
      User.where(name: params[:name])
  - Rails with Arel: use Arel predicates
      users = User.arel_table
      User.where(users[:name].eq(params[:name]))
  - Sequel ORM: use dataset filtering
      DB[:users].where(name: params[:name])
  - Raw SQL: use sanitize_sql_array
      User.where(sanitize_sql_array(["name = ?", params[:name]]))
Secure libraries:
  - ActiveRecord parameterized where clauses
  - Arel query builder for complex queries
  - Sequel ORM with built-in escaping
  - Rails sanitize_sql_* helper methods
Prevention strategies:
  - Never use string interpolation in SQL fragments
  - Use strong_parameters to whitelist allowed attributes
  - Enable Brakeman static analysis in CI/CD pipeline
  - Review raw SQL usage in code reviews
  - Use database roles with minimal privileges

title: Command Injection via Kernel System Methods
description: Detects use of system, exec, backticks, or %x with user-controlled input in Ruby applications.
impact:
Remote code execution through shell metacharacter injection. An attacker
can execute arbitrary operating system commands with the privileges of the
Ruby application process, potentially gaining full control of the server,
reading sensitive files, pivoting to internal networks, or installing
persistent backdoors.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Rails: avoid system() calls in controllers; use background jobs with validated arguments
  - General: pass command and arguments as separate array elements
      system("convert", params[:filename], "output.png")
  - Sidekiq/Resque: validate all job arguments before processing
Secure libraries:
  - Shellwords.escape() for argument escaping
  - Open3.capture3 with array arguments for safe subprocess execution
  - Terrapin/Cocaine gem for safe command line execution
  - posix-spawn gem for safe process spawning
Prevention strategies:
  - Pass command and arguments as separate array elements to system()
  - Use Open3.capture3("command", "arg1", "arg2") with explicit arguments
  - Validate input against strict allowlists of permitted values
  - Never concatenate user input into command strings
  - Run processes in sandboxed environments with minimal privileges
  - Enable Brakeman command injection checks in CI/CD pipeline

title: Unsafe ERB/eval with User Input
description: Detects ERB template rendering or eval with user-controlled content, enabling arbitrary Ruby code execution.
impact:
Arbitrary Ruby code execution via eval or dynamic template rendering.
This is the most severe class of vulnerability: attackers can execute any
Ruby code, read/write files, access databases, make network requests,
and completely compromise the application and underlying server.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Rails: use pre-compiled ERB templates from the views directory; never render user-provided templates
  - Sinatra: use layout/template system instead of dynamic ERB construction
  - Background jobs: validate method names against explicit allowlists before send()
Secure libraries:
  - Erubi gem (safe ERB engine with auto-escaping)
  - Liquid templating engine for user-provided templates (sandboxed)
  - Mustache for logic-less user-controlled templates
Prevention strategies:
  - Never use eval() with user input under any circumstances
  - Use pre-compiled ERB templates loaded from files, not user data
  - Replace send() with explicit method calls or strict allowlists
  - Use a strict allowlist for permitted methods when dynamic dispatch is required
  - Use public_send instead of send and validate method names against respond_to?(:method, false)
  - Apply the principle of least privilege: run application with minimal OS permissions
  - Use Ruby's $SAFE level or Sandboxing for untrusted code (note: $SAFE is deprecated in Ruby 3.x)

title: Mass Assignment / Strong Parameters Bypass
description: Detects ActiveRecord models and controller actions that permit unprotected attribute assignment from user-controlled input, allowing attackers to set privileged fields such as admin flags, role columns, account balances, or foreign keys by injecting unexpected parameters into create or update calls.
impact:
Mass assignment allows attackers to modify any model attribute by injecting
unexpected parameters in HTTP requests. This can lead to vertical privilege
escalation (setting admin=true), horizontal privilege escalation (changing
user_id foreign keys), financial manipulation (modifying balance or price
columns), data corruption (overwriting audit timestamps), and bypassing
business logic constraints. In Rails applications prior to version 4.0,
all attributes were mass-assignable by default, and even in modern Rails,
misuse of params.permit! or to_unsafe_hash reintroduces the vulnerability.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Rails 4+: always use strong parameters with explicit permit lists
      def user_params
        params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email, :password)
      end
      User.create(user_params)
  - Rails 3.x: use attr_accessible in models with explicit attribute lists
      class User < ActiveRecord::Base
        attr_accessible :name, :email, :password
      end
  - API controllers: parse and validate JSON bodies through strong parameters
      def api_params
        ActionController::Parameters.new(JSON.parse(request.body.read))
          .require(:user).permit(:name, :email)
      end
Secure libraries:
  - ActionController::StrongParameters (built into Rails 4+)
  - Pundit or CanCanCan for attribute-level authorization
  - dry-validation for schema-level input validation
  - ActiveModel::Serializers for controlling attribute exposure
Prevention strategies:
  - Never pass raw params directly to create, update, or new
  - Never use params.permit! in production code
  - Define separate permit lists for different user roles (admin vs regular user)
  - Use Brakeman mass_assignment check in CI/CD pipeline
  - Audit models for sensitive columns (role, admin, balance, permissions)
  - Add integration tests that verify unpermitted attributes are rejected
  - Consider using Form Objects or Service Objects to decouple input handling

title: Open Redirect via redirect_to with User-Controlled URL
description: Detects instances where Rails redirect_to is called with a URL derived from user-controlled input such as params, request headers, or cookie values, enabling attackers to redirect authenticated users to malicious phishing sites that harvest credentials or serve malware while appearing to originate from a trusted domain.
impact:
Open redirects enable attackers to construct URLs on a trusted domain that
redirect victims to attacker-controlled sites. This is particularly dangerous
in authentication flows (OAuth callbacks, post-login redirects, SSO return URLs)
where users expect to remain on the trusted site. Attackers can harvest
credentials via convincing phishing pages, steal OAuth authorization codes,
distribute malware under the appearance of a trusted domain, and bypass URL-based
security controls such as CSP or domain allowlists. While classified as medium
severity in isolation, open redirects frequently serve as a critical component
in chained attacks.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Rails: use only_path option to force relative redirects
      redirect_to params[:return_to], only_path: true
  - Rails: validate the host of the redirect URL against an allowlist
      uri = URI.parse(params[:return_to])
      if ALLOWED_HOSTS.include?(uri.host)
        redirect_to params[:return_to]
      else
        redirect_to root_path
      end
  - Rails: use named route helpers instead of dynamic URLs
      redirect_to dashboard_path
  - Devise/OmniAuth: configure allowed redirect origins in initializer
      config.navigational_formats = []
Secure libraries:
  - Rails url_for with only_path: true
  - Devise Omniauthable with strict callback validation
  - rack-protection gem for redirect safety
  - addressable gem for robust URL parsing and host validation
Prevention strategies:
  - Never pass user input directly to redirect_to without validation
  - Maintain a server-side allowlist of permitted redirect hosts
  - Use relative paths (only_path: true) for all post-action redirects
  - Store return URLs in server-side session under a validated key
  - Strip or reject URLs containing @, backslashes, or protocol-relative prefixes
  - Validate redirect targets in integration tests with malicious URL payloads
  - Log all external redirects for security monitoring

title: YAML Deserialization via Psych.load / YAML.load
description: Detects use of YAML.load or Psych.load with user-controlled input, which enables arbitrary object instantiation and remote code execution through crafted YAML payloads that exploit Ruby's object deserialization mechanism. YAML.load in Ruby deserializes arbitrary Ruby objects including those with dangerous side effects in their initialize or === methods.
impact:
YAML deserialization in Ruby (via Psych engine) can instantiate arbitrary Ruby
objects by processing YAML tags like !ruby/object:ClassName. Attackers can craft
YAML payloads that chain gadget objects (such as Gem::Installer, Gem::Requirement,
ERB, or Gem::StubSpecification) to achieve remote code execution. Known exploit
chains exist for every major Ruby version. A single YAML.load call on untrusted
input can lead to complete server compromise, including arbitrary file read/write,
command execution, reverse shells, and denial of service. This vulnerability class
has been exploited in major real-world breaches against Ruby on Rails applications.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Ruby 3.1+: YAML.load now requires permitted_classes by default
      YAML.safe_load(yaml_string)
      YAML.safe_load(yaml_string, permitted_classes: [Date, Time, Symbol])
  - Ruby < 3.1: replace all YAML.load with YAML.safe_load
      YAML.safe_load(params[:data])
  - Rails: use ActiveSupport JSON serialization instead of YAML for user data
      config = JSON.parse(params[:config])
  - Psych: use Psych.safe_load with strict class restrictions
      Psych.safe_load(data, permitted_classes: [Date, Time])
Secure libraries:
  - YAML.safe_load (built-in, restricts object instantiation)
  - SafeYAML gem (monkey-patches YAML.load for safety)
  - Psych.safe_load with permitted_classes whitelist
  - JSON as a safer serialization alternative for user data
Prevention strategies:
  - Replace every YAML.load call with YAML.safe_load globally
  - Use SafeYAML gem to make YAML.load safe by default across the application
  - Never accept YAML input from untrusted sources; prefer JSON for APIs
  - If YAML is required, use permitted_classes with the minimal set of safe types
  - Audit gems and dependencies for internal YAML.load usage on user-controlled data
  - Add Brakeman deserialization checks to CI/CD pipeline
  - Monitor for YAML payloads containing !ruby/object tags in WAF rules

title: XML External Entity Injection via Nokogiri/REXML
description: Detects XML parsing in Ruby applications using Nokogiri or REXML with external entity processing enabled, allowing attackers to read arbitrary files from the server, perform server-side request forgery, exfiltrate data via out-of-band channels, or cause denial of service through recursive entity expansion (Billion Laughs attack).
impact:
XML External Entity injection allows attackers to define external entities in
XML documents that reference local files (file:///etc/passwd), internal network
services (http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/), or remote DTDs for out-of-band
data exfiltration. In Ruby applications using Nokogiri (libxml2 backend) or REXML,
the impact includes: arbitrary file read from the server filesystem, server-side
request forgery (SSRF) to internal services and cloud metadata endpoints, denial
of service via recursive entity expansion (Billion Laughs), and port scanning of
internal networks. On cloud-hosted applications, XXE can access instance metadata
services to steal IAM credentials, leading to full cloud account compromise.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Nokogiri: disable external entity loading with NONET and NOENT flags
      doc = Nokogiri::XML(xml_string) { |config|
        config.nonet.noent.noblanks
      }
  - Nokogiri: use parse options constant
      doc = Nokogiri::XML(xml_string, nil, nil,
        Nokogiri::XML::ParseOptions::NONET |
        Nokogiri::XML::ParseOptions::NOENT)
  - REXML: set entity expansion limits
      REXML::Security.entity_expansion_limit = 0
      REXML::Security.entity_expansion_text_limit = 0
      doc = REXML::Document.new(xml_string)
  - Rails: configure global XML parsing in application.rb
      config.middleware.delete ActionDispatch::ParamsParser
Secure libraries:
  - Nokogiri with NONET | NOENT parse options (default safe in Nokogiri >= 1.13.2)
  - Oga gem (pure Ruby XML parser without external entity support)
  - ox gem with default safe parsing configuration
  - JSON as alternative format where XML is not strictly required
Prevention strategies:
  - Always disable external entity processing in XML parsers
  - Set Nokogiri parse options to NONET | NOENT for all XML parsing
  - Set REXML::Security.entity_expansion_limit = 0 globally
  - Prefer JSON over XML for API communication where possible
  - Validate XML content-type headers and reject unexpected XML input
  - Use Web Application Firewall rules to detect XXE payloads (<!ENTITY, SYSTEM)
  - Audit all XML parsing code paths including those in gem dependencies
  - On cloud deployments, restrict access to metadata endpoints via network policy

title: Server-Side Template Injection via Liquid/Slim/Haml
description: Detects server-side template injection vulnerabilities where user-controlled input is rendered through Ruby templating engines such as Liquid, Slim, Haml, or Tilt without proper sandboxing. Attackers can inject template directives to execute arbitrary Ruby code, access application objects, read environment variables, or traverse the object graph to achieve remote code execution.
impact:
Server-side template injection in Ruby applications allows attackers to inject
template directives that are executed on the server. The severity depends on the
templating engine: Liquid provides a sandboxed environment but custom tags and
filters can leak data or enable denial of service; Slim and Haml allow embedded
Ruby code execution by design, meaning any user-controlled template leads directly
to RCE; Tilt dispatches to multiple engines and user-controlled engine selection
can escalate from safe to dangerous template evaluation. Successful exploitation
enables arbitrary code execution, access to application secrets and environment
variables (including database credentials, API keys), full filesystem access,
and lateral movement to connected services and databases.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Rails: never use render inline: with user input; use pre-defined templates
      render template: "pages/show"
      render partial: "shared/content", locals: { content: sanitized_content }
  - Liquid: use strict mode and restrict available filters/tags
      template = Liquid::Template.parse(content)
      template.render({}, strict_variables: true, strict_filters: true)
  - Slim/Haml: never parse user-controlled strings as templates
      # Instead of Slim::Template.new { params[:content] }.render
      # Use pre-compiled templates with safe variable interpolation
  - Tilt: never allow user-controlled engine type selection
      # Never: Tilt[params[:format]].new { content }.render
      # Always: use a fixed, known-safe engine
Secure libraries:
  - Liquid with strict mode (sandboxed, limited to safe operations)
  - Mustache (logic-less templating, no code execution)
  - Rails ActionView with pre-compiled templates (ERB/Erubi from files only)
  - Markdown renderers (Redcarpet, Kramdown) for user-formatted content
Prevention strategies:
  - Never allow user input to be used as template source in any engine
  - Use Liquid in strict mode for user-customizable templates with curated filters
  - Pre-compile all templates from trusted filesystem sources only
  - Implement Content Security Policy headers to limit template output behavior
  - Separate user-customizable content from template logic using a WYSIWYG editor or Markdown
  - Audit all render calls in controllers for inline or dynamic template usage
  - Use Brakeman render checks and template injection detection in CI/CD
  - If user-customizable email templates are required, use Liquid with a strict allowlist of variables

title: Rust SQL Injection via format! Macro
description: Detects SQL queries built with format! or format string macros
impact: SQL injection can lead to full database compromise
remediation: Use sqlx::query!() compile-time checked queries or diesel's query builder

title: Rust Command Injection
description: Detects command execution with user-controlled arguments in Rust
impact: Command injection enables arbitrary code execution on the server
remediation: Use Command::new with explicit args, never pass user input to shell

title: Rust Unsafe HTML Response
description: Detects unescaped user input in HTML responses using Actix/Rocket
impact: Cross-site scripting via unescaped user input in HTML responses
remediation: Use template engines (Askama, Tera) with auto-escaping, or manually escape output

title: Rust Weak Cryptography
description: Detects use of weak or deprecated cryptographic algorithms in Rust
impact: Weak hash/cipher algorithms can be broken by modern attacks
remediation: Use ring, RustCrypto with AES-256-GCM, SHA-256+, or Argon2 for passwords

title: Rust Insecure Random Number Generation
description: Detects use of non-cryptographic RNG for security-sensitive operations
impact: Predictable random numbers enable session prediction, token forgery
remediation: Use OsRng or ring::rand::SystemRandom for security-sensitive randomness

title: Rust Insecure TLS Configuration
description: Detects disabled certificate verification in Rust HTTP clients
impact: Disabled TLS certificate validation enables man-in-the-middle attacks
remediation: Enable certificate verification using rustls with proper CA certificates

title: Rust Hardcoded Secrets
description: Detects hardcoded passwords, API keys, or tokens in Rust code
impact: Hardcoded credentials can be extracted from compiled binaries
remediation: Use environment variables (std::env::var) or secret management systems

title: Rust Unsafe Deserialization
description: Detects deserialization of untrusted data without type constraints
impact: Deserializing arbitrary types can lead to denial of service or logic bugs
remediation: Always deserialize to specific, validated struct types using #[derive(Deserialize)]

title: Rust Server-Side Request Forgery
description: Detects SSRF via user-controlled URLs in Rust HTTP clients
impact: SSRF enables access to internal APIs, cloud metadata, and internal networks
remediation: Validate URLs against allowlists, block private/loopback IP ranges

title: Rust Path Traversal
description: Detects path traversal vulnerabilities in Rust file operations
impact: Path traversal allows reading/writing arbitrary files on the server
remediation: Use canonicalize() and verify paths start with expected base directory using starts_with()

title: Rust Unsafe Block with Raw Pointer Dereference
description: Detects unsafe blocks dereferencing raw pointers from external input
impact: Unsafe pointer operations can lead to memory corruption, buffer overflows, or code execution
remediation: Minimize unsafe blocks, add bounds checking, consider using safe abstractions

title: SQL Injection via format! in Database Queries
description: Detects SQL queries constructed using format!() or string concatenation in Rust database clients, bypassing the memory safety guarantees that Rust provides for other vulnerability classes.
impact:
SQL injection in Rust applications despite memory safety guarantees. Rust's
borrow checker prevents buffer overflows and use-after-free, but SQL injection
is a logic-level vulnerability. Successful exploitation enables full database
compromise, data exfiltration, and potential OS command execution via database
features (e.g., PostgreSQL COPY TO PROGRAM).
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - sqlx: use compile-time checked queries with sqlx::query!() macro
      sqlx::query!("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", user_id)
  - Diesel: use the type-safe query builder DSL
      users.filter(name.eq(&user_name)).load::<User>(&conn)
  - tokio-postgres: use parameterized queries
      client.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", &[&user_id])
  - SeaORM: use Entity query builder
      User::find().filter(user::Column::Name.eq(name)).one(&db)
  - rusqlite: use named or positional parameters
      conn.execute("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?1)", params![name])
Secure libraries:
  - sqlx with compile-time query verification (sqlx::query! macro)
  - Diesel ORM with type-safe DSL
  - SeaORM with entity query builders
  - rusqlite with params! macro
Prevention strategies:
  - Never use format!() for SQL query construction
  - Prefer compile-time checked query macros (sqlx::query!)
  - Use parameterized queries with bind parameters ($1, ?1)
  - Enable clippy lints and custom lints for format!() + SQL detection
  - Use integration tests to verify parameterized query usage

title: Command Injection via std::process::Command with Shell
description: Detects Command::new with user input passed through shell interpreters or directly as the command/program name, enabling OS command injection.
impact:
Command injection despite Rust's memory safety -- logic bugs still apply.
When user input flows into shell interpreters, an attacker can execute
arbitrary commands. This is especially dangerous in Rust services that
may run with elevated privileges due to confidence in Rust's safety.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Actix-web/Axum: validate and sanitize all path/query parameters before use in commands
  - Tokio: use tokio::process::Command with separate .arg() calls
  - General Rust: use std::process::Command with .arg() chaining instead of shell -c
Secure libraries:
  - std::process::Command with .arg() for each argument (avoids shell)
  - which crate to resolve command paths safely
  - regex crate for input validation patterns
  - shell-escape crate for escaping when shell invocation is unavoidable
Prevention strategies:
  - Pass command and arguments separately to Command::new().arg()
  - Never use shell=true or invoke shell interpreters (sh -c, bash -c, cmd /c) with user input
  - Validate input against strict allowlists using regex
  - Use Path::new().canonicalize() to validate file paths
  - Apply is_alphanumeric() or character-class validation on user input
  - Run subprocesses with reduced privileges using std::os::unix::process::CommandExt

title: SQL Injection in Kotlin JDBC/Exposed
description: Detects SQL injection via string templates in Kotlin database queries using JDBC, Exposed, or other database access libraries.
impact:
SQL injection in Kotlin applications via string template interpolation.
Kotlin's string templates (${ }) make it easy to inadvertently interpolate
user input into SQL queries. This affects server-side (Spring Boot, Ktor)
and Android applications (SQLite), enabling full database compromise.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - Spring JDBC: use PreparedStatement or JdbcTemplate with ? placeholders
      jdbcTemplate.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", arrayOf(name), rowMapper)
  - Kotlin Exposed: use the type-safe DSL
      Users.select { Users.name eq userName }
  - Ktor: use parameterized queries with the database driver
  - Android Room: use @Query with :param placeholders, compiled at build time
      @Query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = :name") fun findByName(name: String): User
  - Android SQLite: use query() with selectionArgs
      db.query("users", null, "name = ?", arrayOf(name), null, null, null)
  - jOOQ: use the type-safe query builder DSL
Secure libraries:
  - Kotlin Exposed ORM (JetBrains) with type-safe DSL
  - Spring Data JPA with @Query and named parameters
  - jOOQ for type-safe SQL construction
  - Android Room Persistence Library with compile-time verification
Prevention strategies:
  - Use PreparedStatement or Kotlin Exposed DSL with type-safe queries
  - Never use string templates to construct SQL queries
  - Enable detekt static analysis with custom SQL injection rules
  - Use @Query annotations with named parameters in Spring Data
  - Apply input validation at controller/endpoint boundaries
  - Use database connection pools with read-only users for query-only operations

title: SQL Injection in Swift Database Queries
description: Detects SQL injection via string interpolation in Swift database clients including SQLite.swift, GRDB, FMDB, and raw sqlite3 C API usage.
impact:
SQL injection in Swift applications through string interpolation in queries.
On iOS/macOS, this primarily affects local SQLite databases, which can contain
sensitive data such as user credentials, authentication tokens, personal info,
and cached API responses. On server-side Swift (Vapor/Kitura), this can
compromise backend databases.
remediation:
Framework-specific fixes:
  - SQLite.swift: use the type-safe Expression API
      users.filter(name == searchTerm)
  - GRDB: use parameterized SQL with arguments
      try db.execute(sql: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", arguments: [userId])
  - FMDB: use executeQuery with arguments array
      db.executeQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", withArgumentsIn: [userId])
  - Core Data: use NSPredicate with %@ format specifier
      NSPredicate(format: "name == %@", userName)
  - Raw sqlite3: use sqlite3_prepare_v2 with sqlite3_bind_text
  - Vapor (server-side): use Fluent ORM query builder
Secure libraries:
  - SQLite.swift with type-safe query builder
  - GRDB with SQL interpolation using StatementArguments
  - Core Data with NSPredicate and %@ substitution
  - Fluent ORM for server-side Swift (Vapor)
Prevention strategies:
  - Use parameterized queries with ? placeholders and arguments arrays
  - Use type-safe query builders (SQLite.swift Expression, GRDB record protocols)
  - Never concatenate or interpolate user input into SQL strings
  - Use SwiftLint custom rules to flag string interpolation in SQL contexts
  - Encrypt local databases with SQLCipher for defense in depth
  - Apply App Transport Security and certificate pinning for data in transit

title: SQL Injection via String Interpolation
description: Detects SQL queries built using Scala string interpolation (s"..." or f"...") with user-controlled variables.
impact:
Full SQL injection enabling data exfiltration, authentication bypass,
and potential remote code execution via database features.

title: Command Injection via Runtime.exec or Process
description: Detects OS command execution using Runtime.exec or scala.sys.process with user-controlled input.
impact: Remote code execution allowing an attacker to run arbitrary OS commands.
remediation:
Use ProcessBuilder with argument lists instead of shell strings:
  val pb = new ProcessBuilder(List("ls", "-la", safeDir).asJava)
Validate and sanitize all user input. Use allowlists.

title: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection
description: Detects XML parsing without disabling external entity resolution in Scala.
impact:
XXE can lead to server-side request forgery, file disclosure,
denial of service, and remote code execution.
remediation:
Disable external entities:
  val factory = SAXParserFactory.newInstance()
  factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true)
  factory.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false)

title: LDAP Injection
description: Detects LDAP queries built with string interpolation or concatenation.
impact: LDAP injection can bypass authentication and access unauthorized data.
remediation: Use parameterized LDAP filters and encode special characters.

title: XPath Injection
description: Detects XPath queries with user-controlled input in Scala.
impact: XPath injection can bypass authentication and extract XML data.
remediation: Use parameterized XPath queries with XPathVariableResolver.

title: Template Injection (Server-Side)
description: Detects server-side template injection in Play Framework or Twirl.
impact: SSTI can lead to remote code execution on the server.
remediation:
Use Play's built-in HTML escaping. Never pass raw user input to Html().
Use @Html only with properly sanitized content.

title: NoSQL Injection (MongoDB)
description: Detects NoSQL injection in Scala MongoDB drivers.
impact: NoSQL injection can bypass authentication and exfiltrate data.
remediation: Use the MongoDB Scala driver's type-safe query builders (Filters).

title: Expression Language Injection
description: Detects Spring Expression Language (SpEL) injection in Scala Spring apps.
impact: SpEL injection can lead to remote code execution.
remediation:
Use SimpleEvaluationContext instead of StandardEvaluationContext.
Never pass user input directly to expression parsers.

title: Log Injection / Log Forging
description: Detects unsanitized user input in log statements.
impact:
Log injection enables log forging, CRLF injection in logs,
and can mislead forensic analysis.
remediation:
Sanitize input before logging. Remove newlines and control characters.
Use structured logging (e.g., logback with MDC).

title: Header Injection / HTTP Response Splitting
description: Detects HTTP header injection via unsanitized user input in response headers.
impact: Header injection enables response splitting, cache poisoning, and XSS.
remediation:
Validate and encode all user input before placing in HTTP headers.
Reject input containing CR/LF characters.

title: Command Injection via Backtick Substitution
description: Detects command injection vulnerabilities where user-controlled input is interpolated inside backtick command substitution or $() subshells in shell scripts. Backticks interpret their contents as commands, so any unsanitized variable expansion within them allows arbitrary command execution on the host system.
impact:
Successful exploitation allows arbitrary command execution on the host
system with the privileges of the running shell process. This can lead
to full system compromise, data exfiltration, lateral movement, and
persistent backdoor installation.
remediation:
- Avoid backtick substitution; prefer $() which is more readable.
- Always double-quote variable expansions: "$variable".
- Use arrays for command arguments instead of string interpolation.
- Validate and sanitize all external input before use in commands.
- Use printf '%q' to escape shell metacharacters.
- Enable shellcheck in CI/CD pipelines.

title: Unquoted Variable Expansion in Commands
description: Detects shell commands where variables are expanded without double quoting, enabling word splitting and glob expansion attacks. When user input flows into unquoted variables used in command arguments, attackers can inject additional arguments, redirect output, or trigger filename globbing.
impact:
Unquoted variable expansion enables word splitting and glob expansion,
allowing attackers to inject additional command arguments, access
unintended files, or alter command behavior through crafted input.
remediation:
- Always double-quote variable expansions: "$variable".
- Use arrays for lists of arguments: "${args[@]}".
- Enable shellcheck SC2086 warning in CI/CD pipelines.
- Use set -u to catch unset variable usage.
- Use [[ ]] instead of [ ] for conditionals.

title: Eval with User Input
description: Detects use of the eval built-in with variables or expressions that may contain user-controlled input. eval interprets its arguments as shell commands, making it one of the most dangerous shell constructs when combined with unsanitized input.
impact:
eval with user input provides direct arbitrary command execution on
the host system. This is one of the most critical vulnerability patterns,
enabling full system compromise with the privileges of the running process.
remediation:
- Eliminate eval usage entirely where possible.
- Use associative arrays or case statements instead of eval.
- If eval is necessary, strictly validate input against a whitelist.
- Use declare -n for indirect variable references (Bash 4.3+).
- Never pass user input to eval under any circumstances.

title: Curl/Wget to User-Controlled URL
description: Detects shell commands where curl, wget, or similar HTTP clients fetch content from a URL constructed with user-controlled variables. This enables SSRF, data exfiltration, and RCE when fetched content is piped to a shell interpreter.
impact:
Fetching URLs from user input enables SSRF attacks against internal
services, cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), and data
exfiltration. When piped to shell, it enables full RCE.
remediation:
- Validate URLs against a strict allowlist of domains and protocols.
- Never pipe curl/wget output directly to a shell interpreter.
- Use --max-time and --connect-timeout to limit request duration.
- Block access to internal IP ranges and metadata service IPs.
- Verify downloaded content integrity with checksums before execution.

title: Dynamic Pipe Chains with User Input
description: Detects shell commands where user-controlled variables are used to construct pipe chains dynamically. Attackers can inject additional pipe segments, redirect output, or chain arbitrary commands by manipulating variables used in pipeline construction.
impact:
Dynamic pipe chains with user input allow attackers to inject
additional commands, redirect output to attacker-controlled
destinations, or execute arbitrary code.
remediation:
- Avoid constructing pipe chains dynamically with user input.
- Use predefined command lists and case statements instead.
- Set pipefail option to detect failures in pipe chains.
- Validate pipe commands against a strict allowlist.

title: Source/Dot Command with User-Controlled Path
description: Detects use of the source or dot (.) built-in with a path derived from user-controlled input. The source command executes a file in the current shell context, meaning any code in the sourced file runs with the current shell privileges and can modify environment variables.
impact:
Source with user-controlled paths allows execution of arbitrary shell
code in the current process context, with full access to all environment
variables, functions, and the calling shell privileges.
remediation:
- Never use user input directly in source/dot paths.
- Validate source paths against a strict allowlist of directories.
- Use realpath to canonicalize paths and prevent traversal.
- Set file permissions to prevent modification of sourceable files.
- Verify file integrity with checksums before sourcing.

title: Awk/Sed with User-Controlled Pattern
description: Detects awk and sed commands where the pattern or expression is derived from user-controlled input. Awk supports system() and pipe operators for command execution, while sed supports the e flag for evaluating pattern space as a command. Both can be weaponized for arbitrary RCE.
impact:
Awk and sed with user-controlled patterns enable command injection
via awk system(), pipe operators, or sed e flag. Attackers can
execute arbitrary commands, read sensitive files, or establish shells.
remediation:
- Use awk -v to pass variables safely instead of string interpolation.
- Validate user patterns against a strict character allowlist.
- Avoid sed e flag which evaluates pattern space as commands.
- Prefer fixed awk/sed programs with parameterized input.

title: SQL Injection via Shell Database Clients
description: Detects SQL injection where user-controlled input is interpolated into SQL statements executed via shell database clients such as mysql, psql, sqlite3, sqlcmd, or mongosh. Shell scripts constructing SQL queries via variable interpolation are highly vulnerable because no parameterized query mechanism exists in shell context.
impact:
SQL injection via shell database clients can lead to complete database
compromise, including data theft, modification, deletion, and potentially
OS-level command execution via UDFs or COPY PROGRAM.
remediation:
- Never interpolate variables directly into SQL strings in shell scripts.
- Use parameterized queries through application-level database drivers.
- Restrict database user privileges to minimum required operations.
- Move database logic to application code with ORM/query builders.

title: Find -exec with User-Controlled Input
description: Detects use of the find command with -exec, -execdir, or -delete actions where user-controlled input influences the path, name pattern, or executed command. The find -exec action runs a command for each matched file, and when combined with user input can be weaponized for arbitrary command execution or destructive file operations.
impact:
Find with user-controlled paths or commands can lead to arbitrary
file deletion, permission changes, or command execution across
the filesystem. Path traversal can expand scope to the entire filesystem.
remediation:
- Validate and canonicalize paths with realpath before passing to find.
- Use -maxdepth to restrict find scope.
- Quote all variables in find arguments.
- Avoid -exec sh -c with user input; use -exec directly.
- Restrict find to specific safe directories.

title: Environment Variable Injection
description: Detects patterns where user-controlled input is used to set or modify environment variables that influence command behavior. Attackers can inject malicious values into PATH, LD_PRELOAD, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, IFS, BASH_ENV, or ENV to hijack command resolution, load malicious libraries, or alter shell parsing behavior for arbitrary code execution.
impact:
Environment variable injection allows attackers to hijack command
resolution (PATH), load malicious shared libraries (LD_PRELOAD),
execute code on shell startup (BASH_ENV), or alter parsing behavior
(IFS). This can lead to arbitrary code execution with elevated privileges.
remediation:
- Never set sensitive environment variables from user input.
- Use absolute paths for commands instead of relying on PATH.
- Clear dangerous environment variables at script startup.
- Set PATH to a known-safe value at the start of scripts.
- Use env -i to start with a clean environment.

title: UNION-Based SQL Injection
description: Detects UNION SELECT injection patterns used for data exfiltration by appending additional result sets to legitimate queries. Covers NULL-padding column enumeration, information_schema reconnaissance, targeted extraction of credential stores and PII, GROUP_CONCAT aggregation, and database-specific system catalog queries across MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and Oracle.
impact:
UNION-based injection allows extracting data from any table in the database
by appending additional SELECT statements to the original query. This can
expose credentials, personal data, financial records, and proprietary data.
Combined with file read/write functions, it may enable server-side file access
or remote code execution via webshell upload.
remediation:
Parameterized Query Examples:

  PostgreSQL (Node.js pg):
    const result = await pool.query('SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE category = $1', [categoryInput]);

  MySQL (PHP PDO):
    $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE category = :category');
    $stmt->execute(['category' => $categoryInput]);

  SQL Server (Python pyodbc):
    cursor.execute("SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE category = ?", categoryInput)

WAF Rules:
  - Block requests containing UNION followed by SELECT keyword
  - Block requests referencing information_schema, sys.objects, pg_catalog
  - ModSecurity: SecRule ARGS "@rx (?i)(union).{1,40}(select)" "id:1002,deny,status:403"

Database Permission Hardening:
  - Revoke SELECT on information_schema for application accounts
  - Revoke FILE privilege on MySQL to prevent LOAD_FILE and INTO OUTFILE
  - Create application-specific database views exposing only required columns

title: Boolean-Based Blind SQL Injection
description: Detects boolean-based blind SQL injection patterns that infer data from observable differences in application response behavior. Attackers construct conditional expressions using AND/OR with IF, CASE WHEN, SUBSTRING, ASCII, and comparison operators to extract data one bit or character at a time based on whether the application returns a valid or error response.
impact:
Boolean-based blind injection enables data extraction one character at a time
through response analysis. Though slower than UNION-based attacks, automated
tools like sqlmap can extract entire databases. The technique works even when
error messages and direct output are suppressed.
remediation:
Parameterized Query Examples:

  PostgreSQL (Go database/sql):
    rows, err := db.Query("SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE id = $1", productId)

  MySQL (Java Spring JdbcTemplate):
    Product product = jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(
        "SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE id = ?",
        new Object[]{productId}, productRowMapper);

WAF Rules:
  - Block requests containing SUBSTRING, ASCII, ORD, MID combined with AND/OR
  - Implement response time anomaly detection
  - ModSecurity: SecRule ARGS "@rx (?i)(and|or)\s+(ascii|substring|substr|ord|mid)\s*\(" "id:1006,deny"

Database Hardening:
  - Use parameterized queries exclusively
  - Implement query execution time limits
  - Monitor sequential requests with incrementing SUBSTRING position parameters

title: Time-Based Blind SQL Injection
description: Detects time-based blind SQL injection patterns that use database-specific delay functions such as SLEEP(), WAITFOR DELAY, pg_sleep(), DBMS_PIPE.RECEIVE_MESSAGE(), and BENCHMARK() to infer data from response timing. Attackers introduce conditional delays to extract data bit by bit based on whether the response is delayed.
impact:
Time-based blind injection allows data extraction through timing
side-channels even when error messages are completely suppressed and responses
are identical. Though slower than other techniques, it is highly automatable
with tools like sqlmap and can extract entire databases given sufficient time.
remediation:
Parameterized Query Examples:

  MySQL (Node.js mysql2):
    await connection.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?', [username, passwordHash]);

  PostgreSQL (Python psycopg2):
    cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s", (username,))

WAF Rules:
  - Block SLEEP, WAITFOR, BENCHMARK, pg_sleep function calls in request parameters
  - Implement response time anomaly detection
  - ModSecurity: SecRule ARGS "@rx (?i)(sleep|waitfor|benchmark|pg_sleep)\s*\(" "id:1005,deny"

Database Hardening:
  - Set statement_timeout in PostgreSQL
  - Set MAX_EXECUTION_TIME in MySQL
  - Configure connection pool idle timeouts below common SLEEP values

title: Stacked Queries SQL Injection
description: Detects stacked query injection patterns using semicolons to append additional SQL statements. Covers destructive operations (DROP, DELETE, TRUNCATE), privilege escalation via user creation and GRANT, data manipulation through INSERT/UPDATE, and OS command execution through xp_cmdshell and COPY FROM PROGRAM.
impact:
Stacked query injection enables executing additional SQL statements including
DROP TABLE, data modification, stored procedure execution, and time-based attacks.
Impact extends to complete database destruction, privilege escalation, backdoor
account creation, and OS command execution via xp_cmdshell or COPY FROM PROGRAM.
remediation:
Parameterized Query Examples:

  PostgreSQL (Python psycopg2):
    cursor.execute("UPDATE profiles SET bio = %s WHERE user_id = %s", (bio_input, user_id))

  MySQL (Node.js mysql2):
    await connection.execute('UPDATE profiles SET bio = ? WHERE user_id = ?', [bioInput, userId]);

WAF Rules:
  - Block semicolons followed by SQL keywords (DROP, DELETE, INSERT, UPDATE, EXEC)
  - Block xp_cmdshell, sp_configure, sp_addlogin
  - ModSecurity: SecRule ARGS "@rx (?i)(;)\s*(drop|delete|insert|update|exec)" "id:1003,deny"

Database Hardening:
  - Disable multi-statement execution (PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES = false)
  - Revoke DROP, ALTER, CREATE, GRANT from application accounts
  - Disable xp_cmdshell on SQL Server

title: Error-Based SQL Injection
description: Detects error-based SQL injection patterns that leverage database error messages to extract data. Uses EXTRACTVALUE, UPDATEXML, XMLTYPE, EXP, CONVERT, CAST, and other functions that produce verbose error messages containing query results when given malformed input. This technique provides faster data extraction than blind methods.
impact:
Error-based injection extracts data in bulk through crafted error messages,
significantly faster than blind techniques. When verbose error reporting is
enabled, attackers can extract entire table contents in a single request per
row. This technique is especially dangerous when combined with CONCAT to
aggregate multiple values.
remediation:
Parameterized Query Examples:

  MySQL (PHP PDO):
    $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = :id');
    $stmt->execute(['id' => $productId]);

  PostgreSQL (Node.js pg):
    const result = await pool.query('SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = $1', [productId]);

Error Handling:
  - Never display raw database error messages to users
  - Implement custom error pages with generic messages
  - Log detailed errors server-side only
  - Disable debug mode in production (DEBUG=false, error_reporting(0))

WAF Rules:
  - Block EXTRACTVALUE, UPDATEXML combined with CONCAT
  - Block CONVERT/CAST with subqueries in request parameters
  - ModSecurity: SecRule ARGS "@rx (?i)(extractvalue|updatexml)\s*\(" "id:1007,deny"

title: Out-of-Band SQL Injection
description: Detects out-of-band (OOB) SQL injection techniques that exfiltrate data through DNS lookups, HTTP requests, or file system operations. Covers MySQL INTO OUTFILE/DUMPFILE, LOAD_FILE with UNC paths, SQL Server xp_cmdshell, Oracle UTL_HTTP/UTL_INADDR, and PostgreSQL COPY TO PROGRAM. OOB techniques are used when in-band and blind channels are unavailable.
impact:
Out-of-band injection enables data exfiltration through DNS, HTTP, or file
system channels even when all in-band output is suppressed. File write
capabilities can deploy webshells for persistent RCE. xp_cmdshell and
COPY FROM PROGRAM provide direct OS command execution on the database server.
remediation:
Parameterized Query Examples:

  SQL Server (C# Dapper):
    connection.Execute("UPDATE profiles SET bio = @Bio WHERE user_id = @UserId", new { Bio = bioInput, UserId = userId });

  Oracle (Java JDBC):
    PreparedStatement stmt = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = ?");
    stmt.setInt(1, productId);

Database Hardening:
  - Disable xp_cmdshell: EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 0; RECONFIGURE
  - Revoke FILE privilege on MySQL
  - Revoke EXECUTE on UTL_HTTP, UTL_INADDR, DBMS_SCHEDULER for application accounts
  - Restrict COPY FROM/TO PROGRAM for application roles on PostgreSQL
  - Implement network egress filtering to block database server outbound connections

title: Second-Order SQL Injection via Stored Data
description: Detects second-order SQL injection patterns where malicious input is stored safely in the database but later retrieved and used unsafely in dynamic SQL construction. Covers stored procedures that build queries from table data, user profile fields used in subsequent queries, and data-driven query construction patterns where previously stored values are concatenated into SQL without parameterization.
impact:
Second-order injection is particularly dangerous because the initial storage
is safe, making detection at the input boundary insufficient. The payload
executes in a different context, often with elevated privileges (stored
procedure owner context). This can lead to privilege escalation, data
corruption, and authentication bypass.
remediation:
Parameterized Query Examples:

  SQL Server (T-SQL sp_executesql):
    EXEC sp_executesql N'UPDATE users SET password = @pass WHERE username = @user',
      N'@pass NVARCHAR(100), @user NVARCHAR(50)', @pass = @newPass, @user = @storedUsername;

  PostgreSQL (PL/pgSQL EXECUTE USING):
    EXECUTE 'UPDATE users SET password = $1 WHERE username = $2' USING p_new_pass, p_stored_username;

Prevention:
  - Parameterize ALL queries, including those using data retrieved from the database
  - Never trust stored data any more than user input
  - Use query builders or ORM methods for all database operations
  - Audit stored procedures for dynamic SQL construction from table data

title: LIKE Injection with Wildcard Abuse
description: Detects SQL injection through LIKE clause manipulation where user input containing wildcard characters (%, _) is not properly escaped. Attackers can inject % to match all records (data exfiltration), craft expensive LIKE patterns for ReDoS-style denial-of-service, or combine LIKE with SQL injection techniques to bypass authentication filters.
impact:
LIKE injection enables data enumeration through wildcard manipulation,
authentication bypass via tautology construction, and denial-of-service
through expensive pattern matching on large tables. While less severe than
full SQL injection, it can expose significant amounts of data through
iterative searching.
remediation:
Parameterized Query with ESCAPE:

  PostgreSQL:
    cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE '%' || $1 || '%' ESCAPE '\\'", [escaped_input])
    -- Pre-processing: escaped_input = input.replace('%', '\\%').replace('_', '\\_')

  MySQL:
    cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE CONCAT('%', %s, '%') ESCAPE '\\\\'", [escaped_input])

Prevention:
  - Always escape % and _ in user input before LIKE clauses
  - Use ESCAPE clause to define escape character
  - Use full-text search (MATCH AGAINST, to_tsvector) instead of LIKE for search features
  - Implement result set limits (LIMIT, TOP) on search queries
  - Rate-limit search endpoints to prevent enumeration

title: ORDER BY Injection
description: Detects SQL injection through ORDER BY clauses where user-supplied column names, sort directions, or numeric indices are incorporated without validation. Since column identifiers cannot be parameterized, ORDER BY clauses are a common injection vector. Attackers leverage this for column count enumeration, boolean-based data inference via conditional ordering, and full SQL injection through subquery or CASE WHEN constructs.
impact:
ORDER BY injection enables column count enumeration (prerequisite for UNION
attacks), boolean-based data inference through conditional sort behavior,
and in some cases full SQL injection through subqueries or error-based
techniques within the ORDER BY clause. It is a common vector because
column identifiers cannot be parameterized.
remediation:
Whitelist Validation:

  Node.js:
    const allowedColumns = ['price', 'name', 'created_at'];
    const sort = allowedColumns.includes(req.query.sort) ? req.query.sort : 'id';

  SQL Server (QUOTENAME):
    SET @sql = N'SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY ' + QUOTENAME(@sortColumn);
    -- Plus: validate @sortColumn against a whitelist

  Python:
    ALLOWED_SORTS = {'price', 'name', 'created_at'}
    sort_col = sort_input if sort_input in ALLOWED_SORTS else 'id'
    cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY {sort_col}")

Prevention:
  - Never directly concatenate user input into ORDER BY
  - Maintain a strict whitelist of allowed sort columns
  - Map user-provided sort keys to safe column names via a dictionary/enum
  - Use QUOTENAME() (SQL Server) as defense-in-depth
  - Validate sort direction is only ASC or DESC

title: Comment-Based SQL Filter Bypass
description: Detects SQL injection techniques that use SQL comments to bypass input filters, WAFs, and keyword detection. Covers inline comments (/* */), MySQL version comments (/*!...*/), single-line comments (-- and #), and comment insertion between SQL keywords to evade tokenization-based detection. These techniques are commonly used to bypass basic SQL injection filters that match on keyword adjacency.
impact:
Comment-based bypasses render keyword-based SQL injection filters ineffective.
Once the filter is bypassed, the attacker can execute any SQL injection
technique (UNION, stacked queries, blind injection) with full impact. This
technique is commonly used against WAFs and custom input filters, making
defense-in-depth critical.
remediation:
Parameterized Queries (primary defense):
  - Use parameterized queries/prepared statements exclusively
  - Comments bypass keyword filters but NOT parameterized queries
  - Never rely solely on input filtering for SQL injection prevention

WAF Configuration:
  - Configure WAF to detect comment patterns within SQL contexts
  - Enable comment normalization (strip comments before analysis)
  - Use semantic SQL parsing instead of regex-based detection
  - Block requests containing /**/ or /*!...*/ in query parameters

Filter Hardening (defense-in-depth only):
  - Normalize input by stripping comments before keyword matching
  - Use SQL tokenizer instead of regex for keyword detection
  - Implement whitelist validation instead of blacklist filtering
  - Detect hex encoding, URL encoding, and mixed-case evasion

title: Swift SQL Injection via String Interpolation
description: Detects SQL queries built with Swift string interpolation
impact: SQL injection leading to data breach or database compromise
remediation: Use SQLite parameter binding (sqlite3_bind_text) or GRDB/SQLite.swift query builders

title: Swift Command Injection
description: Detects OS command execution with user input in Swift
impact: Remote code execution through shell command injection
remediation: Use Process with explicit argument arrays, avoid shell interpretation

title: Swift XSS in WKWebView
description: Detects loading user-controlled content in WKWebView without sanitization
impact: XSS in WebView can access device APIs and steal app data
remediation: Sanitize HTML content before loading, use WKContentRuleList, validate URLs

title: Swift Hardcoded Credentials
description: Detects hardcoded secrets in Swift source code
impact: Credentials in source code can be extracted from compiled iOS/macOS apps
remediation: Use iOS Keychain, environment variables, or secure server-side configuration

title: Swift Insecure Keychain Configuration
description: Detects insecure Keychain access control settings
impact: Data accessible even when device is locked can be extracted by malware
remediation: Use kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly for sensitive data

title: Swift Weak Cryptography
description: Detects use of deprecated or weak crypto algorithms in Swift
impact: Weak hash functions can be reversed or collided
remediation: Use CryptoKit: SHA256, AES.GCM, P256 for signing

title: Swift Insecure TLS Configuration
description: Detects disabled TLS certificate validation in Swift
impact: Disabled TLS validation enables man-in-the-middle attacks
remediation: Enable proper TLS certificate validation, use certificate pinning

title: Swift Unsafe Deserialization
description: Detects unsafe deserialization in Swift using NSKeyedUnarchiver
impact: Unsafe deserialization can lead to arbitrary code execution
remediation: Use NSSecureCoding protocol and NSKeyedUnarchiver with specific class types

title: Swift Path Traversal
description: Detects path traversal vulnerabilities in Swift file operations
impact: Path traversal allows reading sensitive files from the device
remediation: Normalize paths and validate they stay within allowed directories

title: Swift Server-Side Request Forgery
description: Detects SSRF vulnerabilities in Swift Vapor/server-side applications
impact: SSRF allows access to internal services and cloud metadata endpoints
remediation: Validate and whitelist allowed URLs, block private IP ranges

title: Swift Remote Code Execution via Dynamic Library Loading
description: Detects dynamic library loading that could enable code injection
impact: Loading dynamic libraries from untrusted paths enables arbitrary code execution
remediation: Only load libraries from trusted, hardcoded paths within the app bundle

title: SQL Injection via Dynamic SQL (sp_executesql)
description: Detects dynamic SQL without parameterization in T-SQL.
impact:
T-SQL injection can compromise the SQL Server database, access linked servers,
enable xp_cmdshell for OS command execution, and exfiltrate data.

title: Dangerous Stored Procedure Usage
description: Detects use of dangerous extended stored procedures.
impact: Injection attacks can lead to data breach, unauthorized access, or system compromise
remediation: Use parameterized queries, input validation, and output encoding

title: SQL Injection via OPENROWSET/OPENDATASOURCE
description: Detects data access via OPENROWSET with dynamic connection strings.
impact: Injection attacks can lead to data breach, unauthorized access, or system compromise
remediation: Use parameterized queries, input validation, and output encoding

title: Excessive Database Privileges
description: Detects granting of excessive SQL Server privileges.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: Hardcoded SQL Server Credentials
description: Detects hardcoded credentials in T-SQL scripts.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: Guest User Enabled
description: Detects enabling guest user access on databases.
impact: Authentication and authorization flaws can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation
remediation: Implement strong authentication, proper session management, and principle of least privilege

title: Weak Encryption Algorithm
description: Detects use of weak encryption in SQL Server.
impact: Weak cryptography can be broken, compromising data confidentiality and integrity
remediation: Use industry-standard algorithms (AES-256-GCM, SHA-256+, Argon2) and proper key management

title: Trustworthy Database Setting
description: Detects TRUSTWORTHY database setting which can lead to privilege escalation.
impact: Framework misconfiguration can disable security controls and expose sensitive functionality
remediation: Follow framework security best practices, enable security features, review configuration

title: CLR Assembly Without SAFE Permission
description: Detects CLR assemblies with EXTERNAL_ACCESS or UNSAFE permissions.
impact: Framework misconfiguration can disable security controls and expose sensitive functionality
remediation: Follow framework security best practices, enable security features, review configuration

title: Linked Server with Hardcoded Credentials
description: Detects linked server configurations with embedded credentials.
impact: Exposed secrets enable unauthorized access to systems, APIs, and sensitive data
remediation: Use secret management systems, environment variables, and rotate exposed credentials immediately

title: SQL Agent Job with Credentials
description: Detects SQL Agent jobs with embedded credentials.
impact: Exposed secrets enable unauthorized access to systems, APIs, and sensitive data
remediation: Use secret management systems, environment variables, and rotate exposed credentials immediately

title: TypeORM Raw Query Injection
description: Detects SQL injection vulnerabilities in TypeORM raw query methods where user-controlled input is interpolated via template literals or string concatenation instead of using parameterized queries. Covers query(), createQueryBuilder().where(), manager.query(), and getRepository() raw methods with unsafe variable interpolation.
impact:
SQL injection through TypeORM raw queries can lead to full database compromise
including data exfiltration, authentication bypass, data modification, and in
some configurations remote code execution via database features.
remediation:
TypeORM Parameterized Queries:
  - Use query builder: .where("user.id = :id", { id })
  - Use parameterized raw query: connection.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", [id])
  - Use Repository methods: repository.findOne({ where: { id } })
  - Use QueryBuilder with setParameters: qb.where("name = :name").setParameters({ name })

Prevention:
  - Never use template literals with raw SQL methods
  - Enable ESLint rules to flag template literal SQL construction
  - Use TypeORM entity methods (.find, .findOne, .save) instead of raw queries
  - Implement input validation with class-validator or Zod at API boundaries

title: Prisma $queryRawUnsafe Injection
description: Detects SQL injection via Prisma's $queryRawUnsafe and $executeRawUnsafe methods which explicitly bypass Prisma's built-in parameterization. Also detects improper use of $queryRaw with template literals constructed via string concatenation rather than Prisma.sql tagged templates. Prisma provides safe tagged template support but developers sometimes bypass it.
impact:
Using $queryRawUnsafe or $executeRawUnsafe with interpolated user input
completely bypasses Prisma's SQL injection protections. This can lead to
full database compromise, data exfiltration, and data destruction.
remediation:
Prisma Safe Alternatives:
  - Tagged template: prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${userId}`
  - Prisma.sql: prisma.$queryRaw(Prisma.sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${userId}`)
  - Client API: prisma.user.findMany({ where: { id: userId } })
  - Prisma.join for IN clauses: Prisma.join([1, 2, 3])

Prevention:
  - Ban $queryRawUnsafe and $executeRawUnsafe via ESLint rules
  - Use Prisma Client API methods (.findMany, .create, .update) whenever possible
  - Validate all inputs with Zod or class-validator before any raw query usage
  - Code review all $queryRaw calls for proper tagged template usage
