title: NestJS Validation Pipe Bypass Injection
description: Detects injection vulnerabilities in NestJS applications where validation pipes are missing, misconfigured, or bypassed. Covers controllers using @Body(), @Query(), @Param() decorators without ValidationPipe, use of 'as any' to bypass type safety, missing class-validator decorators on DTOs, and direct use of raw request objects that skip the pipe pipeline entirely.
impact:
Missing or bypassed validation pipes allow unvalidated user input to reach
injection-sensitive functions. This can enable NoSQL injection, SQL injection,
prototype pollution, or command injection depending on the downstream sink.
remediation:
NestJS Validation:
  - Use class-validator decorators on all DTOs (@IsString, @IsInt, @IsUUID)
  - Enable global ValidationPipe: app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true }))
  - Use ParseIntPipe, ParseUUIDPipe for path/query parameters
  - Never use 'as any' on request input

Runtime Validation:
  - Use Zod schemas: const schema = z.object({ id: z.string().uuid() }); schema.parse(body)
  - Use class-transformer: plainToInstance(CreateUserDto, body)
  - Enable strict TypeScript: noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks

title: GraphQL Resolver Injection
description: Detects injection vulnerabilities in TypeScript GraphQL resolvers where user-supplied arguments are interpolated into database queries, system commands, or evaluated dynamically. Covers Apollo Server, TypeGraphQL, Nexus, and Mercurius resolver patterns where args or input types flow unsafely into SQL, NoSQL, or OS command sinks.
impact:
GraphQL resolver injection can enable SQL injection, NoSQL injection, or
command injection depending on the downstream sink. The GraphQL introspection
system can help attackers discover injection-vulnerable resolvers and craft
targeted payloads.
remediation:
GraphQL Validation:
  - Use TypeGraphQL @InputType with class-validator decorators
  - Use graphql-shield for resolver-level validation rules
  - Use custom GraphQL scalars (EmailAddress, UUID, DateTime) from graphql-scalars
  - Never pass raw args directly to database queries

Parameterization:
  - Use ORM methods: prisma.user.findMany({ where: { id: args.id } })
  - Use parameterized queries for raw SQL
  - Validate and whitelist filter operators for dynamic queries
  - Implement query depth and complexity limits

title: tRPC Input Injection
description: Detects injection vulnerabilities in tRPC procedures where input validation is missing, uses permissive schemas (z.any(), z.unknown(), z.record()), or is bypassed through type assertions. tRPC provides built-in Zod integration for input validation, but unvalidated or loosely validated inputs can flow into database queries, file operations, or command execution sinks.
impact:
Missing or permissive tRPC input validation allows arbitrary user input to
reach injection-sensitive sinks. Combined with Prisma $queryRawUnsafe or
direct database operations, this enables SQL injection, NoSQL injection,
or system command execution.
remediation:
tRPC Input Validation:
  - Always use strict Zod schemas: .input(z.object({ id: z.string().uuid(), search: z.string().max(100) }))
  - Never use z.any(), z.unknown(), or z.record(z.any())
  - Use z.enum() for known value sets
  - Use z.string().regex() for pattern-constrained inputs

Prevention:
  - Use Prisma Client API instead of raw queries
  - Parameterize all database queries
  - Add ESLint rule to flag z.any() in .input() calls
  - Use tRPC middleware for additional input sanitization

title: Drizzle ORM Raw SQL Injection
description: Detects SQL injection in Drizzle ORM usage where sql.raw(), sql.unsafe(), or template literal interpolation is used instead of Drizzle's safe sql`` tagged template literal. Drizzle provides sql`` for parameterized queries but developers may use unsafe alternatives when constructing dynamic queries with user input.
impact:
sql.raw() and sql.unsafe() in Drizzle ORM bypass parameterization, enabling
full SQL injection. This can lead to data exfiltration, data modification,
and depending on database configuration, remote code execution.
remediation:
Drizzle Safe Alternatives:
  - Tagged template: sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${userId}`
  - Query builder: db.select().from(users).where(eq(users.id, userId))
  - Placeholder: sql.placeholder('id') with prepared statements
  - Filter operators: eq(), like(), and(), or(), inArray()

Prevention:
  - Ban sql.raw() and sql.unsafe() via ESLint rules
  - Use drizzle-zod for input validation: createInsertSchema(users).parse(input)
  - Use Drizzle query builder methods exclusively
  - Code review all sql.raw() and db.execute() calls

title: Deno Subprocess Command Injection
description: Detects command injection vulnerabilities in Deno TypeScript applications where user-controlled input is passed to Deno.Command, Deno.run (deprecated), or subprocess APIs without sanitization. Deno's permission system controls subprocess access but does not prevent injection within allowed commands.
impact:
Command injection in Deno applications enables arbitrary code execution
within the bounds of Deno's permission flags. If --allow-run is granted
without restrictions, attackers gain full system access. Even with
restricted permissions, data exfiltration and denial of service are possible.
remediation:
Deno Security:
  - Use minimal Deno permissions: --allow-run=specific-command
  - Validate all subprocess arguments against allowlists
  - Never use shell mode (sh -c) with user input
  - Use Deno.Command with array args (not shell string)

Prevention:
  - Validate inputs with Zod: z.string().regex(/^[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+$/)
  - Use z.enum() for known command values
  - Implement path validation for file operations
  - Use Deno.permissions.request() for least-privilege

title: Bun Shell Command Injection
description: Detects command injection vulnerabilities in Bun TypeScript applications through Bun.spawn(), Bun.spawnSync(), Bun.$``, and Bun.file() APIs where user-controlled input is interpolated into commands or file paths. Bun's shell template literal (Bun.$``) provides some escaping but can still be vulnerable to injection when misused.
impact:
Bun applications run without a permission sandbox (unlike Deno), so command
injection provides unrestricted OS access. File operation injection enables
reading sensitive files, overwriting application code, or planting webshells.
Combined with Bun's performance focus, exploitation can be rapid and
difficult to detect.
remediation:
Bun Security:
  - Use Bun.spawn with array args (not shell string): Bun.spawn(['convert', input, '-resize', '100x100', output])
  - Validate all file paths against base directory: path.resolve(base, input).startsWith(base)
  - Never use Bun.$`` with unvalidated user input
  - Use Bun.file() only with validated, resolved paths

Prevention:
  - Validate inputs with Zod: z.string().regex(/^[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+$/)
  - Use z.enum() for known command/file values
  - Run Bun applications in containers with minimal privileges
  - Implement path allowlisting for file operations
  - Use seccomp/AppArmor profiles to restrict system calls

title: TypeScript SQL Injection via Template Literal
description: Detects SQL queries built with template literals in TypeScript
impact: SQL injection through TypeScript template literals
remediation: Use parameterized queries with TypeORM, Prisma, or Knex parameter binding

title: TypeScript NoSQL Injection
description: Detects NoSQL injection in TypeScript MongoDB operations
impact: NoSQL injection can bypass authentication or exfiltrate data
remediation: Validate input types, sanitize with mongo-sanitize, avoid $where operator

title: TypeScript Command Injection
description: Detects command injection via child_process in TypeScript
impact: Command injection enables arbitrary code execution
remediation: Use execFile with argument arrays, avoid shell interpretation

title: TypeScript JWT Without Verification
description: Detects JWT decoding without signature verification
impact: JWT decode without verify allows forged tokens to bypass authentication
remediation: Always use jwt.verify() with algorithm restriction and strong secret/key

title: TypeScript Insecure Session Configuration
description: Detects insecure session cookie settings in TypeScript web apps
impact: Insecure cookies can be stolen via XSS or transmitted over unencrypted connections
remediation: Set secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'strict', and use HTTPS

title: TypeScript Hardcoded Credentials
description: Detects hardcoded secrets in TypeScript source code
impact: Hardcoded credentials in source code can be extracted from repositories
remediation: Use environment variables (process.env) or secret management services

title: TypeScript Weak Cryptography
description: Detects weak hashing or encryption in TypeScript
impact: Weak algorithms can be broken, compromising data integrity
remediation: Use sha256+ for hashing, aes-256-gcm for encryption, bcrypt/argon2 for passwords

title: TypeScript React dangerouslySetInnerHTML
description: Detects use of dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user input in TypeScript React
impact: Cross-site scripting through unsanitized HTML injection in React components

title: os.Open with User-Controlled File Path
description: Detects usage of Go's os.Open, os.OpenFile, os.Create, and os.ReadFile where the file path argument originates from user-controlled input such as HTTP request parameters, URL path segments, form values, or JSON body fields. An attacker can inject path traversal sequences like ../../etc/passwd to read or write arbitrary files on the server filesystem. Go does not perform any automatic path validation in its os package functions, making explicit validation essential.
impact:
Successful exploitation reads arbitrary files from the Go server's
filesystem including /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, application configuration
files, environment variables, private keys, TLS certificates, database
credentials, and source code. Write operations via os.Create or os.OpenFile
with O_WRONLY can overwrite configuration, inject code into template files,
or corrupt critical data. Go binaries often run with elevated privileges,
amplifying the impact.
remediation:
1. Clean and validate the resolved path:

   cleanPath := filepath.Clean(userInput)
   absPath, err := filepath.Abs(filepath.Join(baseDir, cleanPath))
   if err != nil || !strings.HasPrefix(absPath, filepath.Clean(baseDir)+string(os.PathSeparator)) {
       http.Error(w, "Forbidden", http.StatusForbidden)
       return
   }
   f, err := os.Open(absPath)

2. Use filepath.Base() for filename-only access:

   safeName := filepath.Base(userInput)
   f, err := os.Open(filepath.Join(uploadsDir, safeName))

3. Use github.com/cyphar/filepath-securejoin for safe joins.
4. Reject inputs containing '..' or path separators.
5. Use file ID mappings instead of raw path input.

title: filepath.Join with Unsanitized User Input
description: Detects usage of Go's filepath.Join or path.Join where path segments originate from unsanitized user input. While filepath.Join calls filepath.Clean internally to normalize separators and remove redundant elements, it does NOT prevent traversal. filepath.Join("/base", "../../etc/passwd") correctly resolves to /etc/passwd if the process has access. Unlike Python's os.path.join, Go's filepath.Join does not have the absolute path override behavior, but traversal sequences still escape the base directory.
impact:
An attacker escapes the intended directory by injecting traversal
sequences through filepath.Join. Since Go's filepath.Join normalizes
but does not constrain traversal, the resolved path can access any
file on the filesystem. This enables reading application configuration,
database credentials, TLS keys, and source code. Write operations can
modify binary executables, configuration, or deploy backdoors.
remediation:
1. Validate the resolved path stays within the base directory:

   base, _ := filepath.Abs(baseDir)
   target, _ := filepath.Abs(filepath.Join(base, userInput))
   if !strings.HasPrefix(target, base+string(os.PathSeparator)) {
       http.Error(w, "Forbidden", http.StatusForbidden)
       return
   }

2. Use filepath.Base() for filename-only operations:

   safeName := filepath.Base(userInput)
   fullPath := filepath.Join(uploadsDir, safeName)

3. Use github.com/cyphar/filepath-securejoin:

   safePath, err := securejoin.SecureJoin(baseDir, userInput)

4. Reject inputs containing '..' or path separators.
5. Use file ID mappings instead of raw paths.

title: http.ServeFile Path Traversal
description: Detects path traversal vulnerabilities in Go's http.ServeFile function where the file path is constructed using user-controlled input. While http.ServeFile includes basic protection by cleaning the URL path with path.Clean, it does NOT protect against traversal when the file path argument itself is derived from user input through other means, such as query parameters, router variables, or custom path parsing. This pattern is frequently found in custom file serving handlers in Go web applications.
impact:
An attacker can download arbitrary files from the server through
http.ServeFile by injecting traversal sequences into the path parameter.
Sensitive targets include application configuration, database connection
strings, TLS private keys, credentials files, and Go source code. On
Linux deployments, /proc/self/environ reveals environment variables
containing secrets. The http.ServeFile function properly handles MIME
types and range requests, making it efficient for attackers to exfiltrate
large files.
remediation:
1. Validate paths before passing to http.ServeFile:

   safePath, err := filepath.Abs(filepath.Join(docRoot, userInput))
   if err != nil || !strings.HasPrefix(safePath, filepath.Clean(docRoot)+string(os.PathSeparator)) {
       http.Error(w, "Forbidden", http.StatusForbidden)
       return
   }
   http.ServeFile(w, r, safePath)

2. Use http.FileServer with http.Dir for directory-constrained serving:

   http.Handle("/static/", http.StripPrefix("/static/", http.FileServer(http.Dir("./public"))))

3. Use filepath.Base() for single-file serving.
4. Implement file ID mappings instead of path parameters.
5. Use securejoin for safe path construction.

title: ioutil.ReadFile / os.ReadFile with User-Controlled Input
description: Detects usage of Go's ioutil.ReadFile (deprecated) or os.ReadFile (Go 1.16+) where the file path originates from user-controlled input. These functions read an entire file into memory and are commonly used for configuration loading, template rendering, and data processing. When the path is derived from HTTP parameters, router variables, or form data without validation, attackers can read arbitrary files. The simplicity of these one-liner file reads makes them especially common in quick handlers vulnerable to traversal.
impact:
ReadFile reads the entire file into memory and returns it as a byte
slice, making it trivial for an attacker to exfiltrate complete file
contents in a single request. High-value targets include: Go application
configuration files, .env and environment files, TLS private keys and
certificates, database credential files, SSH private keys, /proc/self/environ
for environment variable exposure, and application source code. The
memory-efficient read makes even large files like database dumps
exfiltrable.
remediation:
1. Validate path before reading:

   base, _ := filepath.Abs(dataDir)
   target, _ := filepath.Abs(filepath.Join(base, userInput))
   if !strings.HasPrefix(target, base+string(os.PathSeparator)) {
       http.Error(w, "Forbidden", http.StatusForbidden)
       return
   }
   data, err := os.ReadFile(target)

2. Use filepath.Base() for filename-only reads:

   safeName := filepath.Base(userInput)
   data, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dataDir, safeName))

3. Use securejoin for safe path construction.
4. Implement file allowlists or ID-based lookups.
5. Set file size limits with io.LimitReader on os.Open.

title: archive/zip Extraction Path Traversal (ZIP Slip)
description: Detects ZIP Slip vulnerabilities when extracting ZIP or TAR archives using Go's archive/zip or archive/tar packages without validating that extracted file paths remain within the target directory. Go's archive packages do not prevent path traversal by default. An attacker can craft malicious archives with entries containing ../../ paths that write files to arbitrary filesystem locations during extraction, leading to remote code execution via binary or script overwrite.
impact:
ZIP Slip in Go enables writing arbitrary files during archive extraction.
Go binaries often run as system services with elevated privileges.
Exploitation scenarios include: overwriting the Go binary itself for
persistent RCE, writing to system cron directories for scheduled
execution, replacing systemd service units, modifying /etc/passwd or
authorized_keys for persistent access, and deploying reverse shells.
Container environments are also vulnerable if the extraction directory
shares a mount with sensitive paths.

title: net/http.FileServer Directory Escape
description: Detects path traversal vulnerabilities in Go's http.FileServer and http.Dir configuration. While http.FileServer with http.Dir provides basic path cleaning, certain configurations can be exploited: using a custom http.FileSystem implementation without proper validation, combining http.StripPrefix with incorrect prefix patterns, or passing user-controlled values to http.Dir. Additionally, http.FileServer exposes directory listings by default, which aids attackers in reconnaissance. Symlink traversal within the served directory can also escape the intended scope.
impact:
Directory escape through http.FileServer enables access to files outside
the intended static file directory. Combined with default directory
listing, attackers can enumerate the server filesystem structure, identify
sensitive files, and download them. Custom FileSystem implementations
without proper validation are particularly dangerous as they bypass
http.Dir's built-in cleaning. Symlink traversal within the served
directory can access any file on the filesystem even when http.Dir is
properly configured. This aids in reconnaissance and targeted
file exfiltration.

title: FileInputStream with User-Controlled Path
description: Detects usage of Java's FileInputStream, FileOutputStream, FileReader, and FileWriter constructors where the file path argument originates from user-controlled input such as servlet request parameters, HTTP headers, path variables, or multipart form data. An attacker can inject path traversal sequences like ../../etc/passwd to read or write arbitrary files on the server filesystem, leading to information disclosure, credential theft, or arbitrary file write for code execution.
impact:
Successful exploitation reads arbitrary files from the server, including
/etc/passwd, application.properties, web.xml, persistence.xml, private
keys, and database credentials. Write variants via FileOutputStream can
overwrite JSP/servlet files for code execution, modify configuration for
privilege escalation, or corrupt application data. In Java EE environments,
this can expose JNDI datasource passwords and application server credentials.

title: Paths.get with Unsanitized User Input
description: Detects usage of java.nio.file.Paths.get() or Path.of() where path segments incorporate user-controlled input without validation. While Path.normalize() removes redundant elements, it does NOT prevent traversal if the result is not validated against a base directory. Paths.get("/base", "../../etc/passwd").normalize() resolves to /etc/passwd. This pattern is common in modern Java applications using NIO.2 file APIs and is often found in Spring Boot and Jakarta EE applications.
impact:
Exploitation allows reading arbitrary files through NIO Path APIs,
including application.properties/yml with database credentials and API
keys, WEB-INF/web.xml deployment descriptors, keystore files with
private keys, and system files like /etc/passwd. Write operations via
Files.write() can modify application class files, configuration, or
inject JSP web shells. In Spring Boot applications, actuator endpoints
and auto-configuration secrets are high-value targets.

title: Spring Resource Loading Path Traversal
description: Detects path traversal vulnerabilities in Spring Framework resource loading mechanisms where user-controlled input is used to construct resource paths. This includes ResourceLoader.getResource(), ClassPathResource, FileSystemResource, UrlResource, and ResponseEntity with Resource bodies. Spring's resource abstraction does not inherently prevent traversal, and user input in resource identifiers such as file:, classpath:, or direct paths can be exploited to access arbitrary files.
impact:
Exploitation of Spring resource loading enables access to sensitive files
through the framework's resource abstraction. Attackers can read
application.properties/yml with all configured secrets, Spring Boot
actuator credentials, database connection strings, JWT signing keys,
and OAuth2 client secrets. In Spring Boot fat-jar deployments, classpath
traversal can expose embedded configuration. FileSystemResource-based
attacks access the entire filesystem.

title: ServletContext.getResourceAsStream Path Traversal Bypass
description: Detects path traversal vulnerabilities in Java Servlet applications using ServletContext.getResourceAsStream() or ServletContext.getResource() where the resource path contains user-controlled input. These methods are designed to access resources within the web application context but can be exploited to access files outside the web root through traversal sequences. The servlet container's path normalization may not provide complete protection, especially with encoded sequences.
impact:
ServletContext resource access exploitation exposes WEB-INF directory
contents including web.xml (servlet mappings, security constraints, init
parameters), application class files (potential decompilation for source
exposure), persistence.xml (database credentials), context.xml (JNDI
resource definitions), and property files. getRealPath traversal can
access any file on the filesystem. This information enables further
targeted attacks against the application and infrastructure.

title: ZIP Slip via ZipInputStream
description: Detects ZIP Slip vulnerabilities in Java applications extracting ZIP archives using ZipInputStream, ZipFile, or JarInputStream without validating that entry paths remain within the target directory. Java's ZIP API does not prevent path traversal by default, and maliciously crafted archives can contain entries with ../../ paths that write files to arbitrary filesystem locations. This vulnerability class has affected major Java libraries including Apache Commons Compress, Spring Integration, and various build tools.
impact:
ZIP Slip in Java enables writing arbitrary files during archive extraction.
Common attack vectors include: overwriting JSP/Servlet class files for
remote code execution, deploying WAR files to application server auto-deploy
directories, modifying application.properties for configuration injection,
overwriting JAR files in the classpath for persistent backdoor, and writing
to cron directories or systemd paths for scheduled execution. This
vulnerability class has resulted in CVEs in Apache Ant, Spring Integration,
Gradle, and many other Java tools.

title: File.getCanonicalPath Bypass Attempts
description: Detects patterns where File.getCanonicalPath() or Path.toRealPath() are used for path traversal validation but implemented incorrectly, creating a false sense of security. Common bypasses include: checking canonical path without proper prefix comparison, TOCTOU (time-of-check/time-of-use) race conditions where the filesystem changes between validation and access, symlink resolution differences between getCanonicalPath and actual file access, and incomplete startsWith checks that match directory name prefixes (e.g., /uploads-backup matching /uploads).
impact:
Bypassing canonical path validation nullifies the intended security
control while giving developers false confidence. This enables the same
impacts as unprotected file access: reading sensitive configuration,
credentials, and keys; writing to arbitrary locations for code execution;
and filesystem manipulation. The TOCTOU variant is particularly dangerous
in multi-threaded Java applications where race conditions between
validation and file access can be exploited reliably.

title: fs.readFile/writeFile with User-Controlled Path
description: Detects usage of Node.js fs.readFile, fs.readFileSync, fs.writeFile, and fs.writeFileSync where the file path argument originates from user input such as request parameters, query strings, headers, or body fields. An attacker can inject path traversal sequences like ../../etc/passwd to read or overwrite arbitrary files on the server filesystem, potentially exfiltrating sensitive configuration, credentials, or source code, or corrupting critical application data.
impact:
Successful exploitation allows an attacker to read arbitrary files from the
server filesystem, including /etc/passwd, environment files, application
source code, private keys, database credentials, and session secrets.
Write-variant exploitation enables overwriting configuration files, injecting
malicious code into application files, or corrupting critical data. This can
lead to full server compromise, data breach, and lateral movement within the
infrastructure.

title: path.join with Unsanitized User Input
description: Detects usage of Node.js path.join where one or more path segments originate from unsanitized user input. While path.join normalizes path separators, it does NOT prevent traversal — path.join('/base', '../../etc/passwd') resolves to /etc/passwd. Developers often mistakenly believe path.join provides safety, making this a widespread and dangerous pattern.
impact:
An attacker can escape the intended directory scope by injecting traversal
sequences into path segments. Since path.join normalizes but does not
restrict traversal, the resulting path can point anywhere on the filesystem.
This leads to arbitrary file read/write, information disclosure, or
denial of service through file overwrite/deletion.

title: Express Static File Serving Bypass
description: Detects insecure patterns in Express.js static file serving where user-controlled input can bypass the intended directory restriction via res.sendFile, res.download, or improperly configured express.static middleware. This includes direct use of user input in res.sendFile without root option or path validation, custom static file handlers that do not properly constrain the served directory, and misconfigured dotfiles options.
impact:
An attacker can download arbitrary files from the server by injecting
path traversal sequences into file download or static serving endpoints.
Sensitive files such as application configuration, environment variables,
database credentials, TLS private keys, and other users' uploaded files
can be exfiltrated. In severe cases, source code exposure reveals
additional vulnerabilities for chained exploitation.

title: Multer Upload Path Traversal
description: Detects path traversal vulnerabilities in multer file upload configurations where the destination directory or filename callback uses unsanitized user input. An attacker can craft a multipart upload with a filename containing traversal sequences such as ../../../tmp/malicious.js to write files outside the intended upload directory. This can lead to remote code execution if the traversal targets executable paths, or overwrite critical application files.
impact:
Successful exploitation allows an attacker to write uploaded files to
arbitrary locations on the server filesystem. This can result in:
overwriting application source files for code injection, placing web shells
in publicly accessible directories, overwriting configuration files to
modify application behavior, or writing to cron directories for scheduled
code execution. The impact ranges from data corruption to full remote
code execution.

title: ZIP Slip via adm-zip or archiver Libraries
description: Detects ZIP Slip vulnerabilities when extracting ZIP archives using adm-zip, archiver, or similar Node.js libraries without validating that extracted file paths remain within the target directory. A maliciously crafted ZIP archive can contain entries with path traversal sequences (e.g., ../../malicious.js), causing files to be extracted to arbitrary filesystem locations. This is one of the most impactful path traversal variants as it often leads to remote code execution.
impact:
ZIP Slip enables an attacker to write arbitrary files to the server
filesystem during archive extraction. Common exploitation scenarios
include: overwriting application source code or configuration for RCE,
placing web shells in document roots, overwriting crontab entries for
persistent access, and replacing SSH authorized_keys for remote login.
This vulnerability class has led to numerous critical CVEs across
multiple languages and frameworks.

title: Directory Listing via User-Controlled Directory Path
description: Detects usage of fs.readdir, fs.readdirSync, or fs.promises.readdir where the directory path originates from user-controlled input. An attacker can inject path traversal sequences to enumerate files and directories outside the intended scope, revealing the server's filesystem structure, identifying sensitive files for subsequent targeted access, and mapping the application deployment for further exploitation.
impact:
Directory listing allows an attacker to enumerate the server filesystem
structure, revealing filenames, directory hierarchies, and potentially
sensitive file locations. This information is used to identify targets for
subsequent file read attacks (e.g., configuration files, key files, source
code). Even without directly reading file contents, the listing can expose
business-sensitive information through filenames and directory names. It
also aids in fingerprinting the application framework, identifying backup
files, and locating hidden administrative interfaces.

title: file_get_contents / fopen with User-Controlled Path
description: Detects usage of PHP's file_get_contents(), fopen(), fread(), fwrite(), and file_put_contents() where the file path argument originates from user-controlled input such as $_GET, $_POST, $_REQUEST, $_COOKIE, or $_SERVER variables. An attacker can inject path traversal sequences like ../../etc/passwd to read or write arbitrary files on the server filesystem. PHP's file functions also support stream wrappers (php://, data://, file://) which can amplify the attack surface beyond simple path traversal to include SSRF and code execution vectors.
impact:
Successful exploitation reads arbitrary files from the PHP server including
configuration files (config.php, wp-config.php, .env), database credentials,
PHP source code (revealing additional vulnerabilities), private keys, and
system files (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow). PHP stream wrappers amplify the
attack: php://filter can base64-encode source code to bypass binary
detection, php://input enables request body injection, and data:// can
execute arbitrary code. file_put_contents exploitation enables writing
PHP web shells for persistent RCE.

title: include / require with User-Controlled Input (LFI/RFI)
description: Detects Local File Inclusion (LFI) and Remote File Inclusion (RFI) vulnerabilities where PHP's include, include_once, require, or require_once statements use paths derived from user-controlled input. Unlike simple file read, include/require executes the included file as PHP code, making this a direct remote code execution vector. Combined with log poisoning, PHP filter chains, or uploaded files, even local-only inclusion achieves full RCE. This is among the most critical PHP vulnerability patterns.
impact:
LFI/RFI through include/require is among the most critical PHP
vulnerabilities. Impact includes: direct remote code execution by including
uploaded files, log files with injected PHP code, or PHP filter chains;
full source code disclosure of the application; database credential
extraction from configuration files; session hijacking by reading
session files; and with allow_url_include enabled, remote file inclusion
from attacker-controlled servers for instant RCE. This vulnerability
pattern has been the root cause of countless major web application
compromises.

title: ZipArchive Extraction Path Traversal (ZIP Slip)
description: Detects ZIP Slip vulnerabilities when using PHP's ZipArchive class to extract archives without validating that extracted file paths remain within the target directory. The ZipArchive::extractTo() method does not prevent path traversal, and maliciously crafted ZIP files can contain entries with ../../ paths that write files outside the extraction directory. Manual extraction loops using ZipArchive::getFromIndex() or ZipArchive::getStream() are similarly vulnerable. This can lead to PHP web shell deployment and remote code execution.
impact:
ZIP Slip in PHP enables writing files to arbitrary locations on the web
server. The most common and impactful exploit is deploying a PHP web
shell (<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>) into the document root for
immediate RCE. Other scenarios include: overwriting .htaccess for
configuration hijacking, modifying wp-config.php or equivalent files
for credential injection, placing backdoor code in existing PHP files,
and writing to cron directories for persistent access. PHP web
applications are particularly vulnerable because any .php file in the
document root is executable.

title: readfile / file() with User-Controlled Path
description: Detects usage of PHP's readfile(), file(), file_exists(), is_file(), is_readable(), and similar file functions where the path argument originates from user-controlled input. readfile() is particularly dangerous as it reads a file and directly writes it to the output buffer, making it ideal for file download endpoints. file() reads the entire file into an array. Both functions honor PHP stream wrappers, amplifying the attack surface. Even information-leaking functions like file_exists() can be used for path enumeration and timing-based attacks.
impact:
readfile() directly outputs file contents to the browser, making it
the ideal function for file download exploitation. An attacker exfiltrates
configuration files (wp-config.php, config.php, .env), database credentials,
PHP source code, private keys, and system files. file() reads files into
arrays, enabling line-by-line processing of sensitive data. Even
file_exists() leaks information about the server filesystem, enabling
targeted attacks. With PHP stream wrappers, readfile() can also be used
for SSRF via http:// and https:// protocols.

title: realpath() Bypass Techniques in PHP
description: Detects patterns where PHP's realpath() function is used for path traversal validation but implemented incorrectly, creating a false sense of security. Common bypass scenarios include: not checking realpath()'s false return for non-existent files, using strpos instead of str_starts_with for prefix matching (allowing /uploads-backup to match /uploads), TOCTOU race conditions between realpath() check and actual file operation, not accounting for symlinks, and using realpath() on the user input directly instead of the joined path.
impact:
Flawed realpath() validation provides no actual protection against path
traversal while giving developers a false sense of security. Bypasses
enable all the same impacts as unprotected file access: reading
configuration files, PHP source code with credentials, private keys,
and system files. The TOCTOU variant is exploitable in concurrent
request scenarios on shared hosting. Non-recursive blacklist replacement
is trivially bypassed with payloads like ....// which after replacement
become ../ again.

title: SplFileObject Path Traversal
description: Detects path traversal vulnerabilities in PHP's SplFileObject, SplFileInfo, DirectoryIterator, RecursiveDirectoryIterator, and FilesystemIterator where the path argument originates from user-controlled input. These SPL (Standard PHP Library) classes provide object-oriented file operations and may be overlooked in security audits that focus on traditional PHP file functions. SplFileObject in particular provides read/write capabilities, making it equivalent to fopen() in terms of risk but often not covered by static analysis tools.
impact:
SplFileObject provides full file read/write capabilities equivalent to
fopen()/fread()/fwrite(). An attacker can read sensitive files, write
arbitrary content, and create new files. DirectoryIterator and
RecursiveDirectoryIterator enable complete filesystem enumeration,
revealing file names, sizes, permissions, and directory structure.
This information is critical for planning targeted file read/write
attacks. SPL file classes are often overlooked by WAFs and static
analysis tools, making them attractive for attackers bypassing file
function monitoring.

title: open() with User-Controlled File Path
description: Detects usage of Python's built-in open() function where the file path argument originates from user-controlled input such as request parameters, form data, URL route variables, or query strings. An attacker can inject path traversal sequences like ../../etc/passwd to read or write arbitrary files on the server filesystem, leading to exposure of sensitive data, credentials, source code, or destructive file overwrites.
impact:
Successful exploitation allows an attacker to read arbitrary files from the
server filesystem, including /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, application source
code, database configuration files, API keys, private keys, and session
secrets. When open() is used in write mode, attackers can overwrite
configuration files, inject malicious code into Python modules, or corrupt
application data. This leads to full information disclosure, credential
theft, and potential remote code execution through code injection.
remediation:
1. Validate resolved paths against a base directory:

   import os
   base_dir = os.path.abspath('/app/uploads')
   requested = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(base_dir, user_input))
   if not requested.startswith(base_dir + os.sep):
       abort(403)
   with open(requested, 'r') as f:
       content = f.read()

2. Use os.path.basename() for filename-only access:

   safe_name = os.path.basename(user_input)
   filepath = os.path.join(upload_dir, safe_name)

3. Use pathlib with is_relative_to() (Python 3.9+):

   from pathlib import Path
   base = Path('/app/uploads').resolve()
   target = (base / user_input).resolve()
   if not target.is_relative_to(base):
       abort(403)

4. Maintain an allowlist of accessible files.
5. Never pass raw user input directly to open().

title: os.path.join with User-Controlled Path Segments
description: Detects usage of os.path.join where one or more path segments originate from user input. A critical Python-specific behavior makes this especially dangerous: if any segment is an absolute path, os.path.join discards all preceding segments. For example, os.path.join('/safe/dir', '/etc/passwd') returns '/etc/passwd'. Even without absolute paths, traversal sequences like ../../ can escape the intended directory. Developers often mistakenly assume os.path.join provides path safety.
impact:
Exploitation of os.path.join with user-controlled segments can bypass any
intended directory restriction. The absolute path behavior is especially
dangerous as it silently discards the base directory. This enables
arbitrary file read/write, leading to credential theft, source code
exposure, configuration manipulation, and potential remote code execution
through file overwrite. In Django applications, this can expose settings.py
containing SECRET_KEY and database credentials.
remediation:
1. Validate resolved paths against the intended base:

   import os
   base_dir = os.path.abspath(UPLOAD_DIR)
   full_path = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(base_dir, user_input))
   if not full_path.startswith(base_dir + os.sep):
       raise PermissionError("Path traversal detected")

2. Reject absolute paths from user input:

   if os.path.isabs(user_input):
       raise ValueError("Absolute paths not allowed")

3. Use os.path.basename() for filename-only access.
4. Strip leading slashes and '..' before joining.
5. Use pathlib.Path.is_relative_to() for validation.

title: Flask send_file / send_from_directory Path Traversal Bypass
description: Detects insecure usage of Flask's send_file() and send_from_directory() functions where user-controlled input is passed without adequate validation. While send_from_directory includes basic traversal protection, it can be bypassed in certain configurations. Direct use of send_file() with user input is always dangerous. This rule also covers custom file serving handlers that replicate send_file behavior without its protections.
impact:
Successful exploitation allows an attacker to download arbitrary files from
the server through Flask file serving endpoints. This includes application
configuration (settings.py, .env), database credentials, private keys,
source code revealing additional vulnerabilities, and other users' uploaded
files. In production Flask deployments, this can expose the SECRET_KEY
enabling session forgery and CSRF bypass.
remediation:
1. Always use secure_filename() for user-provided filenames:

   from werkzeug.utils import secure_filename
   safe_name = secure_filename(request.args.get('file'))
   return send_from_directory(app.config['UPLOAD_FOLDER'], safe_name)

2. Validate paths after resolution:

   import os
   base = os.path.abspath(app.config['UPLOAD_FOLDER'])
   requested = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(base, user_input))
   if not requested.startswith(base + os.sep):
       abort(403)
   return send_file(requested)

3. Use Flask safe_join() for path construction.
4. Maintain allowlists of downloadable files.
5. Avoid send_file() with user input; prefer send_from_directory().

title: Django FileResponse Path Traversal
description: Detects path traversal vulnerabilities in Django applications using FileResponse, HttpResponse with file content, or StreamingHttpResponse where the file path originates from user input. Django does not provide built-in path traversal protection in FileResponse, making it critical to validate file paths before serving. This includes views that construct file paths from URL parameters, query strings, or POST data for document download functionality.
impact:
An attacker can download arbitrary files through Django file serving views,
including settings.py (exposing SECRET_KEY, database credentials, and API
keys), environment files, application source code, database files (SQLite),
and other sensitive data. With SECRET_KEY exposure, the attacker can forge
session cookies, CSRF tokens, and signed data, leading to full
authentication bypass and privilege escalation.
remediation:
1. Validate file paths against the intended base directory:

   import os
   from django.conf import settings

   base = os.path.abspath(settings.MEDIA_ROOT)
   requested = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(base, user_input))
   if not requested.startswith(base + os.sep):
       raise PermissionDenied("Path traversal detected")
   return FileResponse(open(requested, 'rb'))

2. Use database lookups instead of direct path construction:

   doc = get_object_or_404(Document, pk=doc_id, owner=request.user)
   return FileResponse(open(doc.file.path, 'rb'))

3. Use Django's built-in SuspiciousFileOperation protection.
4. Validate filenames with os.path.basename().
5. Restrict file serving to authenticated users with ownership checks.

title: ZIP Slip via Python zipfile Module
description: Detects ZIP Slip vulnerabilities when using Python's zipfile module to extract archives without validating that extracted file paths remain within the target directory. The zipfile.extractall() and zipfile.extract() methods do not prevent path traversal by default in older Python versions, and maliciously crafted ZIP files can contain entries with ../../ paths that write files outside the extraction directory. While Python 3.12+ added protections, many deployments use older versions.
impact:
ZIP Slip in Python enables writing arbitrary files during archive extraction.
Exploitation scenarios include: overwriting application source code for
backdoor injection, placing WSGI/ASGI handler files for web shell access,
modifying Django/Flask settings for configuration injection, overwriting
crontab or systemd service files for persistent access, and replacing SSH
authorized_keys for remote login. Python versions before 3.12 are
particularly vulnerable as zipfile does not validate entry paths.
remediation:
1. Validate each entry path before extraction:

   import zipfile, os

   def safe_extract(zip_path, dest_dir):
       dest = os.path.abspath(dest_dir)
       with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path) as zf:
           for info in zf.infolist():
               target = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(dest, info.filename))
               if not target.startswith(dest + os.sep):
                   raise ValueError(f"Traversal detected: {info.filename}")
           zf.extractall(dest)

2. Use os.path.basename() for flat extraction:

   for info in zf.infolist():
       safe_name = os.path.basename(info.filename)
       if safe_name:
           target = os.path.join(dest_dir, safe_name)
           with open(target, 'wb') as f:
               f.write(zf.read(info.filename))

3. Upgrade to Python 3.12+ which includes built-in protection.
4. Extract to a temporary directory and validate before moving.

title: shutil.copy with User-Controlled Paths
description: Detects usage of shutil.copy, shutil.copy2, shutil.copyfile, shutil.move, and shutil.copytree where source or destination paths incorporate user-controlled input. An attacker can inject path traversal sequences to copy sensitive files to accessible locations (for exfiltration), overwrite critical files with attacker-controlled content, or move files to achieve denial of service or code execution. The shutil module performs no path validation internally.
impact:
Exploitation of shutil operations with user-controlled paths enables
multiple attack scenarios: copying /etc/shadow or settings.py to a web-
accessible directory for download, overwriting application code with
malicious files, moving critical files to cause denial of service, and
copying web shells into document roots for persistent backdoor access.
The bidirectional nature (both source and destination controlled) makes
this especially versatile for attackers.
remediation:
1. Validate both source and destination against allowed directories:

   import os, shutil

   def safe_copy(src_input, dst_input, allowed_src, allowed_dst):
       src = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(allowed_src, src_input))
       dst = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(allowed_dst, dst_input))
       if not src.startswith(allowed_src + os.sep):
           raise PermissionError("Source traversal detected")
       if not dst.startswith(allowed_dst + os.sep):
           raise PermissionError("Destination traversal detected")
       shutil.copy2(src, dst)

2. Use os.path.basename() for filename-only operations.
3. Implement file ID mappings instead of accepting raw paths.
4. Run file operations in chroot or container isolation.
5. Log all file copy/move operations for audit trail.

title: Path Traversal in ASP.NET File Operations
description: Detects .NET file operations with user-controlled paths, enabling directory traversal to access arbitrary files on the server through ASP.NET web applications.
impact:
Directory traversal in ASP.NET enabling arbitrary file access, including
appsettings.json with connection strings, web.config with machine keys,
and application source code. On Windows, uses backslash traversal (..\\).
remediation:
- Use Path.GetFileName() to extract filename
- Validate Path.GetFullPath(input).StartsWith(allowedRoot)
- Use [FromRoute] with strict routing constraints
- Implement IFileProvider for controlled file access
- Framework-specific validation:
  - ASP.NET Core: Use IFileProvider (PhysicalFileProvider) with root-constrained access
  - ASP.NET Core: Use FileExtensionContentTypeProvider for validated content types
  - ASP.NET Core: Use StaticFileOptions with FileProvider and RequestPath restrictions
  - ASP.NET MVC: Use FilePathResult with Server.MapPath validation against AppDomain.CurrentDomain.BaseDirectory
  - Blazor: Use IWebHostEnvironment.ContentRootPath as the base for file path validation
  - ASP.NET Core: Apply [RegularExpression] attribute on route parameters for filename constraints
- Canonical path validation pattern:
    var fullPath = Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(baseDir, userInput));
    if (!fullPath.StartsWith(Path.GetFullPath(baseDir) + Path.DirectorySeparatorChar))
        return Forbid();
- Handle both forward slash (/) and backslash (\\) traversal on Windows
- Use Microsoft.Extensions.FileProviders for sandboxed file access

title: Command Injection via os/exec
description: Detects remote code execution via os/exec.Command where user-controlled input is passed to shell interpreters or as command arguments without validation. Covers exec.Command, exec.CommandContext, and shell wrapping.
impact:
Remote code execution enabling complete server compromise, data
exfiltration, ransomware deployment, and lateral movement.
remediation:
Avoid shell invocation. Pass arguments separately:
  exec.Command("ping", "-c", "4", validatedHost) // SAFE
  exec.Command("sh", "-c", userInput) // UNSAFE
Use Go stdlib functions instead of shell commands when possible.

title: Dynamic Plugin Loading from User Input
description: Detects plugin.Open with user-controlled paths enabling loading of arbitrary shared objects for code execution. Covers path traversal to malicious plugins and user-controlled symbol lookup.
impact:
Loading a malicious plugin achieves full arbitrary code execution
in the application process with all its privileges and access.

title: Unsafe Deserialization via encoding/gob
description: Detects unsafe deserialization of user-controlled data via encoding/gob, encoding/json with interface{} targets, or custom unmarshalers that may instantiate arbitrary types.
impact:
Unsafe deserialization can lead to arbitrary type instantiation,
method invocation on deserialized objects, and potential RCE if
custom UnmarshalBinary/UnmarshalJSON implementations have side effects.
remediation:
Decode into strongly-typed structs, not interface{}:
  var user UserRequest // typed struct
  json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&user)
Avoid gob for untrusted network data. Validate size limits.

title: Template Engine RCE via text/template
description: Detects code execution through Go's text/template engine when user input is parsed as template source, enabling arbitrary method calls on template context objects.
impact:
Template injection in text/template enables calling any exported
method on objects in the template context, information disclosure
via field access, and XSS when used for web output.

title: Cgo Unsafe Memory Operations
description: Detects unsafe Cgo operations where user-controlled data is passed to C functions without bounds checking, enabling buffer overflows, format string attacks, and arbitrary code execution.
impact:
Cgo vulnerabilities enable buffer overflows, format string attacks,
and memory corruption leading to arbitrary code execution with the
privileges of the Go process.
remediation:
Validate input length before Cgo calls. Use defer C.free:
  input := r.FormValue("data")
  if len(input) > MaxSize { return errors.New("too large") }
  cstr := C.CString(input)
  defer C.free(unsafe.Pointer(cstr))
Avoid C.sprintf; use C.snprintf with bounds.

title: Reflect-based Dynamic Method Invocation
description: Detects reflection-based method dispatch where user-controlled input determines which method to invoke via reflect.ValueOf().MethodByName(), enabling invocation of unintended internal methods.
impact:
Reflection-based dispatch allows invoking any exported method on the
target object, bypassing authorization checks, accessing admin
functions, and potentially executing destructive operations.

title: Runtime.exec with User-Controlled Input
description: Detects usage of Java's Runtime.getRuntime().exec() where the command string or command array includes user-controlled input from servlet request parameters, headers, or request body fields. Runtime.exec() can invoke arbitrary OS commands. When passed a single string, it uses StringTokenizer to split the command (not a shell), but command injection is still possible via argument injection and when the command includes a shell invocation explicitly (/bin/sh -c, cmd.exe /c).
impact:
Full remote code execution on the server:
- Complete system compromise with JVM process privileges
- Data exfiltration from filesystem, databases, and environment
- Lateral movement across the internal network
- Installation of backdoors and persistent access
- Cryptocurrency miners, ransomware deployment

title: ProcessBuilder with User-Controlled Arguments
description: Detects usage of Java's ProcessBuilder where command arguments are derived from user-controlled input. While ProcessBuilder with argument lists avoids direct shell injection (unlike Runtime.exec with a single string), it is still dangerous when user input controls the command name, arguments, or environment variables. Argument injection attacks can exploit option flags in target programs, and explicitly invoking a shell with user input enables full command injection.
impact:
Arbitrary OS command execution via ProcessBuilder:
- Argument injection to manipulate target program behavior
- Environment variable poisoning (LD_PRELOAD, PATH)
- Working directory manipulation for file access
- Full system compromise with JVM process privileges

title: ScriptEngine.eval with User-Controlled Script
description: Detects usage of Java's javax.script.ScriptEngine where the evaluated script code comes from user-controlled input. ScriptEngine supports JavaScript (Nashorn/GraalJS), Groovy, JRuby, Jython, and other languages. Code evaluated via ScriptEngine has access to Java classes via Java.type() or Class.forName(), enabling Runtime.exec(), file I/O, network access, and full JVM compromise from within script evaluation.
impact:
Arbitrary code execution via Java interop in scripting languages:
- Access to Runtime.exec, ProcessBuilder for OS commands
- File system read/write via java.io.* classes
- Network access via java.net.* classes
- Full JVM and system compromise

title: JNDI InitialContext.lookup with User-Controlled Name
description: Detects usage of Java's JNDI (Java Naming and Directory Interface) InitialContext.lookup() where the lookup name is derived from user- controlled input. JNDI lookup with protocols like ldap://, rmi://, dns://, or iiop:// can be exploited to load remote objects, triggering arbitrary code execution via deserialization or remote class loading. This is the same class of vulnerability exploited by Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) and remains a critical RCE vector in Java.
impact:
Remote code execution via JNDI class loading (LDAP/RMI):
- Arbitrary deserialization of malicious Java objects
- Full JVM and OS-level compromise
- Log4Shell-class vulnerabilities affecting the entire infrastructure
- Data exfiltration via DNS JNDI provider

title: Expression Language Evaluation with User Input
description: Detects usage of Java Expression Language (EL), Unified EL, or Spring Expression Language (SpEL) where the expression string is derived from user-controlled input. EL/SpEL provide powerful capabilities including method invocation, constructor calls, property access, type references, and operator overloading. When user input is evaluated as an EL/SpEL expression, attackers can invoke Runtime.exec(), access the ClassLoader, or perform any Java operation available via reflection. SpEL injection and EL injection are common and critical RCE vectors in Java applications.
impact:
Arbitrary Java method invocation via EL/SpEL:
- OS command execution via Runtime.exec() or ProcessBuilder
- File system access via java.io classes
- Spring Bean access and method invocation
- Full JVM and system compromise

title: Unsafe Reflection with User-Controlled Class Names
description: Detects Java reflection patterns where the class name, method name, or constructor arguments are derived from user-controlled input. Class.forName() with a user-supplied class name allows arbitrary class loading and instantiation. Combined with Method.invoke() and Constructor.newInstance(), attackers can instantiate any class on the classpath and invoke any method, including Runtime.exec() and ProcessBuilder.start(). This is a fundamental RCE vector when reflection parameters are controllable.
impact:
Unsafe reflection with user input enables full RCE:
- Arbitrary class instantiation on the classpath
- Any method invocation including Runtime.exec()
- Private method access via setAccessible(true)
- Remote class loading via URLClassLoader
- Full system compromise with JVM privileges

title: child_process.exec with User-Controlled Input
description: Detects usage of Node.js child_process.exec(), execSync(), and related shell-execution functions where the command string includes user-controlled input. Unlike execFile/spawn, exec() invokes a shell (/bin/sh or cmd.exe) to interpret the command string, enabling shell metacharacter injection (;, |, &&, ||, $(), backticks) for arbitrary command execution. This is the most common and dangerous RCE vector in Node.js applications.
impact:
- Full remote code execution on the server.
- Complete system compromise with application's OS privileges.
- Data exfiltration from the server filesystem and databases.
- Lateral movement to other systems on the internal network.
- Installation of backdoors, cryptominers, or ransomware.
- Denial of service through resource exhaustion or system destruction.

title: eval() / Function Constructor with User-Controlled Input
description: Detects usage of JavaScript's eval(), Function constructor, setTimeout/ setInterval with string argument, and other dynamic code evaluation mechanisms where the evaluated code is derived from user-controlled input. These functions compile and execute arbitrary JavaScript code, enabling an attacker to execute any server-side code including file system access, network requests, and process management.
impact:
- Full remote code execution in the Node.js process context.
- Access to require() enabling OS command execution (require('child_process')).
- File system read/write via require('fs').
- Network access for lateral movement and data exfiltration.
- Process control including termination of the server.
- Complete server compromise.

title: Node.js vm Module Sandbox Escape
description: Detects usage of Node.js vm module (vm.runInNewContext, vm.Script, vm.createContext) with user-controlled code. The vm module does NOT provide a secure sandbox -- it is explicitly documented as not being a security mechanism. Attackers can escape the vm context to access the host Node.js process via constructor chain traversal, prototype pollution, or direct process/require access.
impact:
- Full remote code execution via sandbox escape.
- Access to Node.js process object (process.env, process.exit).
- Ability to require() any module including child_process.
- File system access via require('fs').
- Complete server compromise.
- Known CVEs in vm2 enabling reliable sandbox escapes.

title: Dynamic require()/import() with User-Controlled Path
description: Detects usage of Node.js require() or dynamic import() where the module path is derived from user-controlled input. An attacker can manipulate the path to load arbitrary modules from the filesystem, including native modules that execute code upon loading, or modules in node_modules that provide dangerous functionality. Path traversal can be used to reach modules outside the intended directory.
impact:
- Arbitrary code execution via loading malicious or dangerous modules.
- File system traversal to load modules outside intended directory.
- Loading of child_process, fs, or net modules for system access.
- Native addon loading for native code execution.
- Information disclosure via module side effects.

title: node-cron / Scheduler with User-Controlled Expression or Command
description: Detects usage of cron job schedulers (node-cron, cron, bull, agenda, node-schedule) where the cron expression, job name, or executed command/callback is derived from user-controlled input. Attackers can manipulate cron expressions to schedule arbitrary task execution, inject commands into job callbacks, or create denial-of-service conditions through invalid or resource-intensive schedules.
impact:
- Scheduled arbitrary code execution on the server.
- Persistent backdoor via recurring cron jobs.
- Denial of service through resource-intensive schedules.
- Delayed attack execution to evade immediate detection.
- Command injection via job callback manipulation.

title: worker_threads with User-Controlled Code/Path
description: Detects usage of Node.js worker_threads module where the worker script path, workerData, or eval'd code is derived from user-controlled input. Workers execute JavaScript in separate threads with their own V8 instance but share the same process and full Node.js API access. Providing user- controlled code to a Worker enables arbitrary code execution in a separate thread.
impact:
- Arbitrary code execution in a separate thread with full Node.js access.
- Access to file system, network, and child_process from worker thread.
- Resource exhaustion via spawning many worker threads.
- Persistent code execution in background threads.
- Full server compromise via worker with require() access.

title: os.system/os.popen with User-Controlled Input
description: Detects usage of Python's os.system() and os.popen() where the command string includes user-controlled input. These functions invoke a system shell (/bin/sh on Unix, cmd.exe on Windows) to execute the command, enabling shell metacharacter injection for arbitrary command execution. os.system and os.popen are legacy interfaces that should be replaced with subprocess module calls without shell=True.
impact:
- Full remote code execution on the server.
- Complete system compromise with application's OS privileges.
- Data exfiltration from filesystem, databases, and environment variables.
- Lateral movement to other systems via network commands.
- Installation of backdoors, rootkits, or cryptominers.
- Denial of service through system resource manipulation.
remediation:
1. Use subprocess with shell=False and argument lists:
   ```python
   import subprocess
   import shlex

   # UNSAFE:
   # os.system(f'ping -c 4 {user_host}')

   # SAFE: Use subprocess with argument list (no shell)
   def safe_ping(host: str) -> str:
       # Validate input
       import re
       if not re.match(r'^[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9.\-]+[a-zA-Z0-9]$', host):
           raise ValueError('Invalid hostname')
       if len(host) > 253:
           raise ValueError('Hostname too long')

       result = subprocess.run(
           ['ping', '-c', '4', host],
           capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10
       )
       return result.stdout
   ```
2. Never use os.system() or os.popen() with user input.
3. Use subprocess.run() with shell=False (default).
4. Validate user input against strict allowlists.
5. Apply principle of least privilege to the application user.

title: subprocess.Popen/run/call with shell=True and User Input
description: Detects usage of Python's subprocess module functions (Popen, run, call, check_output, check_call, getoutput, getstatusoutput) with shell=True where the command includes user-controlled input. When shell=True, the command string is passed to /bin/sh (Unix) or cmd.exe (Windows) for interpretation, enabling shell metacharacter injection identical to os.system(). This is the most common subprocess misconfiguration.
impact:
- Full remote code execution via shell injection.
- System compromise with application process privileges.
- Data exfiltration, lateral movement, backdoor installation.
- Environment variable access (API keys, database credentials).
- Complete infrastructure compromise in cloud environments.
remediation:
1. Use subprocess with shell=False (default) and argument lists:
   ```python
   import subprocess

   # UNSAFE:
   # subprocess.run(f'ping -c 4 {host}', shell=True)

   # SAFE: Argument list without shell
   def safe_ping(host: str) -> str:
       import re
       if not re.match(r'^[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9.\-]+$', host):
           raise ValueError('Invalid hostname')

       result = subprocess.run(
           ['ping', '-c', '4', host],  # List of args, no shell
           capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10,
           # shell=False is the default!
       )
       return result.stdout
   ```
2. Never use shell=True with user-controlled input.
3. Always pass commands as lists of arguments, not strings.
4. Validate user input against strict patterns.
5. Use shlex.split only for trusted input (not a security measure for shell=True).

title: eval/exec/compile with User-Controlled Input
description: Detects usage of Python's eval(), exec(), and compile() built-in functions where the code string is derived from user-controlled input. These functions execute arbitrary Python code, enabling attackers to import modules, access the filesystem, execute OS commands, and perform any operation available in the Python runtime. eval() is commonly misused for expression evaluation and JSON parsing.
impact:
- Full remote code execution in the Python process.
- Arbitrary module import (os, subprocess, socket, etc.).
- Filesystem read/write access.
- OS command execution via os.system or subprocess.
- Network access for data exfiltration and lateral movement.
- Complete server compromise.
remediation:
1. Use ast.literal_eval for safe expression evaluation:
   ```python
   import ast

   # UNSAFE:
   # result = eval(user_expression)

   # SAFE: For literal values (strings, numbers, tuples, lists, dicts)
   result = ast.literal_eval(user_expression)

   # SAFE: For mathematical expressions
   import simpleeval
   s = simpleeval.SimpleEval()
   result = s.eval(user_expression)

   # SAFE: For JSON parsing
   import json
   data = json.loads(user_json)
   ```
2. Never use eval/exec with user input, even with restricted builtins.
3. Use ast.literal_eval for safe literal evaluation.
4. Use simpleeval, numexpr, or mathparse for math expressions.
5. Use JSON parsing (json.loads) instead of eval for data.

title: __import__/importlib Dynamic Module Loading with User Input
description: Detects usage of Python's __import__() built-in function and importlib module functions where the module name is derived from user-controlled input. Dynamic imports allow attackers to load arbitrary Python modules, including os, subprocess, socket, and other modules that provide system access. This is often used in plugin systems, factory patterns, or when eval/exec are restricted but __import__ is still accessible.
impact:
- Loading of os, subprocess, or other system modules for command execution.
- Access to filesystem via loaded modules.
- Network access for data exfiltration.
- Denial of service via resource-intensive module loading.
- Code execution via module initialization side effects.
remediation:
1. Use an allowlist of permitted module names:
   ```python
   ALLOWED_PLUGINS = {
       'csv_handler': 'myapp.plugins.csv_handler',
       'json_handler': 'myapp.plugins.json_handler',
       'xml_handler': 'myapp.plugins.xml_handler',
   }

   def safe_load_plugin(plugin_name: str):
       module_path = ALLOWED_PLUGINS.get(plugin_name)
       if module_path is None:
           raise ValueError(f'Plugin {plugin_name} not allowed')
       return importlib.import_module(module_path)
   ```
2. Never pass user input directly to __import__ or importlib.import_module.
3. Map user-provided names to a fixed set of approved modules.
4. Use entry_points for plugin discovery instead of dynamic imports.
5. Validate module names against a strict pattern.

title: ctypes/CDLL with User-Controlled Library Path
description: Detects usage of Python's ctypes module (ctypes.CDLL, ctypes.cdll, ctypes.windll, ctypes.oledll) where the shared library path is derived from user-controlled input. Loading a user-specified shared library executes its initialization code (constructor functions, DllMain), enabling arbitrary native code execution. This bypasses Python-level sandboxes since the loaded code runs as native machine code.
impact:
- Arbitrary native code execution at the process level.
- Complete bypass of Python-level sandboxes and restrictions.
- Full system access with application's OS privileges.
- Memory corruption and exploitation of host system.
- Persistent backdoor via loaded native library.

title: Celery Task with User-Controlled Arguments
description: Detects usage of Celery task dispatching where task names, arguments, or serialized data come from user-controlled input. Celery is the most popular distributed task queue in Python. An attacker who can control task names can invoke arbitrary registered tasks, and controlling arguments can lead to command injection within task handlers. The pickle serializer (historical default) enables arbitrary code execution via deserialization attacks.
impact:
- Arbitrary task execution on Celery worker nodes.
- Code execution via pickle deserialization on workers.
- Command injection via task argument manipulation.
- Denial of service through task queue flooding.
- Lateral movement to worker nodes in distributed deployments.
remediation:
1. Use JSON serialization and validate task names:
   ```python
   ALLOWED_TASKS = {
       'send_email': 'myapp.tasks.send_email',
       'process_upload': 'myapp.tasks.process_upload',
       'generate_report': 'myapp.tasks.generate_report',
   }

   @app.route('/api/dispatch', methods=['POST'])
   def dispatch_task():
       task_key = request.json.get('task')
       task_name = ALLOWED_TASKS.get(task_key)
       if task_name is None:
           return jsonify({'error': 'Task not allowed'}), 400

       # Validate and sanitize arguments
       args = validate_task_args(task_key, request.json.get('args', []))
       celery.send_task(task_name, args=args)
       return jsonify({'status': 'dispatched'})

   # In celeryconfig.py:
   CELERY_TASK_SERIALIZER = 'json'
   CELERY_ACCEPT_CONTENT = ['json']
   CELERY_RESULT_SERIALIZER = 'json'
   ```
2. Never use pickle as the Celery serializer.
3. Use JSON or msgpack serialization only.
4. Validate task names against an allowlist.
5. Sanitize and validate all task arguments.

title: Unsafe Java Deserialization
description: Detects unsafe Java/Scala deserialization of untrusted data.
impact:
Deserialization of untrusted data can lead to remote code execution
via gadget chains in the classpath.
remediation:
Use JSON or Protocol Buffers instead of Java serialization.
If Java serialization is required, use ObjectInputFilter:
  val filter = ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter("com.myapp.*;!*")

title: Unsafe Pickle/Kryo Deserialization
description: Detects unsafe deserialization using Kryo or other Scala serializers.
impact: Unsafe Kryo deserialization can lead to remote code execution.
remediation:
Enable registration requirement in Kryo:
  kryo.setRegistrationRequired(true)
  kryo.register(classOf[MyClass])

title: Scala Script Engine Code Execution
description: Detects dynamic code execution via ScriptEngine or code compilation.
impact: Dynamic code execution from user input leads to full RCE.
remediation: Never compile or evaluate user-supplied code. Use sandboxed execution if needed.

title: Unsafe Reflection
description: Detects unsafe reflection with user-controlled class names.
impact: Unsafe reflection can instantiate arbitrary classes leading to RCE.
remediation: Use an allowlist of permitted class names. Never pass user input to Class.forName.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery
description: Detects HTTP requests made with user-controlled URLs.
impact:
SSRF can access internal services, cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254),
and sensitive internal resources.
remediation:
Validate URLs against an allowlist of permitted domains.
Block access to internal IP ranges and metadata endpoints.

title: Unvalidated Redirect to Internal Service
description: Detects proxy or redirect patterns that could access internal services.
impact: Server-side request forgery enables access to internal resources and cloud metadata
remediation: Validate and allowlist URLs, block private IP ranges and cloud metadata endpoints

title: Path Traversal
description: Detects file access with user-controlled paths.
impact: Path traversal allows reading or writing arbitrary files including /etc/passwd.
remediation:
Canonicalize paths and verify they stay within the intended directory:
  val basePath = Paths.get("/safe/dir").toRealPath()
  val target = basePath.resolve(userInput).normalize()
  require(target.startsWith(basePath))

title: Zip Slip Vulnerability
description: Detects unsafe ZIP extraction that doesn't validate entry paths.
impact: Path traversal enables reading or writing arbitrary files on the server
remediation: Canonicalize paths and verify they remain within expected base directories

title: Cross-Site Scripting via Raw HTML
description: Detects XSS via unescaped HTML output in Play Framework.
impact: XSS allows attackers to execute JavaScript in users' browsers.

title: Reflected XSS in Response
description: Detects direct inclusion of request parameters in HTML responses.
impact: Cross-site scripting enables session hijacking, credential theft, and website defacement
remediation: Apply context-aware output encoding and use Content Security Policy headers

title: Hardcoded Secret in Application Config
description: Detects hardcoded secrets in Scala application configuration.
impact: Exposed secrets enable unauthorized access to systems, APIs, and sensitive data
remediation: Use secret management systems, environment variables, and rotate exposed credentials immediately

title: Play Framework Debug Mode in Production
description: Detects debug/development settings that should not be in production.
impact: Framework misconfiguration can disable security controls and expose sensitive functionality
remediation: Follow framework security best practices, enable security features, review configuration

title: Akka Remote Without Authentication
description: Detects Akka remoting configuration without authentication.
impact: Framework misconfiguration can disable security controls and expose sensitive functionality
remediation: Follow framework security best practices, enable security features, review configuration

title: Remote Code Execution via PHP System Functions
description: Detects PHP functions that execute system commands or PHP code with user-controlled input. Covers system(), exec(), passthru(), shell_exec(), popen(), proc_open(), eval(), assert(), backtick operator, and preg_replace with /e modifier across WordPress, Laravel, Symfony, and vanilla PHP applications.
impact:
Full RCE through PHP command execution or code evaluation. PHP applications
typically run as www-data with access to the entire web root, configuration
files, database credentials, and often shared hosting environments. Web shell
installation provides persistent access even after the original vulnerability
is patched.
remediation:
- Add dangerous functions to disable_functions in php.ini:
    disable_functions = exec,passthru,shell_exec,system,proc_open,popen,eval,assert
- Use escapeshellarg() for individual command arguments:
    system('ls -la ' . escapeshellarg($userPath));
- Never use eval() or assert() with user input under any circumstances
- Remove preg_replace /e modifier; use preg_replace_callback instead
- Implement strict input validation using ctype_alnum() or regex allowlists:
    if (!ctype_alnum($input)) { die('Invalid input'); }
- Use Symfony Process component for safe subprocess execution:
    $process = new Process(['/usr/bin/ls', '-la', $sanitizedPath]);
    $process->run();
- Apply open_basedir restrictions to limit filesystem access
- Run PHP with minimal privileges (dedicated user, not root)
- Use PHP-FPM with chroot jails for isolation
- Implement a WAF (Web Application Firewall) to filter malicious input

title: Remote Code Execution via Ruby System Methods
description: Detects Ruby code execution via system, exec, backticks, Open3, IO.popen, or eval with user-controlled input. Covers Rails controllers, Sinatra routes, Grape API endpoints, and general Ruby application patterns including ERB template injection.
impact:
Full RCE in Ruby applications. Rails applications typically have access to
encrypted credentials, database connections, session secrets, and API keys.
The attacker can access the Rails console, ActiveRecord models, and the
entire application codebase including deployment configuration.
remediation:
- Use Shellwords.escape() for shell argument escaping:
    system("ls -la #{Shellwords.escape(user_path)}")
- Pass arguments as arrays to system() to avoid shell interpretation:
    system("ls", "-la", sanitized_path)
- Use Open3.capture2 with separate arguments:
    stdout, status = Open3.capture2("/usr/bin/ls", "-la", sanitized_path)
- Never use eval/instance_eval/class_eval with user input
- Implement strict input validation with regex allowlists:
    raise "Invalid input" unless input.match?(/\A[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+\z/)
- Use Ruby standard libraries instead of shell commands (FileUtils, Net::HTTP)
- Apply the principle of least privilege to the application user
- Consider using Docker containers with read-only filesystems
- Regularly audit Gemfile for known-vulnerable dependencies

title: Remote Code Execution via Shell Eval/Source
description: Detects shell scripts that eval or source content from external/untrusted sources, including curl-pipe-bash patterns, unquoted variable expansion in command context, and unsafe heredoc evaluation. Covers bash, sh, zsh, and POSIX shell patterns in scripts, CI/CD pipelines, Docker entrypoints, and infrastructure-as-code.
impact:
Arbitrary code execution through shell eval or process substitution. Shell
scripts often run with elevated privileges and have access to deployment
credentials, cloud tokens, SSH keys, and infrastructure secrets. CI/CD
pipeline compromise can lead to supply chain attacks affecting all downstream
consumers of build artifacts.
remediation:
- Avoid eval with any external or variable data; restructure logic to use
  case statements or function dispatch:
    case "$action" in
      start) do_start ;;
      stop)  do_stop ;;
      *)     echo "Unknown action" >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
- Download scripts to disk and verify before execution:
    curl -fsSL https://example.com/script.sh -o /tmp/script.sh
    echo "expected_sha256  /tmp/script.sh" | sha256sum --check --strict
    bash /tmp/script.sh
- Use checksums (SHA-256) or GPG signatures for integrity verification
- Quote all variable expansions to prevent word splitting and globbing:
    system "$sanitized_var"  # not  system $var
- Use printf '%q' to safely escape values for shell context:
    safe_val=$(printf '%q' "$user_input")
- Set strict shell options at the top of every script:
    set -euo pipefail
